on behalf of the alde group. the report is about something as basic as the link between citizens, between people - to avoid using a term which is now misleading - and the political project we are trying to develop, and it contains a series of very profound statements, all of which are interrelated and all of which are important. firstly, nationality remains a matter for the member states; there is still a political entity in europe called the 'state'. that's true, even if some of us don't like it very much. if we ignore this fact, we will only be building utopias. however, it must be borne in mind that, in some ways, nationality is also a matter for the european union. it involves all of us. when a state illegitimately refuses to grant citizenship to persons who have been resident on its territory for many years, it is denying them access to european citizenship, which alone enables us and the european commission, without any amendment to the treaties, to assess this question. the member states grant european citizenship: we cannot be indifferent to that. on the other hand, we cannot allow millions of people in europe to contribute to our welfare and wealth with their labour and their taxes without having any political rights whatsoever. the concrete implementation of the solution to this problem is complicated. but we cannot accept that so many millions of people are in that situation: contributing, but without the right to have a say in their own future. i therefore welcome this report. i think it is indeed possibilist, and in some cases goes a little beyond what the treaties allow or what some of us would support: for example, the european parliament and the national parliaments must have the same legitimacy, and so i do not think that at this moment it is possible to ask that certain people be allowed to vote in european parliament elections and not be allowed to vote in national elections. both parliaments should have equal legitimacy and both developments, when they come, must take place at the same time. the commission must do a much better job of publicising the rights which european citizens have today, for example in consular matters and in so many other areas where they do not even know what rights they have. the commission can make a major contribution to this debate by providing transparency on what the individual member states are doing in a field which is and will remain, for the time being, within its competence.

member of the commission. i would like to thank the european parliament and the committee on the environment for the painstaking preparation of this second reading report. i am particularly grateful to mrs korhola for her contribution to the effort to implement the aarhus convention in the community institutions. it is worth noting that, following the guidelines on access to environmental information and public participation, this proposal for a regulation is the third legislative proposal to implement the aarhus convention, this time for the community institutions, and mrs korhola's contribution is valuable. this regulation was proposed in parallel with the decision to ratify the aarhus convention, which contains obligations not only for the public authorities of the member states but also for the community institutions. the provisions already in force in this area therefore needed to be supplemented. the proposal therefore covers all three pillars of the convention, namely access to environmental information, public participation and access to justice. the community became a party to the convention in may 2005, just before the second conference of the parties in almaty. at that time the first reading of the regulation had already been taken and political agreement had been reached at council level with a view to the common position. the common position improves and completes the commission's original proposal in many respects. it also incorporates, either verbatim or in substance, many of the amendments tabled by the european parliament at first reading. in particular, as regards access to environmental information, a new article 6 is added, referring to the application of the exceptions concerning access to environmental information, as proposed by an amendment of the european parliament. the common position also incorporates elements of the european parliament's amendments concerning more detailed requirements for public participation in the preparation of plans and programmes relating to the environment. as regards access to justice, the council simplified the criteria and procedures under which non-governmental organisations can apply for internal review of acts of the community institutions. it is worth noting that it is no longer necessary for these bodies to operate at community level in order to exercise this right. the commission is able to accept these changes, since the present wording retains the obligation of these bodies to have as their main objective the protection of the environment at community level. the commission could also accept changes to the provisions relating to the outcome of internal review and the possibility for non-governmental organisations to bring cases before the european court of justice. the council made these changes in order to avoid a wording which might conflict with the treaty rules on the right of appeal of individuals and associations of individuals. the commission, as guardian of the treaties, shares the council's intention in this respect, since the common position is in line with the aarhus convention, which allows the contracting parties to establish criteria for public access to justice. i hope that agreement on this proposal will be reached soon. we have already come a long way from the full application of the aarhus convention and the adoption of this regulation will demonstrate how much we want it to be applied to the community institutions.
i am speaking on behalf of the group of the european people's party. mr president, i would like to join mrs korhola in her position; i cannot really agree with amendments nos 22, 23 and 25. i believe that the aarhus convention, which is already being implemented in some countries, such as spain, is a victory, of course, for the possibility of transparency, training, etc. i am extremely concerned, however, that positions which depart from the common sense shown by the council and the commission's position are intended to give the ngos, as mrs korhola has said, excessive legal capacity. i believe that democracy should be symmetrical. it is not logical that ngos should have more rights than local authorities in this area. it also seems to me that the regions cannot have the specific capacity that would be given to them here. on the other hand, there is a principle of law, that of direct interest, which is a much debated topic in the history of law and which was usually applied to the family or to some problem that occurred in the territory in question. however, it seems to me that the fact that the direct interest applies to any ngo in europe means that we are entering an infinite area of law, which we would not know where it would end up. i think this can create a lot of problems, especially because, as we know, sustainable development requires direct environmental knowledge, because it is not the same case by case. the first principle, which we have mentioned many times here, is that the concept of sustainable development is comprehensive, it has to refer to a specific place and in one place you can do one thing for economic or social reasons and in another you cannot do it. the fact that ngos, often not located on the relevant site, can claim this right because of their interest in the environment seems to me to be excessive. i therefore agree with the council's position.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, first of all i would like to point out that this report by parliament, which is intended to facilitate the work of adapting the aarhus convention, is a necessary and appropriate instrument. i therefore acknowledge the efforts of the rapporteur and the other members to adapt this convention to the mechanisms currently available in the member states and the community institutions, in order to ensure the legitimate right to information and environmental justice. in this respect, we believe that better access to information and greater public participation in decision-making will make it possible to implement such decisions more effectively and will contribute to raising public awareness of environmental problems. the convention will have to strengthen transparency, accountability and good governance in areas of public action as diverse as energy, agriculture, transport or tourism, through the recognition of a series of rights aimed at ensuring the effective participation of citizens in public decision-making processes. such information should provide sufficient knowledge to participate actively and consistently in the various administrative procedures. it should also recognise the right to pursue any administrative or judicial remedy deemed appropriate where it is considered that such rights have been infringed by public administrations. as regards the specific aspects of the report, i believe that ngos should not be subject to excessively restrictive requirements as regards access to justice, such as the requirement to work internationally and, above all, the requirement not to have been registered for more than two years for the submission of applications. i think in many cases that would be a grave injustice. on the other hand, in the interests of the universalization of justice, i think we should reject the possibility that the european investment bank can refuse access to environmental information, since the aarhus convention provides that exceptions must be interpreted restrictively and the inclusion of the term 'banking' extends this concept of confidentiality. in fact, the directive on public access to environmental information does not provide for specific rules for banks. i would like the commission to agree to these two specific points because they seem to me to be the most important. i hope that this regulation will be implemented as soon as possible, to ensure access to justice in all environmental matters.

mr president, commissioner, for a person or a country, ties with neighbours are of the utmost importance. relations with neighbouring countries are also important for the european union. it must be positive relations, framed by the objective of achieving a circle of peaceful, prosperous, human rights-respecting, stable countries around the union, which share our principles of democracy and the rule of law. the achievement of such a circle is necessary in the interests of the union, as the commissioner has just acknowledged. with globalisation and interdependence, it is clear that no wall can isolate the european union from its neighbours; hence the importance of an active and generous neighbourhood policy. i believe that, as mr tannock's report shows, and i certainly appreciate his work, the specific neighbourhood policies should differ fundamentally according to the neighbouring country in question. the difference should not depend on the continent to which the country belongs; otherwise we would have the impression that there is a first-level neighbourhood policy and a second-level neighbourhood policy for the non-european mediterranean neighbours. this would be a mistake, since many of these mediterranean countries have very close and longstanding relations with the union, closer and longer than those which the union has with several european countries which are also the object of the neighbourhood policy. these mediterranean countries expect, in accordance with our commitments, the closest possible relationship with the union. they also need our greater cooperation to overcome their backwardness in terms of institutional democratic development, economic and social growth, etc. but the european policy of closer neighbourliness also implies the promotion of reforms geared towards democracy, respect for human rights and the market economy. and there must also be progress on such matters as economic openness, border control, cooperation in the fight against terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration. it is clear that progress in these areas will benefit the neighbouring countries concerned and the whole region. mr president, allow me to make one further comment. i am very sorry that at the barcelona summit last november the level of participation of our neighbours in the southern mediterranean was disappointing. i think they have missed a great opportunity to show their interest in strengthening their relations with the union. but beyond this disappointment, we must look to the future and to the strategic imperatives of the union. this calls for our giving priority attention to our neighbors, not only in their interest but also in our own.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his report and the motion for a resolution on the future of the lisbon strategy, with regard to the gender perspective. it is a very useful contribution to our common agenda for growth and jobs. you clearly and very appropriately highlight what gender equality policy can bring to the lisbon strategy. the persistence of large gaps between women and men is indeed a matter of great concern. it is essential to continue our efforts and to consolidate the integration of the gender dimension in all policies, gender mainstreaming. the need to tackle gender disparities in employment or training and, in particular, the pay gap and its causes, must be at the heart of our concerns. it is important to address structural inequalities between men and women in order to ensure equal participation of all in economic and social life. this requires better implementation of community law. but it is important to tackle all the factors that cause these disparities, such as the predominance of women in lower-paid sectors, the persistence of stereotypes, especially in education and training, or, as you have very well demonstrated, the difficulty of reconciling work and private life. issues of work-life balance are a key element of equality issues. they must cover all possible aspects: childcare and dependent persons, adjustment of working time, new forms of work, etc. and men must be fully involved in the conciliation measures. the duty of good governance which we have, in particular through good coordination of the different policies, through partnership between institutions and with the relevant actors, and through statistical and analytical monitoring of our policies, is also underlined. the commission fully shares these views, as reflected in the annual report on equality between women and men presented since 2004 at the spring summit. all the above are identified as priorities for action in the future. the commission's commitment to gender equality will also be reflected in the commission's forthcoming roadmap for gender equality. it will in particular highlight the aspect of governance, the importance of which you yourself have very usefully stressed. the commission also ensures continuous monitoring of equality policy through analyses and studies, as well as the development of specific statistics. studies are regularly carried out by experts. these studies are published. in 2005, a study focused on the reconciliation of work and private life. finally, the commission analyses the member states' national reform programmes from a gender perspective in order to make an important contribution to the 'employment' chapter of the annual monitoring report.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, the lisbon strategy, which was merged with the sustainable development strategy in gothenburg, aims to achieve economic growth, social cohesion and poverty reduction in the union and, to this end, it establishes that the three complementary pillars on which it must be based are economic, social and environmental. all three are equally important, commissioner. given that social inclusion within the lisbon strategy specifically concerns women, i welcome and congratulate mrs estrela on her report, because it is an excellent opportunity to remind the council and the commission of the need to impregnate all union policies with a transversal dimension in terms of the gender perspective. as the report explicitly states, there is a need for better coordination between the policy of an integrated approach to equality between women and men on the one hand and the lisbon strategy on the other, in order to systematically take into account the gender perspective in the achievement of the ambitious lisbon objectives, in particular in the broad economic policy guidelines, the employment guidelines, environmental policy - see reach directive - , internal market policy - see bolkenstein services directive - and finally in the policies for the integration of immigrants. on the other hand, the link between the beijing platform for action and the lisbon strategy is also obvious, so the need to harness the productive potential of european workers is key to delivering on both agendas. finally, as has also been said, we support the amendment tabled by mrs gröner and mrs estrela, which calls on the commission to make the reconciliation of work and private life one of its priorities in the roadmap for equality between men and women, which is currently under discussion, and to review, in collaboration with the member states, the social partners and other actors, directive 96/34/ec as regards its suitability and effectiveness. such review should focus on how to improve the situation of women and men in order to achieve work-life balance for both women and men, which would be a key factor in achieving gender equality in all aspects of life.

mr president, i am the co-author, as the panel indicates, of a proposal, which we have signed by several groups, in support of the extradition from chile to peru of the fugitive former dictator, fujimori, for reasons of defending human rights, of fighting against impunity and, also, to help strengthen democracy in peru. the evidence, the evidence and the documentation, which has been provided not only by the peruvian government and judicial authorities but also by international human rights organizations, is so overwhelming in terms of the murders, torture, corruption and abuse of power by former president fujimori, who, during ten years of authoritarian rule, many of which were dictatorial, oppressed the peruvian people, that i believe that this extradition will take place, especially given the enormous prestige of the chilean judiciary. however, the fact that an institution such as the european parliament is supporting this process will also undoubtedly help to create an international and binational climate between the two countries, whose relations are not easy, in the right direction. we have therefore contributed to supporting this resolution, and i am doing so now with these words and with my vote.

member of the commission. mr president, the current political situation in cambodia remains of serious concern. since the lifting of parliamentary immunity for mr sam rainsy, the leader of the in the country. the commission and eu member states have agreed to a number of measures to respond to the situation. following the issuing of a strong eu declaration on the subject, the eu intends to working group on cooperation in the areas of institution-building, administrative reform, governance and human rights in order constructively to engage the cambodian authorities on these issues. the missions of eu member states in cambodia, will continue to monitor the situation very closely. the international community, especially the eu which had such a vital role in the establishment of put our political dialogue on hold and interrupt our development programmes to the detriment of the poor people in cambodia.

try to bring about change by means of coercive measures which would only increase the economic hardship of the cuban people. in order to promote peaceful change in cuba, the european union has engaged expression and association. political measures are useless if they are not effective on the ground. the council has therefore changed some of the modalities of its policy so that it can have a real impact, particularly with regard to the intensification of dialogue with the peaceful opposition. these close contacts have been very well received by the peaceful opposition. in line with the council conclusions of 31 january 2005, the luxembourg and the united kingdom presidencies, and in particular the european union representation in havana, have given new impetus to relations with the opposition and independent sectors, focusing, inter alia, on key medium-term issues of the transition. this includes, inter alia, enhancing dialogue with key members of the peaceful opposition, in particular with regard to their concrete plans for the future, and other means of supporting independent and civil society organisations. at the same time, the council has clearly condemned unacceptable behaviour on the part of the cuban authorities towards european politicians and visitors. the presidency has raised the issue of access to ministries in havana and has pointed out to the cuban government that it cannot expect any dialogue if it denies access to the european union's embassies and refuses to recognise or speak to eu interlocutors. the council also reaffirmed its readiness to continue a constructive dialogue with the cuban authorities on the basis of reciprocity and non-discrimination, including on the issue of visas for visits by representatives of the respective governments. the presidency of the european union expressed its regret in a public statement that the cuban authorities had prevented the so-called 'ladies in white' (damas de blanco) from travelling to strasbourg to receive the european parliament's 2005 sakharov prize for freedom of thought. cases like this, as well as the government's refusal to allow osvaldo payá to travel to participate in the ngo forum on freedom of expression in december, make it clear that the cuban authorities are violating the right to freedom of movement for their own citizens, as enshrined in article 13 of the universal declaration of human rights. the council regretted that no further progress had been made in the release of political prisoners. it condemned the imprisonment last summer of other members of the peaceful opposition and the measures taken by the cuban authorities to restrict freedom of expression, assembly and the press. the council maintains its call on cuba to release all political prisoners. the eu intervened in the situation of prisoners who had started a hunger strike to protest their conditions of detention. in this context, i would also like to recall, finally, the active and continuous role played by the eu, with the strong support of the european parliament, in the united nations commission on human rights. last year the european union tabled a resolution on cuba.
the european union is not bound by an association or cooperation agreement with cuba. this is not the case for a cause attributable to the european union, nor to many members of this parliament, who have endeavoured to preserve the capacity for dialogue and dialogue with the authorities and the people of cuba. the regrettable events, such as the ban on the ladies in white attending the european parliament or the increase in repression, as stated in the text of the resolution which this parliament will adopt tomorrow, against independent journalists, as recently denounced by reporters without borders, peaceful human rights activists, clearly show the systematic disregard for the most basic rights on the island. the resolution therefore says that these events undermine the aspirations to improve relations between the european union and cuba, the main objective of the changes introduced by the council in january 2005 in the common position, and asks the council, mr president-in-office, to act accordingly. and i remind you, mr president-in-office, that when you approved the lifting of the measures accompanying the council's common position, you called for the immediate and unconditional release of the people who were detained, and now the situation of those people has worsened. andrei sakharov said, madam president, that often the voices that count the most are the ones that are not heard. and i believe, madam president, that this parliament has once again had to take the floor precisely to make the cause of freedom its own and to defend and make known in this house, which represents the citizens of the european union, those people who are fighting in cuba for their freedom and for their dignity.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president-in-office of the council, our group welcomes the fact that the context in which this debate on cuba is taking place reasonably ensures a fairly broad commitment to a motion for a resolution. we have always believed that there is a broad basis in this parliament and in the institutions of the union for agreement and for a good direction in relations with cuba. as a group, our position is very clear: firstly, in the present context we can only confirm that the cuban authorities have not given the expected signals in relation to the improvement of human rights in the country. secondly, we are faced with the impossibility of awarding the sakharov prize to the ladies in white and we must therefore urge the cuban authorities to allow this group to visit europe at the invitation of the european parliament. at the same time, we believe that the president of parliament should be instructed to take all possible steps to ensure that the prize is actually awarded. we believe, however, that in the present climate of relations the prospects for progress are better today than under the council's previous policy, which led to a dead end, as has been - to say the least - the policy of sanctions and embargo for decades. we are committed to maintaining the council's current policy with two objectives: firstly, to maintain firmly the demand for human rights in cuba, the release of prisoners of conscience and of the peaceful opposition and respect for democratic freedoms and, secondly, to maintain and increase the relationship and dialogue with all the political and social sectors in cuba which are involved or interested in the relationship with europe and in the evolution of the country, the inevitable changes that we are going to see in cuba in the near future.
on behalf of the green group, i agree that there are many alarms that the cuban regime continues to apply a policy of repression against dissenting opinions, arbitrary imprisonment of opposition groups, constant harassment of anyone who expresses a position contrary to the governmental one. the repression of groups which have been stigmatised by the regime, such as homosexuals and certain intellectuals, is also worrying. the specific case before us, the regime's ban on the ladies in white leaving the country to receive the sakharov prize, is another example of this worrying situation. however, as has already been said, the policy of blockade and isolationism to which various western powers have subjected cuba for decades has only served to strengthen the hard-line sectors of the regime. i therefore welcome the decision of the council of the european union in june 2005 to offer cuba a new forum for political dialogue. the aim was, among other things, to begin to prepare the ground for what many of us hope will be an imminent transition to democracy. those of us who have endured a dictatorship know how difficult it is to build a democracy, especially when those who should be your allies from the outside turn their backs on you. in this sense, it is encouraging to see how more and more community, university and scientific groups are appearing, both in rural and urban environments, under the roof of churches or in educational and social centres; groups that did not exist before and whose work can make a valuable contribution to political development in cuba. it is time for the cuban regime to understand that its future does not lie in maintaining the status quo, but in facing in a serious and credible way the transition which the cuban people themselves are demanding above all. the european union must therefore make it very clear that our intention is to help cuba to enter modernity by way of democracy, and that is why we must not fail to call for the release of all those sentenced to long prison terms for peaceful opposition to the regime.

the next item is the debate on the oral question to the council on the national management declarations responsibility of the member states for the implementation of the budget of the european union, by szabolcs fazakas, terence wynn and jan mulder, on behalf of the committee on budgetary control (o-0102/2005 b6-0347/2005).
the president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i am grateful for this opportunity to explain to you the council's position on this important question, namely the statement of assurance to be given by the european court of auditors on the implementation of the community budget, and may i begin by stating the obvious fact that the administration of the community budget is complex and, as such, unique in the world. it covers a wide range of administrative levels, from the various commission services to the central, regional and local administrations of the member states and the individual final recipients. it is in the interest of all concerned to contribute to sound budgetary management, including the budgetary and discharge authorities. like the european parliament, we in the council have repeatedly expressed our disappointment with the state of affairs, particularly in connection with the discharge procedure. after extensive consultation in the council and in the council bodies, the council adopted conclusions on the commission communication on the roadmap on 8 november, and i can assure you that this was not an easy task. this document summarises the conclusions of a two-day meeting of a group of experts from all member states, representing the respective ministries of finance, the operational authorities and the audit authorities, organised jointly with the commission. this preparatory work provided a good basis for in-depth discussions in the council bodies and proved useful in reaching agreement in the form of the council conclusions mentioned above. i assume you have already read this document, so i will just highlight the most important points. i would like to conclude by addressing the issue of declarations to be made by the individual states, although i know that this is a particularly important question for you. i'm asking you to be patient. in its conclusions, the council underlines that a number of efforts have already been made to improve the efficiency of budgetary management: the introduction of internal audits, stricter rules on the accountability of the commission's authorising officer, the implementation of the integrated administration and control system, to name a few. in view of the importance of the structural funds in the budget of the european union, i would also like to draw attention to the work done to set up payment agencies and to further develop internal and ex post controls in the field of structural operations. one of the first points mentioned in the council conclusions is the balance of responsibilities between the commission and the member states in the implementation of the budget of the european union, in accordance with the provisions of the treaty, which must be taken into account when improving the controls and guarantees in this area. the council also considered it essential that this improvement builds on existing control structures and aims to improve the cost-benefit ratio and simplify the systems. the council considers that an effective integrated internal control framework, based on the principles set out in the court's opinion on the so-called single audit, provides assurance as to the risk of error in the underlying operations. one of the main points in the council conclusions concerns the improvement of control systems. member states and the commission should optimise the effectiveness, economy and efficiency of the current control systems. without prejudice to the specific features of administrative provisions in the various member states, the council shall promote the pursuit of general principles and common elements for internal controls. the council considered that member states should continue to carry out and improve controls in cooperation with the commission on funds managed under shared responsibility. this should take into account the responsibilities under the treaty, the financial regulation and the corresponding provisions of the sectoral regulations. for example, some member states are prepared to take measures under the confidence pact as provided for in the context of structural fund programmes. the council is the assembly of the member states, and i speak for all the member states, not just for the council itself. as you know, the commission services have published a first analysis of the shortcomings of the internal control framework of the commission services in relation to the control principles set out in the court of auditors' proposal for an internal control framework of the community. in the context of shared management, the council asked the commission to assess the implementation of the applicable rules on sampling of forwards, paying agencies and the activities of settlement bodies. the council conclusions suggest that the commission, in cooperation with the member states, should assess the current level of sectoral and regional controls and the relevance of existing declarations. i now come to the subject of audit. when establishing the internal control framework, a distinction must be made between internal control and external audit. the ec treaty alone is the basis for any cooperation between independent supreme audit authorities, as these authorities are not part of the internal control framework. this is important. some control authorities are ready to discuss with the court how they can make a greater contribution. i can assure you that all the member states have agreed to do their utmost to reduce the risk of errors and to strengthen controls. the commission and the member states should ensure that their approach to the integrated internal control framework is based on common control standards and should discuss together how to implement those standards most effectively. the council calls on the member states to discuss bilaterally with the court of auditors the results of its das audits in order to eliminate systemic problems. it called on the commission to report to the council on solutions to problems faced by several member states. finally, and this is particularly important, the court has proposed that the european parliament and the council should reach a common understanding of the acceptable risks of the underlying operations. the council's conclusions attach great importance to this uniform understanding. the council looks forward to further steps in this respect. i come now to a subject of the greatest importance to us all: simplification. there is a need for simplification in terms of harmonisation of control principles, legislation and control requirements in relation to the rules to be adopted for the 2007-2013 programming period. the council considers that simplification should never lead to an increase in the current administrative and control costs. it must, on the contrary, lead to the elimination of multiple internal controls by different parties involved in the control framework. finally, i would like to turn to the very important issue of declarations in the context of the decentralised management of eu funds. the council considers the existing declarations at operational level to be a means of providing assurance to the commission and ultimately to the court of auditors. they must be useful and cost-effective and can be taken into account when it comes to achieving a positive das. care must be taken not to jeopardise the existing balance between the commission and the member states. i'm aware that you expected more in this regard. but you will agree with me that the text as a whole can be regarded as a substantial and significant advance. in order to continue to take this matter forward, the council has agreed to examine, at the time of the 2004 discharge, the action plan drawn up by the commission to remedy the shortcomings of the current control framework. the council conclusions of 8 november will of course be followed by further steps in 2006. the achievement of a positive das is, as i have said, an important and very ambitious goal which cannot be achieved overnight. i think that these council conclusions are an important step towards that goal. they also confirm that the council will continue to support the commission in its efforts to contribute actively to financial management at all levels. some of you may feel that the council should have gone a step further. i can understand that. but remember that the presidency was bound to the necessary unanimity on this matter. thank you for your attention.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, already during the entire period of the work of this commission we have a common concern to get a positive das. it has not been possible. this is a very link. this proposal was rejected last november and now we have to think about what to do next, because the problem will continue to exist. the commission adopted an action plan on 17 january and has ‘member states should designate a national coordinating body per policy area which can (…) provide all stakeholders with an overview of the assurance available in respect of community actions under shared and indirect management in their member state. the cooperation of member states is necessary when ensuring such a provision in forthcoming legislation, and steering its implementation via implementing rules and guidance’. maybe this can be a solution or a least an intermediary solution that can link together the technical levels, the paying agencies and the audits and provide good evidence for overall discharge.

i am very aware of the difficulties of this proposal, mr president, as rapporteur for the committee on fisheries, and it is not for nothing that parliament has played a key role in unblocking it after its presentation just over two and a half years ago, even finding a procedure which has allowed a compromise between the commission and parliament to overcome the difficulties of the proposal and which has even had the support of most of the sector and national administrations. it is incomprehensible that, in a situation of such consensus, the council should be delaying since april last year the adoption of what is probably the most important package of technical measures to be adopted at this time. the consequences of this irresponsibility are manifold: the mediterranean is the only community area which is still far from being associated with the minimum concepts of responsible fishing and sustainable development, when in other community waters much more drastic action is already being taken in its name. it is shameful that the mediterranean fishermen themselves, in their vast majority, have understood better than the council the urgent need to regulate this fishery, despite the price they will have to pay. the credibility of the council is therefore completely called into question. we are also in danger of failing to meet our international obligations within the two regional fisheries organisations operating in the mediterranean. and, mr president, how can we propose to third countries more restrictive management measures when we are not able to implement them in our own territory? i therefore ask you, mr president-in-office of the council, in addition to telling us about the timetable, a question to which you have not yet answered, to explain to this parliament why, without a blocking minority, the council is unable to take a decision on this matter.

world today. it is a form of violence that knows no geographical barriers or age limits for the victims, nor does it make any distinction of class, cultural or family background; it is the most widespread crime in the world, and the european commission and the institutions of the european union have an institutional and moral duty to react firmly against it. i particularly appreciate this report because it deals with the main issues that the european institutions have to deal with. the commission has taken a number of initiatives to help member states implement effective prevention and response policies to eradicate violence against women. we are developing legal instruments to encourage close cooperation between the member states in policing, in defining crimes, which often do not coincide, and of course in strengthening the instruments to prosecute and eradicate these crimes from civil society, as well as to ensure more effective protection for victims of violence. most of the actions mentioned in the report fall within the framework of the daphne project, which we all know: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the daphne programme, which the commission intends to continue and develop further, covers all forms of violence, including domestic violence, which is one of on behalf of the green group, mr president, i am very sad to have to hold this debate on violence against women, because it means that this is an active issue, a living issue. the report by mrs carlshamre, whom i congratulate on her work, reminds us, among other things, that violence against women is a scourge that knows no nationality, religion, social status or economic level; on the contrary, as has also been said, it is a universal phenomenon, linked to the inequalities existing in our societies in the distribution of power and gender roles. that is why the response must be forceful, here in europe and in other countries where, as in mexico or guatemala, the situation has reached such levels that even 'feminicides' are being spoken of. the time for rhetoric and condemnation, however, is long gone. the time for action is now, to take action on behalf of victims, to implement proactive and preventive strategies and to establish effective, proportionate and dissuasive criminal sanctions. but for these measures to be effective, they must be provided with the necessary human and economic resources. a few days ago we celebrated the first anniversary of the law on gender violence in spain. this is an opportunity to insist, as the carlshamre report does, that violence against women must be regarded as a clear violation of the most fundamental human rights and that, in addition to reactive measures, holistic programmes must be established which seriously address the issue of the distribution of roles in our society and, in particular, the perception still held by many men that women are merely objects at their disposal and that, as such, they have the right to beat or abuse them, if not to kill them. in short, the real problem, i'm afraid, is still in the heads of many men, and that's where action is needed.

the next item is the report (a6-0017/2006) by mr thijs berman, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council directive laying down minimum requirements for the protection of chickens kept for meat production (com (2005) 0221 - c6- 0190/2005 - 2005/0099 (cns)).
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the members of the committees that have dealt with this matter, but i would also like to thank the rapporteur, mr berman, for the very valuable work he has done and for all the efforts he has made to bring this initiative to a successful conclusion. i know that the proposals, when they reach the stage of decision, may not fully satisfy all parties. some would like us to move more in one direction, some might feel that we haven't made enough progress, others might think that we should be more conservative and that we have already gone too far. but i think that this proposal, as it is shaped by many of the amendments that have been tabled, is a balanced, a rational proposal, which balances on the one hand the need for better treatment of animals, for animal welfare, particularly for the chicken sector, but at the same time takes account of the economic cost and the burden that it may cause to industry and to the businessmen in this sector. but first of all, we must not underestimate the close link between animal welfare and animal health, and this is particularly important now that we are discussing the measures to be taken to combat avian influenza, which has now reached - even wild birds - in the european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the animal welfare system is not disrupted. there is much better surveillance, much better identification of health problems that may occur, and of course this means, in practical terms, less disease for the animals, less death, less unsuitable chickens in this case, so less loss and less cost. so it may, on the surface, look like a cost to the businessmen, to the producers, to the farmers, but it is actually a benefit, which will lead to savings and economic benefits for the producers. i would also like to point out that the world bank has recently published a report which shows the economic benefits of implementing animal welfare policies and how there is also an economic benefit to be gained from these policies. the second point i would like to make is of course the question of aid to producers. it is particularly important that they do not bear all the costs, but european consumers are prepared to spend more if they know that certain products have been produced in accordance with animal welfare and good animal treatment practices. and through labelling, voluntarily at the beginning - we will present a report on mandatory labelling - producers will be given the opportunity to exploit the very fact that they are pursuing a policy which resonates with european citizens and, indeed, on the basis of our studies and research, they can charge a little more because european consumers are prepared to spend more. of course, there is also the general multi-pronged strategy, the strategic plan for animal welfare, which was recently adopted by the commission and will be discussed in parliament. this proposal may predate this action plan, but it is consistent with the principles and philosophy and proposals of this action plan. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i know that european producers may often feel that they are at a disadvantage vis-à-vis third countries. there is a continuing effort to introduce welfare and animal welfare terms and conditions into international trade. it's not easy; we promote it. the recent adoption by the world organisation for animal health of principles on the welfare of animals is a first step in this direction and we will intensify our efforts in this direction. however, given the very high level of sensitivity of european consumers, we believe that labelling will be able to give an advantage to european producers. it will not be a disadvantage to have animal welfare policies. on the contrary, it will give them access to the very large european consumer market.

mr president, state aid is a legitimate instrument of public policy. in so far as they provide a unique advantage and differentiated treatment, their establishment requires a stricter justification than other alternatives and a refined design that ensures their effectiveness and coherence with the union's policies and objectives as well as its international commitments. the reform of public aid in the period 2005-2009 must take into account that, even if regional aid contributes to real convergence, there are large internal differences in income and opportunities between europe's regions. the result of the hökmark report is fairly balanced. i would like to see the need to link the reform of regional structural aid with the reform of the structural funds regulations until 2013, emphasising their complementarity, and to advocate the maintenance of appropriate support measures for the regions affected by the statistical effect without discrimination. i welcome the proposal to raise the de minimis threshold, which will eliminate red tape and favour smes in particular.

member of the commission. mr president, i welcome this report on the human rights and democracy clause in european union agreements prepared by the honourable members of this house, and especially by mr agnoletto, and the resolution before parliament today. human rights clauses have been inserted systematically into external agreements since 1995 and, ten years on, it is timely to take stock of what has been achieved. all eu institutions need to work together to this end, and i emphasise my commitment to an ongoing, but also very practical, dialogue with the council and parliament, for which this report provides a good basis. i shall begin by underlining how much has already been achieved: it must be said that the glass is more than half full. after often difficult discussions and very difficult negotiations, the commission has secured the inclusion of a human rights and democracy clause in, as you said, more than 50 agreements, covering over 120 countries. a notable example is, indeed, that of articles 9 and 96 of the cotonou agreement. in the field of trade policy, the special incentive arrangement for sustainable development and good governance, known as ‘gsp+’, provides additional benefits for countries that implement, inter alia, certain international standards in human and social rights; so it is a positive incentive. the impact of human rights clauses is already evident, and many of our human rights activities are supported by their mere existence. human rights feature prominently in every political dialogue with our partners. human rights subcommittees are being established with a growing number of partners, and, indeed, the european union neighbourhood policy action plans contain highly detailed sections on human rights. the commission, as part of the troika, makes numerous démarches on human rights issues every year, and the european initiative on democracy and human rights funds human rights projects throughout the world. the commission is also funding numerous technical assistance projects with an impact on human rights, ranging from, for instance, improving police training to modernising the judicial system in partner countries. the rule of law is one of the most important areas where i think we can really make a difference. i would also like to mention how active both member state embassies and commission delegations are in this regard. eu heads of mission collectively draw up human rights fact sheets periodically, report on the implementation of the various eu human rights guidelines and make detailed analyses of developments in particular countries concerning human rights and democracy. more and more frequently, political reporting from the commission delegations is covering human rights issues. assessing the effectiveness of the human rights clause to date needs to be done in a comprehensive manner. the human rights and democracy clause is, in itself, an important way of demonstrating the shared commitment of the european union and its partners to upholding, and also to promoting, human rights. the human rights clause opens the door to developing a deeper and more intensive dialogue on human rights issues. moreover, the existence of these clauses may, in some cases, even help deter potential human rights violations. as far as sanctions are concerned, i would like to underline that the frequency of imposition clearly depends less on the wording of the human rights clause than on the political will of the member states, as well as of the other states. i agree that, when sanctions are not implemented in response to serious breaches of human rights, the credibility of the eu’s human rights policy could be damaged. for its part, the commission would sometimes like to see a more robust use of these clauses but the solution is not, however, to include more clauses in the agreement. instead, we need to build up awareness and the consensus throughout the european union on the importance of human rights issues relative to other priorities. this report therefore makes a valuable contribution in this regard. as regards parliament’s involvement in negotiating or suspending an agreement, you will be well aware that these procedures are clearly established by the treaty and reflect the interinstitutional structure of the european union. parliament already plays an invaluable role in focusing attention on human rights issues, through the extremely active work of the subcommittee on human rights, through its annual report on human rights in the world and through the many resolutions and debates on particular human rights issues. moreover, i very much welcome the suggestion that interparliamentary delegations should take up human rights issues much more systematically. i think that there, too, you have a great role to play. i also favour revising the format of the current eu annual report on human rights in order to make it a fully interinstitutional report and to include an analysis of the application of human rights clauses. in conclusion, let me reiterate that the success of human rights clauses should be measured by the progress made in engaging partners in a genuine dialogue and in consultations on human rights, and the resulting improvements in human rights. over the last ten years, human rights clauses have provided an indispensable foundation for developing a truly effective human rights dialogue with our partners because it is in this way that these countries slowly change their behaviour. that does not mean, of course, that there is no room for improvement: there is always room for improvement, and i look forward to this debate today and to an ongoing and active debate with parliament. we are in a listening mood, but we would also like to contribute to improving human rights in the world. member of the commission. mr president, since its birth two years ago, this proposal has been in the headlines. both its supporters and its opponents see it as a symbol. during all the controversy about this proposal, which focused on a relatively small number of issues, it was easy to forget that there are many other areas in which, i believe, broad agreement exists and in which the benefits of the proposal are recognised. firstly, thanks to administrative simplification, it will be easier to establish a business in the eu. this is crucial for fostering entrepreneurship, a vital element in promoting growth and jobs. service providers will be able to obtain information and to complete administrative formalities through single points of contact in any member state, thus simplifying, accelerating and reducing the cost of the authorisation process and obviating the need to deal with different levels of authorities. it will also be possible to fulfil these procedures electronically, so that businesses save time and avoid incurring considerable costs in having to make visits in person – sometimes several times – in order to complete the necessary formalities with the relevant authorities. secondly, it will be good for consumers. improving consumer confidence is a key component in boosting the possibilities that the internal market offers them. they will benefit as key information about businesses and the service they are providing will be made easily available. this will enable them to make informed choices when they are purchasing services. rights of consumers are clearly set out, and any discrimination on the basis of nationality or place of business must be removed. thirdly, member states will have to implement administrative cooperation to ensure that businesses are properly and efficiently supervised across the eu, while avoiding duplication of control. this legal obligation will be underpinned at a practical level by an electronic system enabling authorities to exchange information directly and efficiently. these, amongst many others in the draft directive, are provisions which will bring forward significant benefits, both for businesses and consumers – i know that you have never lost sight of this. in assessing the amendments adopted in the lead committee’s opinion, and the further amendments tabled since, the commission is taking a opinion of the committee on women's rights and gender equality. mr president, there is nothing wrong with wanting to reduce unjustified barriers to the free movement of services within the framework of a single market, as long as this is done in a responsible way, ensuring that it does not undermine social and environmental rights, and moving towards a european-wide harmonisation of services legislation. but as it stands, this proposal for a directive poses many risks, many of which have already been mentioned. as rapporteur for the committee on women's rights and gender equality, i will refer specifically to those relating to the gender dimension. the risks for women are mainly related to the creation of female employment and to their working conditions, as well as to their status as consumers of services. firstly, the implementation of the directive in its current form would undoubtedly have negative effects on female employment, especially in sectors with a predominantly female workforce. what is needed today, and this has been said on several occasions, is more investment in training and therefore more public spending, and not, as this directive suggests, simply more competition. it is also worrying that the commission has not carried out an analysis of the social and labour impact, especially in view of the effects we have seen in other previous liberalisations, which have led to the destruction of many jobs and in many cases have also eroded social cohesion. on the other hand, the liberalisation of health and social services could lead to a deterioration in social welfare and health care coverage in favour of private insurance, which would particularly affect women as the main consumers of these services. finally, the application of the often mentioned country of origin principle to service providers could lead to abuse and manipulation, since in the areas which are not harmonised at european level, which are the majority, this principle would allow the coexistence of several national regimes and would also allow the juxtaposition, where appropriate, of 25 national regulations, which would have the effect of consumers not knowing to whom and when to complain.
mr president, commissioner, throughout this afternoon much has been said about the need to open up the services market in the european union and also about the need to remove barriers in order to achieve, or put into practice, some of the objectives set out in the lisbon strategy. the services directive is not only necessary but essential. but what requirements should this directive, this text, have in order to fulfil the mission we have given it? in my view, it should first set out clear criteria which give legal certainty to all, consumers and businesses, and above all, which give legal certainty in particular to small and mediumsized enterprises, which make up the majority - 80 or 90% - of the business community in the european union. and it would also be necessary for this text, which is clear, and which is legally secure, to be applied in all the countries of the european union. i must say that in my view the text which was adopted in the committee on the internal market and consumer protection met these requirements. but i must say that at the moment i have my doubts that the compromise texts that have been agreed meet the requirements of clarity and legal certainty. finally, mr president, i would like to make a brief comment. throughout this afternoon there have been those who have tried to oppose two models in europe: those who claim to defend - and are the only defenders of their own - the european social model and those who defend the need for competitiveness and competition. i want to say that the best social policy is one which generates economic growth and job creation. i want to say here that the only danger that can be posed to the european social model is a european union without economic growth, based on old prejudices and unable to compete with other economies, because if we do not grow, it will be impossible for us to maintain our social policy.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by expressing my appreciation for the very good work done on the report we are discussing today. in particular, i would like to thank mr machakis for his extremely constructive and substantial contribution to it. i should like to briefly refer to the main purpose and objectives of the mercury strategy. the main objective of the strategy is to reduce mercury levels in the environment and human exposure to mercury, and in particular to methyl mercury in fish. mercury and its compounds are highly toxic to humans, ecosystems and wild birds. high doses can be fatal in humans but even relatively limited doses can have serious effects on human health. the strategy has the following objectives: reducing the quantities of mercury available by limiting the supply and demand of mercury; addressing the long-term problem of limiting mercury surpluses and stocks to products still in use or stored in recent years; protection against exposure to mercury; improving understanding of mercury problems and of the mandatory uses; supporting and promoting international action to address mercury. in recent decades, many actions have been taken at community level to address the mercury problem and to reduce emissions, uses and exposure to mercury. at the same time, this and whatever we have done so far is not enough. there is still much to be done. in preparing the strategy, the commission paid particular attention to identifying the most important aspects of the mercury problem which remain and the areas where further action by the european union could be taken. the main areas examined and for which action is proposed in the short term are: the supply of mercury to the market and its export; mercury surpluses from the chloride alkali industry; the use of mercury in measurement and control equipment; mercury emissions from coal combustion. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the mercury problem is not eliminated. the current levels are due to past mercury emissions and it will take time for these levels to stabilise even if there are no new mercury emissions. i would also like to stress the importance of international action, in conjunction, of course, with initiatives taken at european union level. mercury is a global pollutant and the commission intends to organise an international conference on 26 and 27 october this year in brussels to strengthen the international capacity to deal with this issue. in conclusion, i would like to thank mr machakis and parliament as a whole again for their work and to reiterate my commitment to helping to shape even stronger european union policies for better health and environmental protection.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, we share your objectives, mr matsakis, both the elimination of mercury emissions at european level and the ban on exports of mercury, which, like its components, is a highly toxic substance for humans and the environment, as has already been said here. although the european union is the world's leading exporter of mercury and a ban on its exports will contribute considerably to curbing trade and reducing global reserves of this metal, i call on the council to continue the european union's participation in international forums and activities, to make bilateral commitments and to undertake projects with third countries, especially in the field of technology transfer, to tackle the problem of mercury pollution. in this context, the adoption of legally binding measures at international level would be desirable. i also ask the commission to raise public awareness by organizing information campaigns on the health risks of exposure to mercury and the environmental problems that this substance can cause, since i fear that citizens are still not sufficiently informed about its toxicity. another aspect which particularly concerns me is the use of mercury in the form of thiomersal in vaccines, as it could have harmful effects on human health, and we should take note of the fact that countries such as denmark have not used it in childhood vaccines since 1992. i am glad that the council conclusions recognize the environmental and social problems resulting from the closure of the long-running mercury mines in almadén, as well as the possibility of using these almadén mines as a deposit for the safe storage of existing stocks of metallic mercury or secondary metallic mercury resulting from european industry, never from its waste, thus taking advantage of existing infrastructure, manpower and know-how. i can only thank the rapporteur and all the other rapporteurs, because they have done a really excellent job.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate mr matsakis and also the other rapporteurs on their excellent work. mercury is a toxic element with negative health effects and therefore the commission proposes that it be safely contained, while reducing its use and ending its trade, but as the communication rightly says in point 9 there are many gaps in its effects on human health, on how it spreads or accumulates in the environment, on its toxicity and on the sensitivity of ecosystems. i think it is important and a priority that all these questions be investigated and that decisions be taken on a scientific basis and not on mere assumptions, more or less alarmist, amplified by the media. the only region in europe that produces mercury, although its mines are now closed, is almadén. this region was very prosperous, thanks to the mercury that was extracted from its mines since the time of the romans, and it is now depressed, also because of the mercury. it should therefore be compensated by specific measures, infrastructures and support which can partially mitigate the effects of the measures taken. this is where, among other things, the safe storage of liquid mercury to be withdrawn from the market should be located. the chloroalkaline industry has signed an agreement to completely end the use of mercury by 2020. this agreement must be respected and its implementation monitored. as a matter of curiosity, i would simply like to say that i have lived in the almadén region, that i have often taken mercury in my hands, that i have had mercury amalgam fillings, that i have removed myself for aesthetic reasons, and i can assure you that i have not had any health problems, nor do the people who live there, nor the animals, nor the plants, because, as the toxicologists say, the poison is in the dose.

the next item is the debate on the oral question to the commission on the free movement of workers and transitional periods by istván szent-iványi, graham watson and ignasi guardans cambó, on behalf of the group of the alliance of liberals and democrats for europe (o-0013/2006 - b6-0012/2006).
vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all, the accession treaty provides for a nuanced approach and clear solutions which allow both the long-term residents directive and the transitional arrangements for the free movement of workers to be applied in full legal compatibility. let me explain this in detail. first of all, there is the question of first-time access to the labour market. in such a case the accession treaty – during any period in which any old member state applies transitional measures – provides that it must give preference to nationals of the new member states over third-country nationals as regards access to the labour market. the second situation concerns nationals from the new member states who are already resident in an old member state. in that case the accession treaty again provides that nationals of new member states who already reside and work in a member state applying transitional measures must not be treated in a more restrictive way than those from third countries also resident and working in that member state. this means that where by virtue of the directive, a third-country national has been given long-term status, the accession treaty operates so as to ensure that the old member states must treat citizens from new member states who are already legally resident and working in the territories at least according to the standards guaranteed in the directive – thus including the right of free access to the labour market. the same logic also applies in the third situation covered by the directive: movement by long-term residents between member states. here the rule is the following: workers from a third country who are long-term residents in a new member state should not be treated more favourably than nationals of that state. in other words, in the situation of mobility to a second member state, an old member state cannot give free access to its labour market to a long-term resident who is a third-country-national if and where the same free access is not given to a national of a new member state. the same applies to equivalent situations between two old member states. in both cases of mobility between member states, if both the national of a new-member-state and the long-term resident are subject to national measures such as a work permit, community preference would operate in favour of the national of the new member state, who is a european citizen. from the above, it results that the rights provided by the directive can be reconciled with the provisions of the accession treaty. there is no need to submit proposals to change the rules, because it is impossible to have less favourable treatment for citizens of the new member states of europe. the commission agrees, however, that there is a need for better information clarifying the issue to be sent to the member states and i intend to do this by sending all member states a letter clearly stating the existing rules.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, mr commissioner, i believe that, regardless of the responses to what is happening or the interpretations of the directive, this is also a good opportunity to speak out, and i join those who think that this problem will not be solved until we have finally ended this transitional period, which hopefully will end as soon as possible, so that all europeans are equal and we make the mobility of workers an important tool for our competitiveness, for our employment and for the construction of the european union. i therefore join those who call for an open door policy, the sooner the better, and i think that in this sense it is very interesting - and as a spaniard i welcome it - that the government of my country has announced that it is lifting the restrictions that existed during this transitional period. we have done so, commissioner, because we are a country with a certain experience, being a country of immigration and a country of emigration. in addition, in these two years it has once again become clear that these restrictions imposed on the countries of central and eastern europe by the europe of the fifteen must be lifted, for reasons of justice and solidarity, but also for reasons of rationality and common sense, today more than ever, in this year of mobility. first, we look at justice and solidarity. we spaniards also had seven years of transition and we felt humiliated and unfairly treated by a situation that was not justified, because it was shown that a lot of those xenophobic and racist speeches were wrong. there was no flood of workers. spanish workers have never created problems in the host countries; on the contrary. and we have seen in the last two years that the same thing is happening to workers in the new member states: not only do they not create problems, but they are solving labour shortages, improving their skills and improving the overall idea of europe. that is why, commissioner, i am asking that the study carried out by the european commission should help to ensure that more countries lift the restrictions and that the day comes when europe is truly a europe of all european citizens and all european workers have the same rights, because that is the logical thing to do, because it is very good for mobility and because europe needs mobility if it is to win the battle of productivity and competition against the united states. we need to create that great market of free citizens in which there will be no problems and which will also allow us to improve our competence, improve our capacity and improve the lives of our citizens, so that, in addition to solving the concrete problems, we try to have a little vision of the future, commissioner, to remove those barriers.

(applause from the centre) but if the european union is acting rightly, please do so with a minimum of red tape and in an understandable form. we are, after all, the heirs to a great legal and administrative tradition in europe. this should be an incentive to finally look at the bureaucratic rules. we have created enough opportunities with the zeal we have shown for regulation. it is therefore good that the european commission has launched a major programme to reduce the current number of paragraphs and to simplify european law. i have just had a good talk with commissioner verheugen on this. the citizens will also appreciate greater transparency in the european will-building process. today, decision-making at union level is often miles away from citizens. many people have difficulty understanding who in europe is responsible for what and who is ultimately responsible for what. this leads to apathy or even distrust, both of which are harmful. but citizens do not want to be just understanding spectators, they want as much democratic participation as possible beyond the european elections. they want to be heard and they want to be able to take the initiative to influence the action of the european institutions. now you will say: subsidiarity, transparency, democratic participation, the right of citizens' initiative - all the content of the european constitutional treaty. indeed, and the treaty contains much more good and right. and this should not be given up lightly, even in view of the fact that 14 member states have already agreed to the treaty. "everyone is his own neighbor" will not be sustainable here. the european commission has presented a green paper on energy policy. i'm very pleased. we need to make good decisions on this matter quickly. the debates i am talking about, which will ensure a good future for the european union, are already under way. i would like to give a small example of this: a few weeks ago i met with six other european presidents in dresden. we have continued a dialogue initiated by the former portuguese president sampaio. and we talked to young people, a hundred students from seven european countries, and we asked them, "what do you think of europe?" what benefits do you see in this and what expectations do you have of the european union and its members? these students were not handpicked. they had been found by chance through a call for tenders . but the young people were well prepared. they had been consulting for a day and a half and called the result of their own discussion their 'dresden requests for european cohesion'. they are thinking, for example, of a uniform electoral system and they want a european house of history. they propose to spend five per cent of gdp on research and science.
