author. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr commissioner, the footwear industry is an important economic sector in the european community, known worldwide for the excellence of its products. it is a sector composed mainly of small and mediumsized enterprises, often located in regions where they are the largest source of employment. in 2005, there were more than 11 000 companies directly or indirectly employing more than 500 000 workers, producing around 700 million pairs of shoes, representing 10% of world production. it should also be noted that in response to the opening-up process, the footwear industry has undergone extensive restructuring, concentrating its production mainly in the higher price range. i would say that the clearest european specialty is the leather industry. as in the case of textiles, the impact of the liberalization process has been important in ending the quota system. the control system introduced by the commission clearly shows that imports, particularly from china, but not only from china, have grown dramatically. last year, the figures in terms of value and quantity exceeded on average 450% of import growth and in some cases 900%. the average price of imported footwear has fallen significantly, but the selling price of the products has not, which does not support the thesis, which we think is important to defend, of who are the real beneficiaries of the trade liberalization process. in principle, they should be consumers. a year ago, the european footwear confederation lodged a complaint about dumping practices in leather footwear. this is one of the largest cases brought in the european union and involves many industries worth over €800 million. on 23 february the commissioner, mr mandelson, announced to the press that the commission was going to recommend an increase in tariffs of 19.4% for china and 16.8% for viet nam. children's footwear and other footwear, which represent a very large part, were not subject to such measures. the fact is that the commission took an unprecedented decision, introducing provisional anti-dumping duties for a period of five months. it should be noted that, given the unit value of the products, this is not a measure that can be considered unreasonable either, it is a relatively small percentage. i will not go into the dumping issue any further. however, as chairman of the committee on international trade, i would like to make a few comments on an initial concept, namely the need to respect the rules we have set ourselves within the wto, both within and outside the community. i am aware that this is more than just a case of dumping. in some cases, the survival of the sector in europe is raised and also the possibility that relocation is an appropriate response to developments. as you know, in these cases everyone has his reasons; now, it is inconceivable that the whole of european industry should move outwards. at the same time, it should be noted that china is seeking to obtain market economy status in the wto framework. there are aspects of the community investigations which indicate that in this case china has clearly failed to comply with its wto obligations, both in the field of subsidies, more or less covert, and in the field of counterfeiting. so, commissioner, this is an opportunity to demonstrate to the citizens that the commission will do everything in its power to ensure that trade rules are respected, including, if necessary, recourse to the dispute settlement body in the wto. these market distortions are not limited to the hunting sector. there are reasonable grounds to suspect that certain illegal interventions in support of chinese exporting companies are routine. commissioner, in view of the expectations of the industry concerned and the sensitivity of european public opinion, i would like to know what action the commission will take to ensure that the wto rules are respected by this country. political considerations should not prevail over technical conclusions in an anti-dumping case. the measures you have proposed are controversial. the european industry and certain member states are not satisfied with its proposal.the objections to the 'creativity' shown by the commission in applying its well-established anti-dumping rules and practices are public. i don't know if these allegations are true. what i do know is that anti-dumping investigations are based on laws which must be faithfully applied without any parallel considerations. i can tell you in conclusion, commissioner, that the committee on international trade of the european parliament will be following this whole process very closely, because we believe that the step taken by the commission is an initial step, but that it must be completed with a favourable attitude so that china or other countries, such as vietnam, can have more opportunities in international trade, but respecting together the rules we have set ourselves.
mr president, the european footwear sector is experiencing two difficulties: on the one hand, it is suffering from unfair practices, and on the other hand, commissioner, it is still facing difficulties in terms of tariffs and other barriers in practice when it comes to accessing third country markets. i believe that all this calls for effective action against dumping, which allows us to react in a fair but at the same time agile way, so that we avoid, as has happened with textiles, that between taking measures and not taking measures, speculative movements occur and we promote a greater increase in imports in the end. the commission's proposal on the anti-dumping proceeding concerning footwear originating in china and vietnam is a reasonable and balanced expression, but it contains surprising elements that many people cannot understand, such as the exclusion of the measures you have proposed for children's footwear, which, as you know, is not in many cases used only by children, and also for special technology sports footwear (staf). in the event of dumping, duties should be imposed which are effective in ensuring fair competition and, in this respect, the level of duties and their practical application should be based on their effectiveness, i.e. the effective elimination of dumping.

vice-president of the commission. the question concerns interest rate policy and monetary policy. on behalf of the commission, i must say that monetary policy – and therefore decisions on interest rate changes – is the sole responsibility of the european central bank. its independence is enshrined in the treaty. it is the european central bank’s primary objective to maintain price stability in the euro area by ensuring that medium- to long-term inflation expectations in the euro area remain solidly anchored at levels consistent with price stability. the european central bank supports economic growth and job creation in the euro area. the current level of interest rates across the entire maturity spectrum remains low by historical standards, both in nominal and real terms. as regards the last part of the question on the economic outlook, in its last interim forecast the commission expected economic growth in 2006 to accelerate to between 1.9% and 2% in the euro area, which is close to estimates of the area’s potential growth rate. however, the commission is cautious about commenting on the policies of the european central bank, as that is the bank’s sole responsibility.

for the european union remains to further reduce unemployment by almost 19.5 million people, increase productivity and increase growth potential. this albeit moderate recovery in the economy is an functioning of the process of the renewed lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. all member states have developed their national reform programmes rapidly and thoroughly. these programmes, which are mr president, the outcome document of the united nations summit in september provided a basis, in some cases a minimum, on which to build institutional reforms. this is what happened with the human rights council: only the commitment to create it was reached, the rest was up in the air. it was difficult to reach an agreement within a few months to launch the body to replace the discredited commission on human rights. president eliasson's final proposal, which has just been voted on with broad support in new york, is the fruit of difficult negotiation. it was not an optimal proposal - it fell short of european ambitions - but it creates a new body that is certainly better than what we have now. the members of the new council will be elected by an absolute majority of the assembly, which means that a minimum of 96 votes is required. in addition, during their term of office, all members of the council will be subject to scrutiny and may even be suspended, as has been said. the frequency and duration of the meetings will also be much higher than those of the present commission on human rights, as we have requested. the new council is therefore a clear step forward in relation to the unhrc. i have to say, however, that i regret that the quota of countries allocated to the western european group is less than what we enjoyed in the commission. mr president, i would have liked to see this proposal by mr eliasson adopted by consensus, but it has finally been put to the vote. i am very sorry that the united states has voted no. it is a key country in the united nations and i hoped that the initiatives would succeed so that they would be associated with mr eliasson's proposal and that the new council would finally be born with the support of washington. but i am glad that they have in any case ensured their constructive cooperation with the new council. the work and functioning of the council will also be reviewed after five years, which will enable us to overcome the shortcomings of the new mechanism, one of the most ambitious objectives of the outcome document of the september summit. mr president, the fight against poverty is a priority in this document and i would like to remind you that poverty should be considered, as this parliament has already said, as a violation of human rights, because it is an attack on the dignity of the person and prevents the enjoyment of other basic rights.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, as our rapporteur has rightly said, i believe that quality is the great asset of european agriculture. in the face of a global market in which we must compete, increasingly, for low labour costs, low environmental and hygiene requirements, i.e. lower prices, i believe that quality must make the difference. for this to happen, we need - and we are working on it - a quality guarantee and certification system which is simpler, easily recognisable and trusted by consumers, both in europe and beyond. the recognition of these qualifications abroad, in the wto, is also essential to establish a market for high-quality agricultural products. we are on this, and i think the work done in the committee on agriculture and rural development supports this position. the first challenge is to further strengthen the system of our consumers and producers. a more flexible system is needed, with clearly defined deadlines and procedures, and with a proper allocation of powers. i think that the consumer's perception is as important as that of the industry itself, which must be shown the economic advantages of a high-quality market: the security of a rating system that controls well products that do not meet the conditions set and an agile and not too burdensome procedure. i think that the issue we are dealing with is very important, especially for countries like mine, which are pioneers in organic farming. i think that the subject deserves, as i have said, wider consideration, which we must tackle as soon as possible after the wto requirements have been met, by simplifying access to the system for products from third countries. in the further study and reflection that we will have in this house, i believe it is essential to listen to the sector and to be attentive to its needs, always thinking of the projection towards the global market of our products and of our quality, which are the values of a truly competitive european agri-food sector.
mr president, the report on designations of origin, geographical indications and traditional terms which the executive committee has presented to us states that the commission's intention in drawing up the report was to clarify procedures and to adapt community legislation to a world trade organisation ruling. the protection of geographical indications is of course of great importance, because it is essential to inform consumers correctly about the quality, origin and production methods of the products they consume. it therefore seems logical that consumers themselves should be spared confusion and that the use of the community logo on products from third countries should not be authorised. we have also an obligation as members of this house to defend the diversity and richness of europe's gastronomic heritage, which has, up to now, enjoyed an international reputation. the judgment of the world trade organisation court must be complied with - there is no doubt about that, that is what it is for - and the regulation must be amended to ensure that it is in line with those requirements. however, as long as the wto itself does not include the international system of geographical indications in the debate and we therefore do not have an international register of geographical indications, it does not seem very sensible for the amendments to our community regulation to go beyond what is strictly necessary. in addition, it is necessary to ensure that changes to the regulation do not lead to delays in registration and discrimination between the european union and third countries, because the community authorisation procedure requires very high quality and food safety requirements to be met. could the commission give assurances that products from third countries meet the same standards? i honestly don't think so. i therefore believe that the amendment tabled by the ppe-de should be supported and i also believe that the differences in conception between the member states on health systems must mean that farmers and producers are not the only ones who pay for the extension of the rules on food hygiene to cover designations of origin.
member of the commission. mr president, the commission thanks the committee on legal affairs for its question and mr lehne for doing a great job here this evening. he presented his views quite clearly. the commission recognises the special role of the legal sector in the good administration of justice and in promoting access to justice – by the way, in response to the example cited by mr lehne, the commission also recognises that supermarkets are very important and very honourable members of our community – we are certainly not challenging this. but we are saying that we need to look afresh at the current regulation of the sector to see what can be modernised to promote new types of services and new ways of doing things. that is in the interests of the users of these key services. so we are proposing that member states use a proportionality test to see how far current regulations are all really serving the public interest. this approach fully respects the subsidiarity principle. it allows for national circumstances, and the special characteristics of the legal sector, to be taken fully into account. the commission certainly agrees with the need for some regulation. i repeat: our initiative is about better regulation, not deregulation. we also recognise that it is the member states’ right to determine the balance between state rules and self-regulation by professional bodies. on the question of the right of member states to fix tariffs, i would underline the position of the commission in its report of february 2004. in our view the arduino judgment suggests that state measures delegating regulatory powers to professional bodies in order to fix tariffs can be challenged under the competition rules – for example, articles 3(1)(g), 10(2) and 81 ec – if the state does not have the final word and exercise effective control of the implementation of these tariffs. we are expecting further clarification on this when the court delivers its preliminary ruling in the macrino case (case c-202/04). finally, there are the internal market rules. these are at issue in another case pending before the european court of justice, the cipolla case (case c-04/04), again concerning the member states’ responsibility for price fixing. the commission considers that minimum prices for lawyers’ services are a restriction on the freedom to provide services because they neutralise the competitive advantage of service providers from other member states. moreover, we see no justification for minimum prices under the proportionality test, since they do not per se guarantee quality, access to justice, or good ethical conduct.

author. mr president, there are many opportunities now opening up in africa to settle accounts with a past that is often bloodstained. however, moving towards peace requires clearly combating impunity and this, in turn, implies bringing out the truth, however painful, and doing justice. the pinochet and milosevic trials, although imperfect and sadly unfinished, are clear indications of the direction that things should take in africa too. names like charles taylor, mengistu haile mariam or hissène habré, among others, must be added to the list of former dictators who have to appear before national and international justice. there are already some mechanisms for accountability through ad hoc tribunals for the perpetrators of crimes and atrocities, such as those in place in rwanda and sierra leone. but unfortunately, the lack of resources, in some cases of political will and certainly of capacity, often makes these courts inefficient and insufficient. the fight against impunity is without doubt one of the pillars of the union's human rights policy. we must therefore remember that without an international criminal court that establishes individual responsibility as a mechanism for enforcing the law, acts of genocide and flagrant violations of human rights will often go unpunished. we therefore also urge the african union states which have not yet ratified the rome statute to do so and to draw up as soon as possible an action plan for its effective implementation. it would be pretentious - and i do not intend to do so - to give lessons to africa from europe, when we too have many open or badly solved cases of impunity or insufficient justice for former dictators. but i do firmly believe that this is a task that must be tackled universally, jointly from europe and from africa. without truth, without justice and without reparation to the victims, peace is but a dream, but fighting against impunity can help us, one day, to make that dream a reality.

común la ilusión de las distintas partes de esta casa, de las distintas familias políticas de esta casa, para buscar soluciones a los problemas que tiene la gente. y ésa es la diferencia fundamental entre unos y otros, señor presidente; no nos engañemos. y, en eso, los partidos políticos juegan una función capital: partidos políticos en europa que han surgido, en realidad, de los grupos parlamentarios de esta casa, como surgieron también, en su origen, en los distintos estados nacionales. el origen de los partidos políticos está en los grupos parlamentarios de esta casa. y yo creo que, si un problema tienen los partidos políticos europeos, es que siguen siendo, en realidad, federaciones, asociaciones, de partidos políticos nacionales. ésta es la realidad. es verdad que hemos progresado en los últimos años, pero no suficientemente. es verdad que tenemos que hacer muchas más cosas. y ¿por qué? porque yo creo que los partidos políticos a nivel europeo pueden ser capaces de animar el debate europeo y de evitar que cualquier debate sobre temas europeos a nivel nacional se convierta en un debate sobre temas domésticos, que es lo que vemos que sucede una y otra vez. yo creo, por ejemplo, que si el consejo europeo hubiera atendido la petición de este parlamento de celebrar, ahí donde se celebraran, los referendos sobre la constitución europea el mismo día, habríamos conseguido hablar de temas europeos y no de temas domésticos. pero, mirando hacia el futuro, señor presidente, yo creo que, en un momento en el que cada vez somos más los que sentimos la necesidad de las disposiciones de la constitución europea, los partidos políticos europeos, en esta fase de reflexión —y me alegro de que esté aquí la vicepresidenta, señora wallström, que encabeza desde la comisión estas iniciativas—, tienen que desempeñar un papel muy importante. vamos a tener aquí, el 8 y el 9 de mayo, el primer foro interparlamentario. pues bien, yo creo que el papel de los partidos políticos europeos va a ser clave para unir las sinergias de los diputados europeos y los diputados nacionales e ir en la dirección que queremos la mayoría de los que creemos que la constitución europea es necesaria para hacer avanzar a europa. por tanto, ahí tenemos unos grandes retos, y evidentemente los grandes retos —el señor onesta tenía razón— necesitan, al final, no solamente buenas palabras, sino también colmar sus necesidades financieras. yo creo que este informe del señor leinen, a quien quiero felicitar expresamente, pone de relieve cuáles son las dificultades que tiene el reglamento y cuáles son las fórmulas que tenemos que utilizar para superarlas mejor. y, por eso, el grupo del partido popular europeo, señor presidente, va a apoyar el informe del señor leinen y vice-president of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to thank mr lehne for his report. the commission wholeheartedly welcomes parliament’s interest in the common frame of reference – on behalf of the pse group. i think that the time is right for this debate, mr president, because it is a subject which really invites us to reflect; we have very little in our hands. it is not a heated debate about something that is going to be done now: it is something that the commission is beginning to do and that we in parliament are supporting. we are probably among the few here who believe in this aim or in this possibility, but i believe that a unified market, an internal market of the european union, is not possible without contractual rules. and when i say contractual rules, i mean precisely that: rules. i am concerned about the commissioner's statements that we do not know what kind of legal instrument we are going to have. there is no soft law in the european union; the great advantage of the european union is that it has developed a solid law, a positive law, which is applied by the courts of justice, and which we must be precise about. the most important thing in law is legal precision: precision as to the nature of the obligations and precision as to the content. and so i think it is important that we start thinking now about definite legal instruments which have a binding value and are not purely recommendatory. neither self-regulation nor co-regulation nor soft law can solve the legal problems that arise in this area. and in this respect the commission's report does not only refer to the possibilities of contract law, but to a review of the acquis in the field of consumer protection. i think we must bear in mind that at the moment no one can think that, in matters of recruitment, the consumer can be treated in the same way as a company. the relationship between consumers and businesses is of a different legal nature and the existing legal systems have to recognise this. and that is what the amendments by my colleagues mr berger and mr patrie are aimed at: they are aimed at maintaining a certain degree of consumer protection. in any case, i should like to thank mr lehne and mrs wallis for the work they have done and also to thank the commission for continuing along this path, because i believe that the future of the european union will have to be shaped by private law, as mr gargani has said, and, above all, at the most immediate stage, by binding contract law and not by mere recommendations.

focuses on issues relevant to our citizens, for the improvement of their living conditions, and that it acts proactively, that is, anticipating and promoting change and not just reacting to it.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would also like to mention the initiative of mr michael cashman on the regulation of public access to documents, a report which runs parallel to this one but goes in the same direction. the council has a credibility problem at the moment. on the one hand, the political leaders of the member states support article 1.2 of the treaty on european union, and have even signed the treaty establishing a constitution for europe, which states that the council's decisions must be taken in the most transparent, open and close to the citizen. but the reality is very different. the council itself refuses to open its legislative meetings to the public and the media. the european ombudsman is right to say that this is a case of maladministration, concluding that the council has not provided any valid reason for not opening the door to its deliberations. to increase the interest and engagement of ordinary citizens in the european union, and in the face of the present constitutional crisis, europe needs bold and imaginative measures to bring european affairs closer to everyone. first of all, it must open its doors to public debate; however, the council does not want to do that. if millions of europeans could watch their ministers on television openly discussing european issues such as the energy crisis, the services directive, the retention of personal data or stem cell research, we could arouse much more interest in european issues and we could awaken from the slumber millions of europeans who show very little interest in european current affairs. public opinion is locked into narrowly national debates. this report adopted by the committee on petitions fully supports the recommendation of the european ombudsman, who considered that the principle of transparency should apply not only to the deliberations of the council but to all cases in which the european parliament is involved, including consultations and issues relating to individual rights and freedoms and those falling within the third pillar. last october, the european ombudsman published a report calling on the council to reconsider its refusal to meet in public when it is taking legislative decisions. to this end, the ombudsman asked the council to amend its rules of procedure in order to guarantee the media and the public access to its debates. however, despite the recommendation of the british presidency, the council has taken no action to change its rules of procedure in order to promote transparency. the leaders of the member states can therefore continue to say in brussels the opposite of what they say to their voters at home. the implications of this openness which we want could be profound for the council and would change the nature of the council. ministers would have to speak out under the scrutiny of the press and in front of millions of people. this would be the best way of making european democracy visible and of waking us up from the current lethargy and boredom. the council could even start with a pilot programme, explaining how decisions are taken and how the procedure is carried out in front of millions of people, in front of the television cameras. i would like to ask the presidency of the council and the commission the following question: are they prepared to propose concrete initiatives to enable open and transparent discussions and decision-making in the council? if not now, when? the citizens and the european parliament are asking the council for light and stenographers. the council has the floor. please open the doors. europeans want to be involved.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the integrated economic guidelines are at the heart of the new growth and jobs policy with which we are seeking to advance the lisbon agenda. they are integrated because they reflect the recognition that we cannot achieve more growth and more jobs for europe unless we closely link macroeconomic, microeconomic and employment policy objectives. the economic guidelines provide the framework within which the member states and the community institutions draw up their plans for implementing the strategy for growth and employment. they were first put forward by the commission last year and i am grateful that the european parliament is working hard on these guidelines because they are indeed a compass for what we intend to do and what should be the basis of our action beyond the year. the strategy for growth and employment which we have been trying to implement for about a year is a completely new process. it is not yet easy to assess the elements of this new process definitively, but one thing can be said - with caution - already today: the member states have largely followed the priorities set out in the integrated economic guidelines in their national reform programmes, and the commission has done the same in its proposal for a community action programme. it is important to note that the growth and employment strategy is based on a three-year cycle. this means that there is no intention of changing the guidelines every year. adjustments to changed realities and consequences of the experiences we have had are of course possible and necessary. however, we do not see any reason to change the present guidelines for 2006. they are and remain a solid basis for the discussions which the commission is now having with the member states, and these discussions are about actually implementing the national reform programmes. as regards the individual pillars of this strategy, my colleagues almunia and špidla will say a few words on the macroeconomic and employment aspects. i would like to turn briefly to the microeconomic part and point out that there is still important progress in some areas. this is particularly true of the key issue for europe's economic future, namely the transition to a knowledge society, the transition to an economy based on innovation, research and development. that is why we have insisted so strongly on the need to impose quantitative targets on research and development expenditure. you know that the results of the national reform programmes in this area have been somewhat disappointing. it would have brought us to an average of 2.2 percent in 2010; the commission has already proposed a reduction of the ceiling on the quantities of cereals. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if these commitments are maintained, we would reach 2.6% in 2010. that's better, but i'm telling you, clearly, not good enough. the commission will therefore continue its pressure at this point. the european council of last week, which will be discussed here tomorrow, also discussed and decided on important parts of the implementation of the strategy. i would like to draw your attention in particular to the council decisions on the promotion of small and mediumsized enterprises, the improvement of legislation and energy policy. there is a question that has occasionally been discussed in the context of the guidelines, which is whether or not the commission should issue country-specific recommendations in its future evaluation of the national reform plans. we did not do this in the first round for a very obvious reason, because we did not know what the national reform programmes would look like. i would like to make it clear, however, that the possibility of including country-specific recommendations in future progress reports is of course part of the commission's toolbox and that we will use this tool if necessary. but the most important thing for me at the moment is that we all work together to make it visible to the wider european public that we have a common strategy for growth and jobs, that we have common priorities and that we work together to achieve those priorities. mr. president, there was a time when laws were made by the gods; the gods made perfect laws. then the gods got tired and men started making laws, and laws are imperfect. so, at the present moment, whether a law is good or bad is not decided by anyone but ourselves, and the only criterion for knowing whether a law is good or bad is democracy, the criterion of the majority, because, as rousseau said, "it is reasonable that the majority should decide, and not the minority". this principle is established in modern democracies, where democracy is representative and parliaments legislate; they may be wrong, but the only criterion of legitimacy is the parliamentary majority. based on this, i think the biggest danger at the moment for democracy is technocracy associated with economic interests - what is called self-regulation and co-regulation - which is a way of putting the general interests in the hands of the particular interests of a few, and it is something to be remembered. of course, this parliamentarian, who has been elected after many legislatures, would not be willing to renounce his legislative responsibilities in favour of subcontracting and technocratic interests.
member of the commission. obviously, when this legislation was enacted, by way of exception to the rule that had been established, under which it was no longer possible to effect transfers of vessels to third countries, it was made subject to certain significant restrictions, one of which related, for example, to the length of the vessels. i remember the discussion here in parliament that we should not allow a situation where vessels would be transferred to third countries stricken by the tsunami without imposing any conditions because that could, in actual fact, increase the fishing effort and therefore intensify the problems that existed in certain fisheries in those third-country waters, but that the vessels should be suitable and appropriate to the fisheries that were traditionally carried out in those countries. therefore, we had restrictions with regard to the size of vessels, the age of vessels, the fact that vessels should not use towed gear and other conditions relating to ecological resource management and seaworthiness. having said that, i must underline the fact that the responses we have received from the member states on why it was not possible to identify vessels for transfer to sri lanka were either that there were no appropriate vessels available among those to be decommissioned in certain member states, or that decommissioning was not foreseen in certain other member states, or that the incentives provided for the transfer of vessels were not sufficiently attractive. i must also underline the fact that this was a commission initiative aimed at trying to help the countries affected by the tsunami, with regard to the fisheries sector specifically, if there was scope to do so. there was an element of additionality which was therefore the main thrust of the assistance, albeit under the general umbrella of development cooperation rather than under the fisheries portfolio. it was an ‘optional extra’ that was not taken up. i must underline that the end result was that certain individual member states gave assistance to the tsunami-affected countries by providing funds for the acquisition of vessels which have been purchased without any control measures. the end result today is that there is a significantly larger fleet in the tsunami-affected areas, which creates much more pressure on the fishing effort than before and creates further problems. rather than moving in the direction of sustainable fisheries, according to the information we have, there are significantly more problems than there were before.
member of the commission. yes, obviously it is important to try to strike the right balance between the needs of the countries that would be affected by such disasters and long-term assistance, which should aim not to create further pressures or difficulties for those countries by trying to help rebuild the economy in a sustainable way. we are trying to do this specifically with regard to fisheries; however, unless there is closer coordination between commission initiatives and the individual initiatives of member states, the chances are that the possibility of success will be limited.
member of the commission. mrs miguélez ramos’ question concerning the ban on the use of deepwater fixed gillnets to the north and west of britain and ireland follows a number of written questions on the same subject from her and from mrs fraga estévez and mr varela suanzes-carpegna. the ban, which took effect on 1 february 2006, was introduced in the tac and quota regulation that was adopted at the council in december 2005. it was proposed in response to the report of the deepnet investigation, which highlighted the potential damage that those fisheries may be causing to deepwater sharks and other species. the deepnet report was carried out by reputable scientific organisations in ireland, the united kingdom and norway, and so was taken seriously by the commission. in parallel to the prohibition in community waters, at its annual meeting in november 2005, the north-east atlantic fisheries commission adopted an identical prohibition of deep-sea gillnets in its regulatory area from 1 february 2006. first, i should like to reassure you that this ban is intended as a temporary measure in response to serious concerns about the practices of some of the participants in such fisheries and in particular about the impact of those practices on vulnerable species such as deep-sea sharks. those species are in such a poor state and take so long to recover their numbers once depleted that the commission has to react very quickly without waiting for definitive scientific advice from the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries (stecf). the prohibition was originally envisaged as an emergency measure in september but deferred until the december council to give time for consultations. unfortunately, no concrete suggestions for alternative measures were presented in time for inclusion in the proposal discussed at the council in december. i am aware that most of the fishermen using such gear behave responsibly and that it is a minority who are causing concern. for that reason, i would like to introduce measures to regulate the activity of deep-sea gillnets at the earliest opportunity. the commission has already had some feedback on possible approaches, especially from the north-western waters regional advisory council, which suggests an earlier reopening of the hague fishery and a limited number of vessels participating in the monkfish and deep-sea fisheries with observer coverage. the commission services will meet with the north-western waters regional advisory council and scientists on friday, 7 april 2006, where we will discuss those possibilities. depending on the outcome of that meeting, a proposal to allow a limited fishery under an observer programme could be made in may 2006. the data collected by such a programme could then be made available to the stecf, which will address the issue in late june or early july. the geographical limits of the prohibition were determined by the coverage of the deepnet study. i am aware that there may be similar problems in other areas, but we currently have no information that would justify enlarging the area of the prohibition. that is another reason for bringing in effective legislation applicable in all areas as soon as practicable. unfortunately, the prohibition is bound to create economic difficulties for the fleets concerned. no transitional measures to mitigate the effects of the ban have been planned, but i would encourage member states to make full use of the possibilities that are already available for the temporary cessation of activities under the financial instrument for fisheries guidance to help those most severely affected.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what i really wanted to ask you is whether there is any possibility of amending this decision immediately, whether there is any possibility of amending the tac and quota regulation so that at least the flying boats - which are engaged in cod fishing in a way that you yourself have acknowledged, in letters i have seen, is not aggressive - can return to those waters; and what time limits does the commission envisage for the definitive regulation of fixed gillnets, so as not to leave the sector in uncertainty. because, commissioner, this decision has had and continues to have very negative effects, especially socioeconomic ones.
member of the commission. as i said in my previous response, the negotiations were conducted by the commission with the representatives of the government of the kingdom of morocco. the authorisation that we had from the council was to negotiate with morocco. the negotiations concluded with an agreement which entails that any fisheries carried out in waters within the jurisdiction of the kingdom of morocco should benefit the communities directly adjacent to where the fisheries are carried out. it is therefore the responsibility of the kingdom of morocco to see to it that any benefits deriving from fisheries carried out in waters adjacent to the polisario front area would go to the communities living there.

member of the commission. on the basis of the european council agreement dating from 16 and 17 december 2005, the situation of the outermost regions for the period 2007-2013 is as follows. for the parts of europe concerned, there will be a higher co-financing rate under the structural funds and the cohesion fund. it will be 85%, both for regions under the convergence objective and for those outermost regions which are part of the regional competitiveness and employment objective. there will also be a specific additional financial allocation to help finance operating aid to offset the additional costs which are incurred in these regions due to their geographical location. the co-financing rate under this additional allocation will be at the level of 50%; this additional allocation amounts to eur 35 per year per capita in each of the seven outermost regions. we then have specific situations as regards individual outermost regions. there is madeira, which will be keeping the status of a phasing-in region, but at the same time will benefit from more generous financial transitional arrangements, similar to those of the statistical phasing-out regions. there are also the canary islands, which will benefit from an additional envelope of eur 100 million over the period between 2007 and 2013. with regard to territorial cooperation – the objective set for the policy – all the outermost regions will be eligible for the transnational strand of the european territorial cooperation objective, and the french outermost regions, like the canary islands, will be eligible for the cross-border strand. in addition, madeira, the azores and the canary islands will benefit from special provisions applicable to portugal and spain. as you know in the case of portugal, madeira and the azores will also be eligible for the cohesion fund, as also for the temporary application of the n+3 rule for the period 2007-2010. in the case of spain and the canary islands, that means they will also be eligible for the cohesion fund and for an additional allocation that was awarded to spain in the form of a technological fund. the participation of the canary islands would be by decision of the government. as you may know, the outermost regions can also benefit from specific measures, which aim at supporting traditional sectors of these regions. there will be specific measures for agriculture in the outermost regions of the union, as well as specific treatment under the rural development policy, in particular concerning the intervention rates of the new european agricultural fund for rural development. on top of that, of course, there are the ordinary instruments that exist under our policies, and all the regions will have access to all the community programmes envisaged under all the titles of the european budget. those in brief are the specific measures available under the new financial perspective for the outermost regions.

mr president, as a european and catalan i fully support the need to reinforce historical memory in order to avoid future disasters while we learn from our past. in mr takkula's report there is a proposal to finance historical sites related to the main totalitarian regimes that europe endured during the 20th century – nazism and stalinism. i agree with him, but we would also like to extend this proposal to other aspects directly related to this kind of authoritarianism. in our case, in the catalan country, we suffered franco's dictatorship which was closely related in origin to nazism and italian fascism. the only president of a democratic nation killed as a consequence of world war ii was lluís companys, president of the catalan autonomous government. the first civilian population bombed indiscriminately by hostile aircraft was guernica, the emblematic town in the basque country. if we neglect franco's regime and other dictatorships in southern europe and the need to rescue the historical memory of this dark period of our history, we avoid discussing the consequences of dictatorships, some of them very disturbing for the european union, even today.

president of the republic of malta. mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, it is both a pleasure and an honour for me to address your institution. as a representative of one of mr president, i would like to share my thoughts with you on a number of other issues. i will start by reflecting on the european constitutional treaty. we must accept that there were some shortcomings in the way the constitutional project was proposed, even if these difficulties have more to do with form than substance. for example, for new member states the constitutional project seemed to have arrived too early and too quickly. the time aspect also counts. and indeed, for countries that were painstakingly preparing for membership, the prospect of changing the rules of the treaty seemed like a game-changing exercise when the finish line of the marathon race was in sight. i know that the constitutional treaty was supposed to speed up decision-making in the union of 27, but it is clear that citizens of some of the member states saw it differently. the union they had grown up in had changed with the enlargement of 1995, and changed even more with the enlargement of 2004 and - against the background of globalisation - with the enlargement of the union. the constitutional project seemed to bring with it a state of uninterrupted change. in retrospect, therefore, it might have been wiser to give this important project more time, not only until the 10 new states had found their feet, but also until all 25 members had had time to adapt to the new realities of the european union. the question, however, remains how to break out of the current impasse. it goes without saying that the expressed wishes of the peoples in the two countries that have not accepted the constitutional treaty must be respected. the same applies to the decisions of the 14 countries that have ratified it. in countries, for example, the constitutional treaty was adopted unanimously by our national parliament, thereby sealing once and for all our commitment to partnership, and clearly breaking away from previous divisions. this is the time to debate and share our views on the road ahead with a number of scenarios. one scenario is to stick to the commitment made by the signatory heads of state or government to try to find a solution within the european council if four out of five member then we can see clearly how we should move forward. another scenario could include the drawing up of a european charter from the first two sections of the constitutional treaty. this could offer european citizens a clear and concise document with which they can better identify. the other section, the constitutional treaty, can be considered to have been largely ratified by the existing treaties. another scenario could include strengthening the protocol's role of national parliaments in particular extending their consultative role with regard to the european project. of course, there are other options that could be considered. this is the purpose of this time of reflection. let's not get carried away. mr president, political leadership in europe we often talk about a lack of political leadership in europe. this is not due to a lack of initiatives, certainly not in europe. this may be due, if nothing else, to a lack of coherence between the initiatives. why can we expect political leadership if some initiatives lack coherence? what is the coherence of stressing solidarity on the one hand, and failing to provide adequate financial means on the other? what coherence do we have if we remove borders on the one hand and rebuild barriers on the other? what coherence is there if we call for collective action, but then leave countries in difficulty to go it alone? i do not think that a lack of political leadership can be attributed to individual community institutions, whose initiatives and perseverance speak for themselves. if anything, any lack of trust in them should be addressed. confidence is not like talent, it is not born with us, it has to be earned. we therefore need to ask ourselves what we can do to regain confidence in the european union and its institutions. this can be done by rebuilding a link with the people. and here i praised the work of the commission which has gone to the hard work of bridging the gap with citizens through plan d. as a directly elected institution at european level, the european parliament is ideally placed to support the work of the commission. building a link with citizens is not a matter of words. it is a matter for the more informed. and if europe communicates better, it will be better placed to reflect the aspirations of europeans and to deliver on all that affects them. mr president, in addition to communicating better, to strengthen trust we also need to be more efficient in the areas in which the european union is already engaged. we can also strengthen confidence by showing that the european union can and must engage in new common initiatives in areas where we are facing new challenges that cannot be tackled by individual countries alone. we must continually ensure that the european union adds more and more value to its member states and its citizens. but more importantly, we can build confidence by showing that, in our policies, in our decisions, in our actions both internally and externally, the european union is capable of giving a voice to reason. by this i mean a union that consistently shows a sense of balance and fairness in developing its policies, in its decision-making, and also in its actions with other countries around the world. in this respect there is enough evidence to make me optimistic that trust can indeed be regained because the union is showing that it is willing to be on the side of reason. let me give you some examples: as a maltese, i am also an observer of the way the european union seeks to balance the interests of large and small countries. i have always been convinced that the european union is not the size of your country of origin that counts, but the strength of your ideas and the clarity of your vision. size counts, too, of course. but the european union is unique in the way it develops a model of governance that balances the interests of the big and the small and often combines these interests in common interests. this is a value to be noted. it deserves to make europe what it is, rich in diversity and respectful of the evident differences of its members. this may also explain why small countries are so closely linked to the european project and to the community method. the european union is increasing the influence of small countries: strengthen their identity, and not least their linguistic identity, and really open up the wide horizons of the rest of europe and the world. the european parliament too must continue to build this balance and take account of the particular interests of small countries. the european union cannot and should not be a directorate of large countries. the services directive is another example of where the european institutions are standing out as a voice of reason. i commend the work of this parliament in reaching a compromise on such an important initiative. the wide endorsement of the european council is also a valid testimony to your work. now that a workable compromise has been found, it is time to bring the legislative process to a swift conclusion, so that european citizens can reap the real benefits of the internal market for services. the initiative under the common energy policy to meet the major challenge of adequate energy supply is another desirable development for which the commission should be commended and supported. it is such initiatives that show that europe is indeed worthy of trust. but there are other challenges where europe has moved too slowly and where action at european level is increasingly needed. in these areas we need to work harder to give voice to reason, to strike a fair balance and thus strengthen trust. i feel that the european commission's work on the development of a maritime policy is of particular importance because it seeks to put europe's intrinsic maritime advantage at the top of the agenda. aside from being from an ancient maritime nation, i am convinced that europe's maritime heritage is still not sufficiently exploited at european level. we need to adopt a holistic approach. we must not let short-term interests in certain areas overshadow our leading position in maritime issues in their globalisation. we should strive to lead the maritime world rather than trying to create our own privileged space within it. confidence must be earned not only from within the union but also from outside. and here too we must demonstrate our ability to strengthen trust through justice. our euro-mediterranean policy is a clear example. the complexity of this region, which we share with our neighbours, and its intrinsic link to the middle east peace process, call us more than ever to be a voice of reason. the recent incidents following the publication of certain bad-luck cartoons have been a step backwards in this respect. but they give us an opportunity to rebuild trust also at this level. another challenge comes from the obvious but inevitable consequences of globalisation. the answer to this challenge cannot be found in protectionism or in the abandonment of what has been achieved so far. there must be a fair balance between the inevitable consequences of free trade on the one hand, and the assertion of europe's core values, and not least our social model, on the other. finding such a balance is no easy task. but we cannot forget that it is europe's sense of balance and reason that is distinguishing it more than other actors in the international arena. another challenge that is more visible at the human level is the challenge of irregular immigration. a few days ago a delegation from your institution visited my country as part of parliament's ongoing work touring countries in europe and beyond to examine the scale of the challenge of irregular immigration. this is a problem that is currently placing a heavy burden on the capacity of a number of member states, and not least my own country, to cope with the seemingly unstoppable influx of people, coming mainly from sub-saharan africa. as your delegation has seen, even when talking to immigrants and asylum seekers, the problem is as real as it is urgent. on the one hand, the mediterranean is facing a human catastrophe in which hundreds of people are drowning trying to reach europe, while thousands more are living in uncertainty and difficult conditions after doing so. at the same time, countries receiving a strong inflow are seeing their capacity and resources stretched to the limit. it is clear that the problem is not just malta's, nor is it the problem of any one country alone. it is a common challenge that requires a collective effort. however, i would like to emphasise that malta's problem is more acute, as malta is the most populous member state. europe urgently needs an immigration policy that can offer a more concrete response to this problem in all its complexity. a response that offers the typical european solidarity with the people involved in this drama, with the countries of origin, but also with the first arrivals in europe who do not have the means to face this problem alone. i therefore thank the european parliament, and the members of the delegation to malta, for putting this item on parliament's agenda and for heeding the country's call for urgent action. mr president, if we are to build trust we must appear to be responding effectively to the interests of the people. and to do that we need to recognize the mood of the people. political leaders should not follow the people but lead them. but they should also not move too fast, or they will leave people behind and be cut off from the realities of the world. here too a balance must be found. there are a number of values that distinguish europe from other continents and the european union from other regional integration projects in the world. europe is already distinguished by its full commitment to the values of peace, tolerance, human rights and solidarity. the european union is becoming increasingly distinctive as a voice of reason among its neighbours and in the world. europe's voice of reason requires us to go beyond the boundaries of our national egos and to work together for our common good. we must continue to preserve this value both in our action among ourselves and with other countries. this is the europe that citizens expect from us and this is the europe they are ready to trust. thank you.

the next item is the oral question to the commission by mr brok, mr moscovici and mr van orden, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the accession of bulgaria and romania to the european union (o-0034/2006 - b6-0019/2006).
member of the commission. mr president, before giving more substantive responses to the questions by mr brok, mr moscovici and mr van orden, i would like to begin by expressing my sympathy for all people affected by the floods that recently hit bulgaria and romania and countries falling outside the scope of today’s debate, in particular serbia. i can assure you that the commission is following the situation with the greatest attention and is ready to offer advice and support in tackling the impact of the floods once the damage has been assessed, as we did last year in the case of bulgaria and romania. (applause) concerning the first question as to whether the rhythm of reform in bulgaria and romania is such that they will be ready for accession by january 2007, the commission is currently assessing the progress made in both countries and is not yet in a position to confirm the answer to this critical question. as i said to the committee on foreign affairs on 3 april, the commission will report on developments until the end of april, so the cut-off date is 30 april, the end of this week. the full factual basis will therefore be available in the first two weeks of may. the commission will then provide an in-depth analysis on 16 may, and we will then be ready to discuss our assessment further with the honourable members of parliament. however, let me underline the priority of all priorities. the completion and implementation of judicial reform and concrete results demonstrating that these have a real effect on the ground are of paramount importance for our assessment. systemic conditions, structural conditions that show that the reforms are irreversible need to be in place. these are the critical yardsticks, since a fully functioning justice system underpins the functioning of the whole of society and the economy in its entirety. on the basis of our objective and balanced assessment, the commission will make a proposal on 16 may for a carefully calibrated decision that will maintain the momentum of essential remaining reforms up to and beyond accession of the two countries. i ask for the support of the parliament and the council for this rigorous and fair position. concerning the second question on the reform of the judiciary and the fight against corruption and organised crime, both countries have shown determination to undertake necessary reforms in this field. in romania we note significant progress, as romania has continued to pursue the implementation of its legal package of 2005. i fully agree with mr moscovici that the rigorous monetary mechanism and the safeguard clause of postponement have provided very strong encouragement and an incentive, and these have produced very tangible results in the case of romania. in bulgaria amendments have been made to the constitution, reducing the scope of the immunity of members of parliament and establishing the leading function of the prosecution service in most investigations. however, there remains ambiguity concerning the independence of the judiciary and there is a serious backlog in cases related to organised crime. as regards the fight against organised crime in bulgaria, there are still very few investigations and prosecutions. the competent authorities seem in general to have a reactive instead of a proactive attitude. therefore, urgent attention is needed in this area. the same is true concerning money laundering in bulgaria. finally, on mr brok’s question concerning the safeguard clauses and monitoring, safeguard clauses are meant to tackle the possible negative consequences that may persist due to shortcomings in bulgaria and romania after accession. safeguards may for instance involve temporarily suspending specific rights under the eu acquis which are directly related to the shortcomings of a new member state. a number of safeguards are already provided in existing community legislation, for instance in the area of food safety or transport. in addition, the accession treaty contains three safeguard clauses: a general economic safeguard clause, a specific internal market safeguard clause and a third one which relates to justice and home affairs. without going into details of how they can be invoked, by way of example i will take the internal market safeguard, which is specifically designed to deal with cases where a new member state fails to fulfil commitments made in the accession negotiations. if such a failure causes or risks causing a serious breach in the functioning of the internal market, the commission may take appropriate measures to deal with that situation, even before accession, with entry into force upon accession. it is important to note that this does not require a unanimous council decision; it requires a commission decision based on our objective risk assessment of a candidate country’s possible shortcomings. it is clear that, in order to have a meaningful system of safeguard clauses, we also need a monitoring mechanism and, in its role as guardian of the treaties, the commission will assume this duty and will verify the implementation of eu legislation in the two countries. (applause)

mr president, i would like to share with the commissioner a concern i have on the current market situation in romania by giving him an example. last year i visited rafo, the third biggest oil refining company in the country, and by far the biggest firm in the poor moldavia province. the company is trying to overcome major financial problems that have been accumulating since its privatisation in 2001. members of its administrative board made me aware of the pressures and obstructions they get from the romanian government to continue with the company’s activities. although in july last year a new investor clearly expressed its willingness to clear rafo’s nominal debt to the romanian authorities, until now the government has not shown any interest in this offer. moreover, the government’s demand for advanced vat payments for imported raw materials – which makes rafo the only company in romania to have its operation conditional on paying vat in advance – poses a serious threat to the company’s viability. this discriminatory treatment, which is against free market rules and which questions the impartiality of the romanian government towards the companies competing in the market, is still maintained in spite of the solvency and serious intentions of the new investors.

policy in general. this basis is the right of israel to exist within secure and recognized borders and the right of the palestinian people to self-determination. the so-called oslo process and the road map have given concrete expression to this right of self-determination towards an independent palestinian state side by side with israel. the european union is therefore firmly committed to the two-state solution. all policy measures, including all european union support measures, have been put at the service of these principles. these principles continue to apply and the council believes that the peace process can only be carried out in accordance with these principles, which i would like to reiterate. firstly, there must be a clear rejection of any form of violence to resolve the conflict in favour of a comprehensive negotiation process. secondly, israel's right to exist must be recognized and, finally, the obligations of the existing agreement, including the road map, must be recognized. these are the principles which guide the council in its middle east policy. the european union therefore continues to support the peace policy of the palestinian president abbas, who was elected directly by the people by a large majority. the council has followed events in the middle east very carefully in recent months. the hope, of course, was that a newly elected palestinian government would be guided by these principles which i have mentioned. the council has been very careful to see whether there is any movement in this direction. unfortunately, we have to note today that the hamas government has shown no clear willingness to accept this basis for european union support unconditionally - nor has the response to the suicide bombing in tel aviv earlier this week been encouraging. at the same time, the council also has an interest in continuing to support the palestinian people and their basic needs. in this tension between the fact that the palestinian people have elected a government which does not stand on the basis of the principles governing the european union, on the one hand, and the effort not to abandon the palestinian people, on the other hand, the policy of the council and the commission must move. i would like to say explicitly that the commission has acted very responsibly in this respect and, as a precautionary measure, has suspended organizations and international organizations to maintain aid to meet the basic needs of the palestinian people, including health and education. the major donors - and the union remains the largest donor - will continue to try to maintain aid without having to direct funds to the palestinian government institutions. so there will be no funding directly to the government and no funding through the government. the world bank has also carried out a study on the effects of reduced aid, including the effects of the israeli government's withholding of palestinian customs and tax revenues. the council has unequivocally called on the israeli government to take measures to improve the humanitarian and economic situation of the palestinians, and in particular to transfer the revenue from customs and taxation, which is the main source of revenue for the palestinian authority. we must of course ask ourselves: 'is there an alternative to this policy? other we believe that, given that hamas is an organisation that is on the list of terrorist organisations and shows no signs of moving towards recognition of the fundamental principles i have mentioned, the european union has no choice but to pursue a policy of - hopefully temporarily - suspending direct payments to the government. the priority will continue to be that the new palestinian government shares with us the basic principles which are indispensable for a successful peace process. a two-state solution without a democratically-based and functioning palestinian authority is by definition unthinkable. we must therefore hope to work towards this and also give clear signals so that the palestinian government will also be guided by these principles in the medium and long term. it is also important that the the constitution of a euro-latin american assembly which can give democratic legitimacy to parliaments as the promoters and legitimators of this relationship, and we would like, mr president-in-office recommended, as was done in the past with the euro-mediterranean assembly. we also call for a renewal and updating of the ministerial political dialogue and recommend the adoption of a renewed bi-regional political agenda, to include new issues: threats to governance, the fight against terrorism and organized crime, the preservation of the environment and natural resources, the reconciliation of the positions of the member states of the european union with those of latin america at the united nations, and many other issues that have to be reflected in initiatives such as the signing of a euro-latin american charter for peace and security. but, mr president, political dialogue and political will will eventually dry up and be reduced to nothing if they are not accompanied by actions which enable us to move from words to deeds, and this is where summits - there are too many summits - fail and are much criticised. and one area where we can clearly move from words to deeds is that of association agreements, with their commercial aspect. it is clear that we must make progress on the mercosur agreement, which unfortunately has not been made before, but not for reasons attributable to the will of the european union: we should set out in vienna a realistic timetable for concluding that agreement. i have to say quite frankly, madam commissioner, that from the european parliament's point of view the time for political dialogue and cooperation agreements with the andean and central american communities is long past, and we recommend that the decision be taken in vienna to move on to the phase of association agreements. i know that at the moment, with venezuela's decision to leave the andean community, there may be some uncertainty, but now more than ever, the european union needs to send a clear and well-defined message in this direction, so as not to give the right to those who are betting against the integration processes. i would like to end, mr president, quickly, so as not to waste time, by mentioning two initiatives: the european investment bank facility, which we would like to have named after the commissioner, because of her tenacity, for having favoured a completely innovative social cohesion fund in the history of the european union; and an initiative which we do not want to see go to waste: the biregional solidarity fund, a fund which will not cost the union any money, because we are not asking for additional aid, a fund which is supported by the european parliament, by the latin american partners. although we are not asking for a 200% commitment to this fund, we are asking at least for it to be studied and for it to be taken into account in the conclusions of the minutes. mr president, the european union cannot be looking over its shoulder in a policy of self-contemplation like the myth of narcissus: it must send a clear and well-defined message at the vienna summit of our commitment to a region that expects a great deal from us. we also expect the commissioner's commitment and the commitment of the council presidency in office, so that, with the efforts of all, this vienna summit will be a success.

between our two institutions, because we are all convinced that indeed strengthening is timely, important and necessary for the following reasons: firstly, latin america is one of the few regions in the world that can be considered a natural ally of the european union, especially because of the common values. secondly, there are many challenges that can be tackled more effectively through a reformed partnership and one of these is the lack of social cohesion, which affects both europe and latin america. i think it is very important that we make further progress in this area and i hope that there will be real results. thirdly, i hope that today's debate on latin america will be a positive signal to our partners, a guarantee that europe maintains a strong interest in its region. we need strong, solid and reliable partners in latin america. let me now turn to the next unfinished business, which is the vienna summit. this summit takes place in a context of important challenges and exchanges, and also changes, in latin america and the caribbean. most of the countries in the region have adopted democratic systems, have embarked on ambitious economic and social reforms and have great potential for development, but unfortunately there are still great social weaknesses, mainly due to the fact that economic progress has not reached the majority of the population and this is actually leading, or has led, to disillusionment with some democratic governments, because of their inability to comply with the terms of the social pact. much attention has been paid to the emergence of new political movements in latin america, which some see as a direct threat to traditional political, economic and social structures. these phenomena need not be viewed in negative terms, but rather in the context of a development towards a more equitable society. i think it goes without saying that it is important that this transition is carried out through existing and reliable democratic institutions. and i think the vienna summit is a great opportunity to achieve this visibility and to have this dialogue about social cohesion, but also about regional integration and multilateralism. it is against this background that the bregenz meeting took place and i am very glad that it was really successful. we must now move forward with the establishment of a network of association agreements between the european union and the countries and regions of latin america. i would therefore recommend that the member states first negotiate with central america. this decision still depends on a clear demonstration by the central american countries of progress in their own integration strategy, but i am very optimistic, and i believe that these decisions will be formalised at the meeting of the central american heads of state and government to be held from 5 to 7 may. as far as the andean community is concerned, as we know, the situation is unfortunately more complex, after venezuela left the community a few days ago. i have personally spoken to president morales and we still hope that the internal meetings within the can will open the way to progress. as regards mercosur, i am aware that the situation is much more difficult, but i still hope that vienna will at least give a strong political impetus to progress in the negotiations which are taking place in parallel with the doha negotiations. we intend to consolidate all our cooperation in economic and development activities through assistance programmes and we would like to have very substantial and significant support from the european investment bank, which would be 4 billion euros. we also hope that vienna will be the occasion to announce the creation of a transatlantic parliamentary assembly between the european union and latin america. i think it will be very important and will also allow people to come closer together in the future. finally, madam president, it is the responsibility of all of us to ensure that the partnership between the european union, latin america and the caribbean is stronger, more effective and has a long-term future.
