on behalf of the pse group. mr president, there is discomfort in the committee on development over the difficulties encountered with the european commission and the council in the handling of the development cooperation instrument. we adopted the first mitchell report over a year ago in the committee on development and have since blocked it in the face of the good words of the commission and council that they would heed our arguments and criticisms of the commission's initial proposal. however, despite some efforts and progress, these proposals have not been put into practice and have not been translated into any text submitted by the commission to parliament. three were the main drawbacks of what we have been proposed. firstly, it did not seem reasonable to have a single instrument for development cooperation and cooperation with the developed world. we were concerned that the resources earmarked for the development of the countries of the south might be diverted to cooperation with the countries of the north. the council and the commission seem to be moving closer to our approaches on this point. the second point raised was more serious. we could not accept that parliament should lose powers already assumed in the sixteen instruments which it was now intended to compress into one or two. the whole process of european integration has been a constant effort to consolidate democratic progress in the interinstitutional relationship, which has mainly been achieved by giving parliament greater powers in decision-making. we were surprised, and almost indignant, at the approach taken by the commission, which puts efficiency and democracy in opposition. the aim has been to reduce parliament's powers on the grounds that they complicate the process and make it less the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the debate has already shown that the energy community treaty is a historic treaty and not a one-way street in terms of its benefits. it is not that we are giving these countries something, as it were, the european union also has something. it is important - and this was also said by mr buzek, for example - that this is a european issue, not just a question of the countries of south-eastern europe or the european union. that is certainly not how an integrated energy market can work. this treaty not only contributes to energy security and supply but also to greater stability in europe as a whole. as you know, the austrian presidency has in recent months been trying to work more closely with the countries of south-eastern europe and the countries of the western balkans, to make progress in the interests of stability and peace in europe. it is perhaps interesting to recall that the treaty establishing the energy community was deliberately modelled on the european coal and steel community, which was the nucleus of the european union. it was also mentioned here, for example, by mr paasilinna, that the energy community treaty has addressed the very local and specific energy and environmental concerns of south-eastern europe. a number of speakers raised environmental concerns, such as the higher death rates due to harsh winters and environmental degradation from emissions from old power stations, the use of wood for domestic fires with the resulting deforestation and the unsustainable use of wetlands and watercourses for hydroelectricity generation. there is a european interest, and it was also mentioned in the debate that we need to think beyond the region of south-eastern europe - the caspian sea was mentioned here. i should like to mention in this connection that the presidency met all the representatives of the central asian countries in kazakhstan as part of a troika mission and also undertook a mission to the south caucasus. in both regions, the question of energy is of particular importance, whether they are producers or transit countries. it was also called 'nabucco', another important project that will help to ensure europe's energy security. doubts were also expressed. it's all legitimate, of course. but i think that the question of this treaty must be seen in the context of the european union's overall efforts in this region of south-eastern europe. i would remind you that all the countries that are part of this treaty are involved in the stabilisation and association process, which of course also includes respect for human rights, fundamental rights and other provisions of the european union. the purpose of this network of agreements we have concluded with south-eastern europe is to introduce these countries to the values of the european union, including, of course, the values enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights. i therefore believe that the energy community is a unique achievement, a successful project which we want to continue to make successful. that's what i heard from most of the reports. there is no doubt that europe must speak with a common energy policy voice to third countries and that the integration of our neighbouring countries into the european internal market must be further promoted. i want to leave no doubt - i said so in my first speech - that parliament has a central and important role here, and that it is not the council that is trying to restrict parliament's rights - which we cannot do, since there is an interinstitutional structure - but that we are also actively interested in involving parliament and working with it. we will therefore involve parliament in all the important matters affecting the energy community, in accordance with the ec treaty but also, as i have already said, in a very comprehensive interpretation of these provisions. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament.
member of the commission. mr president, i shall try to address some of the issues touched upon during the debate about the new countries that could join the community in the years to come. i really believe that turkey is close to joining the community. it has been working towards this since the creation of the community. it has not signed up to it, but we shall continue to work with it. it is quite important for turkey as a candidate country – we have started negotiations with it and it is also a very important transit country – that it could and should sign this treaty. two countries – ukraine and moldova – have also expressed interest in joining. the issue of affordability is very important because energy prices should be accessible to the citizens of these countries. article 33 of chapter iv addresses this issue as far as the community can address it. in the process of creating the community we have devoted attention to social issues. i agree that the social approach in europe should definitely be directed more closely at countries that aspire to a vision that may one day come much closer to that of the european union. a memorandum of understanding is a good first step in that direction. we have looked carefully at renewables and energy efficiency: chapter vi addresses this issue. on kyoto, article 13 in chapter iii – even if it does not say very much – covers this and the provisions on renewables and energy efficiency in the treaty will definitely help to achieve the kyoto goals. concerning privatisation, the community does not impose any type of action in this area: any decision on privatisation will be taken by these countries’ governments. concerning prices, i think these countries are already paying extremely high prices for energy. an energy community could bring down prices because of the new investments it will bring in. it will also help with regard to collecting payments, because there is a lot of money owed. there is also diversification: these regions pay some of the highest gas prices to the supplier. the supplier in these regions does not worry too much about price affordability. this means that the energy community could bring much more stability – at least to prices – and could even reduce prices for consumers. in addition, an acquis communautaire brings public service obligations, which means addressing issues for the more vulnerable people in society. investments from the world bank – the eib is also very active in this region – and other investors will come as soon as the treaty is approved and ratified. i think there has been some misunderstanding about foreign policy. this treaty does not address that issue at all. the treaty states that in some cases when energy is bought from third countries, the energy community could apply some restrictions if these countries neglect the environment or social issues. this provides an opportunity. this treaty in no way restricts the powers of the countries that participate in the treaty to take independent foreign policy decisions. it is very fair to look at these issues, because we cannot afford, if we want to promote sustainability, to buy energy from a third country where environmental standards are neglected and, as a result, the price of energy resources is perhaps cheaper. so i think there has been some misunderstanding. i really believe that this treaty serves the interests of the region and of the european community and i really hope that the countries that participate in this community will benefit greatly from it.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the committees on regional development, the environment and agriculture and the respective rapporteurs, mr galeote quecedo, mr berend, mr capoualas santos and mrs estrela, for their hard and constructive work. recent trends seem to indicate a growing vulnerability of the european union to disasters, and natural disasters in particular. the incidence of extreme weather events and related natural disasters is increasing, perhaps fuelled by the effects of climate changes. this year again, floods have raged in central and eastern europe with four countries – slovakia, hungary, romania and bulgaria – requesting assistance through the community mechanism for civil protection. i am proud to say that european solidarity and generosity has once again mitigated the affliction those countries had to suffer. the four reports rightly point out the human, environmental and financial costs of such disasters. the commission therefore very much welcomes the european parliament’s initiative to examine the various aspects involved, with a joint effort by no less than three parliamentary committees. the jointly organised hearing earlier this spring has certainly made a valuable contribution to this process. the reports rightly consider a whole range of measures aimed at improving risk prevention and the response to crises. the commission agrees with the recommendations regarding the need to adjust action in the area of prevention and management of natural disasters, as well as the need to coordinate community instruments. in fact, the reports reinforce the commission’s integrated approach to its policy on disasters, which includes instruments regarding prevention, immediate response and more longer-term, solidarity-based action. this approach is intended to strengthen the eu’s capacity and effectiveness in preparing for and responding to major disasters, while avoiding duplication of effort. some of the proposals contained in the reports have already been endorsed through the commission’s action. we are now proposing even more concrete ways to act. our recast of the council decision establishing the community mechanism for civil protection is the legal embodiment of a number of proposals put forward in these reports. these proposals are consistent with the rapid response and preparedness instrument. the recent barnier report also explores certain forward-looking suggestions for our response to disasters. the commission also welcomes the progress on the negotiations for the proposed floods directive on the assessment and management of floods and the positive vote in the recent envi committee meeting. the commission would equally welcome strong support from this house for a directive that gives all citizens a right to the same approach and level of ambition for flood risk protection, prevention and preparedness, regardless of where they live in the community: in transboundary or national river basins, or in the coastal areas of the community. not only are floods on the increase with changes to our climate, but droughts have become more prevalent in europe. at the request of a number of member states, the commission is analysing the issues of water scarcity and droughts. options are under consideration and we expect that a commission staff paper will be available shortly. another relevant instrument for the future could be life+, the new financial instrument for the environment. it aims, inter alia, to support the efforts of member states in the field of forest fire prevention, mainly through the implementation of knowledge-related measures such as training and awareness-raising campaigns. equally, the commission is prepared to cofinance prevention measures under the cohesion and rural development policies. member states are invited to include appropriate actions in their programmes for the forthcoming period, where prevention will be one of the priorities. under the rural development pillar, member states can also implement specific measures to restore the potential of forestry or agricultural production. under the rural development programmes, they can also request that a ‘severe natural disaster’ be recognised as force majeure, in order to derogate from certain conditions under the ‘agri-environment’ measures. those possibilities continue in the new programming period from 2007 to 2013. we must not forget, though, that natural disasters are not the only threat the union is faced with. it must be prepared for and able to respond effectively to challenges. major man-made disasters, major threats to public health and acts of terrorism might require just as much of a common european response. for the commission, it is sometimes difficult to explain why the union should be absent in some circumstances. the lack of a concrete expression of union solidarity has already been a source of embarrassment to the union during some of the traumatic events of recent years. the commission is therefore particularly grateful for the widespread support expressed in mr berend’s report for extending the eu solidarity fund to non-natural disasters and for enlarging the scope of eligible operations accordingly. the solidarity fund created in 2002 has generally worked quite successfully, if judged against the objectives and conditions set out in its legal basis. aid has been granted in 21 cases, concerning 15 member states and candidate countries. those who criticise the solidarity fund as being ineffective or too slow have a point. however, experience since 2002 has also led the commission to the view that the existing fund has a number of shortcomings and that modifications to the current regulation are necessary. that is why we have proposed a new solidarity fund regulation. the new proposal is based on the current solidarity fund, while introducing a number of modifications aimed at widening its scope, making the fund more transparent, and introducing a number of operational improvements, in particular the possibility of making advance payments so that the fund reacts more quickly and effectively. the commission nevertheless considers that the fund must remain limited to public emergency intervention. insured or private damage, including agricultural damage, should not be compensated. the ‘polluter pays’ principle and third party liability must continue to apply. as with the current fund, the new proposal is based on the subsidiarity principle. the eu should intervene only when a state is considered to be no longer in a position to tackle a disaster alone. consequently, there should be a relatively high threshold for european intervention. today this threshold is defined in terms of direct damage, which must exceed eur 3 billion, or 0.6% of gni. with the new proposal, the commission has therefore sought to improve the transparency and simplicity of the criteria governing the mobilisation of the solidarity fund. that would help the national authorities to have a clearer idea of when the fund is likely to be able to support them in recovering from a disaster. alongside the enlarged scope, a major element of the proposal is therefore a new definition of the criteria for triggering the fund. the operationally complicated regional criteria would be abolished in favour of only quantitative criteria. in compensation for the loss of the regional criteria, the quantitative threshold would be reset at eur 1 billion, or 0.5% of gni, whichever is the lower. this would increase the predictability of the european union’s solidarity fund decisions, thus reducing the workload in the member states in preparing applications for support that have little or no chance of success. solely in the case of truly unexpected and exceptional situations, such as those where physical damage is limited, for instance terrorist attacks or major public health crises, the new fund could be mobilised by a political decision of the commission, to be confirmed by the european parliament and the council.

mr president, a new stage is opening in nepal after 10 years of civil war and almost 13 000 deaths. king gyanendra's decision in february 2005 to dissolve the government and declare a state of emergency has been the final straw in the nepali's patience. and, let's say it loud and clear, it was the demonstrations for democracy and peace that forced this change. these demonstrations, which were severely repressed by the police and which left several people dead and many injured, have forced the king to abandon the de facto military dictatorship, to restore parliament and to hand over the administration to a government formed by a multiparty alliance. a new opportunity now looms on the horizon to reach a peace agreement with the maoist guerrillas, who had previously announced certain ceasefires that had been rejected by the king; now, instead, the ceasefire has been accepted. what we do hope is that the temporary nature of this ceasefire will soon become permanent. in the meantime, the change of arms in the political arena is to be welcomed, as evidenced by the agreement the maoists have signed with the multiparty coalition, to hold elections for a constituent assembly soon. this resolution also allows us to welcome the government's repeal of the royal decrees restricting freedom of the press and imposing strict controls on ngos and to demand the release of all political prisoners, journalists and human rights activists still in prison. the european union must be very attentive and wisely accompany this process. for example, the new government has decided to freeze the purchase of military aircraft and weapons by the previous administration; member of the commission. mr president, after nine fruitless efforts to join the world health organisation as an observer, taiwan has indicated that it is now considering lowering its ambitions and asking instead for meaningful participation in the work of the who. that means that taiwan has decided that, in this area, substance and pragmatism are more important than legal form. that is the position the eu supports. in may 2004, the irish presidency, explaining why the eu did not support a vote on the issue of taiwan’s observer status in the who, asked the who secretariat for taiwanese officials to be involved in technical work and meetings of the who where appropriate. the irish presidency referred to the who principle of the ‘enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health’ as one of the fundamental rights of every human being and also to the precedent that had been created by the involvement of and practical cooperation with health officials from taiwan during the sars crisis, which could serve as an example. in particular, in view of the arrival of avian influenza and the risk that implies, the austrian presidency, after discussion with member states and the commission, again took up the issue of practical cooperation with the who. subsequently, on 2 may, eu representatives in geneva had a very constructive meeting with the director-general of the who. in fact, over the last year, representatives from taiwan have participated in a number of technical meetings taking place under who auspices. our clear understanding is that the who secretariat is prepared to further explore possibilities for taiwan’s meaningful participation in the technical work of the who. we can only welcome this and will follow the matter with great interest.

prime minister of belgium. mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, i would first of all like to thank president borrell fontelles and all those who took the initiative in inviting me here today to begin a series of debates which you will be holding. i would like to thank you first of all for organising this initiative, and i have already noted in the introduction that the vitality of the european parliament is still the same as it was in 2001, when i came as president of the european council to defend the decisions of our presidency. i am very flattered, mr president, by the invitation, but this initiative certainly shows something else, namely the commitment and perseverance of the european parliament. i would like to remind you that your parliament has played an important, if not decisive, role in the work of the convention. i am very pleased that the european parliament is taking this initiative and with it is taking up its responsibility to shape the future of europe. i would not like to begin, ladies and gentlemen, my speech on the future of the european union without first reminding you of a date from the recent past, namely 1 may 2004, just two years ago. a milestone in the history of europe. i would say that it is a real highlight for the european union. sixty years after the division of power in yalta, forty-eight years after the hungarian uprising, forty-three years after the building of the infamous berlin wall, thirty-five years after the prague spring, it was a great day, because that day meant - states or a strengthened european democracy based on an active european commission and a fully-fledged european parliament, which is the essence of a european democracy. let me illustrate, mr president, the crucial importance of this turning point in the main challenge which concerns us, and i believe that the main challenge which concerns us at the moment is the modernization of the european economy. if we look at the figures, what are they today and what do they tell us? the average growth of gdp in europe has reached 2.3% over the last ten years, compared with 3.3% in the united states. in europe, total employment increased by 9% over the same period. in the united states, this increase was 14%. much more strikingly - we must admit this - if, in the 1980s, per capita income in europe and the united states was still at the same level, today, european income is 30% lower than its american counterpart. and i have not yet touched on the case of china, india or japan, which we talk about a lot. last year, china recorded an economic growth of nearly 10%. the european union's trade deficit is still in surplus, but we are also seeing deficits with the asian region of over 100 billion euros. and this deficit is expected to increase in the years ahead. the european union's response to this problem is the lisbon strategy. the objectives pursued by this strategy are not in doubt, i repeat, not in doubt. europe must become 'the most competitive knowledge economy in the world'. but the method adopted to this end, which allows the member states to design themselves the way forward to achieve this objective, is ineffective. the facts show that in many areas we are getting weaker and weaker in the race. the reason is simple. the lisbon strategy uses the open method of coordination, a form of intergovernmental approach based mainly on best practice, benchmarking and peer review. with the exception of the formulation of certain general objectives, the role of the european institutions is limited to the preparation of the classification and tables for drawing up the report. this is precisely what others are saying in their reports: the world competitiveness centre (imd) or the world economic forum (wef) are the most important. the only difference between the reports drawn up under the lisbon strategy and those of these economic institutes is that the latter show that almost all european countries are in recession. some people will say that this is naturally the consequence of the high value of the euro. but it is above all the consequence of a lack of common reforms in the european union. in short, while we aspire to make our knowledge economy the most competitive in the world, it is clear that our competitiveness is in danger of diminishing every day. i must conclude by saying that i tried to defend myself in the council, but also, already, in the european parliament, for example when i had been invited by the economic and monetary committee. this conclusion is clear as day: the intergovernmental method, without commitments, which forms the basis of the lisbon strategy, is not working properly. (applause from the centre) we need a more binding and community approach. a socio-economic governance in the proper sense of the term. a common socioeconomic policy for europe, the union drawing up the guidelines for the necessary reforms. these reforms are all the more indispensable if we are to face the growing competition from the new growth poles and safeguard the social model of which we are so proud in europe. these reforms require interventions in industry, innovation, research, taxation, but also in the labour market, pension systems, social security, health care, to name a few. the method to be followed, and i do not want ambiguity in the subject, cannot be confined to blind harmonization; i am against blind harmonization, or to say the other things, a standardization which conceals the diversity between the member states. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. the nun! what i am advocating is the implementation of a convergence policy, an approach similar to the one which came to fruition with the stability and growth pact and led to the introduction of the euro, because this is what was at the heart of the stability pact: the commission has already done so. unlike harmonisation, which is based on absolute values and which ignores the diversity of europe, convergence opted for the fixing of the minimum and maximum levels, the fourchettes, of a framework within which the various member states of the union must operate and modernise their economies. the maxima are indispensable for instilling a will to reform in the member states. the minimum is indispensable to prevent social dumping. convergence also enables the various member states to follow a progressive evolution in parallel and the union to regain its competitiveness vis-à-vis the other growing regions of the world, although it avoids deadly internal competition and the union is not forced to renounce its social component. i also believe that the european citizen will thus be able to find in the union a solid partner, a federation of peoples and nations capable, this time, of providing a response to the challenges of globalisation. in any event, by radically overturning the lisbon strategy and by reinforcing it with a more explicitly community-wide approach, the union will be able to resume the successes of the past. it must be recognised that neither the internal market nor the euro would have been possible without a powerful community engine. it must be said today that for the internal market this motor is in the form of the principle of mutual recognition and qualified majority voting as developed by mr delors. the euro, for its part, owes its introduction to the maastricht criteria and the standards of the stability and growth pact, as well as to being a community engine. ladies and gentlemen, if a new community economic strategy of this type is highly desirable for the union, it is certainly indispensable for the euro area. in the long term, a common currency and a monetary union are bound to succeed if they are not relayed by a common approach to social and economic challenges. in fact, a lack of reforms in one country will inevitably have negative repercussions on the health status of other countries, and therefore the whole area. if one were to doubt the necessity of economic governance at least in a monetary union, one need only imagine the united states of america with a single currency, the dollar, with a central bank, the federal reserve, but where socio-economic policy would be different in each of the fifty states. "unbearable", that would be our judgment. or, this situation is unmanageable, we are experiencing it today, at the level of the european union, or at least in the euro zone. and then there is the question of why we are not experiencing the same economic growth as other regions of the world! that is why i have been calling for some time, mr president, for an initiative to be taken to strengthen approach. but if that were to prove impossible, what i fear every day a little more, it is out of the question to undertake anything. moreover, when i speak of the eurogroup, i am referring not only to the current members of the eurozone, but also to all the countries which have been called upon by a conventional clause to join the eurozone. in other words, no one is excluded from membership and participation in the euro area. what could such a strengthening of the euro area look like to create the socio-economic governance that is so lacking in the union? i also think that the reinforcement belgian prime minister. mr president, i should like to thank all those who took part in this debate. i will start with the question of statement 30 because that statement has a rather strange history. the principle of four fifths of the member states was already included in the original proposals tabled by the prodi commission. however, it appeared to say that if four fifths of the member states ratified the treaty, then we were moving forward, which was, of course, unacceptable to some members of the european council. subsequently, the convention and then the intergovernmental conference wanted to retain this concept of four fifths. how was it to be presented? we could not say that if four fifths of the member states ratified the treaty, we were moving forward, because that would ultimately mean abolishing the unanimity rule, which will have to be done one day. the americans did it in 1787 at the convention of philadelphia. it was a seizure of power by nine of the thirteen states that existed at the time. so what did it take to keep the concept of four-fifths? the final decision was to adopt the formula 'the european council shall deal with the matter' in the declaration annexed to the treaty, whereas in reality the concept of the four fifths has a very different origin, since the original aim was not to organise a debate within the european council. the reason for this concept, which goes back to the convention, to the proposals of the prodi commission, and which was not finally taken up in the final text, either by the convention or by the intergovernmental conference, was to find a solution to a particular situation. who was the concept of the 'new' really meant to be? certainly not to the french, but rather to that part of the union which is on the side of mr kirkhope and others, at any rate a part on the other side of the channel. that's what we thought. we said: if everyone says yes and the british say no, we will still meet again in the european council to continue. this was the motif behind the concept of four-fifths. and it is these unfortunate french people who are voting no who are confronting us with the problem of the application of the four fifths. i agree with the substance of the matter: the ideal would be to have a system in which unanimity has disappeared and is replaced by something else, a european referendum or a four-fifths majority, for example. but to do that, we must go through referendums, through popular consultations, and this also in the countries that said no. the reason i'm talking about a second way is there. you can do anything: continue the ratification, very well, i ask; use the four-fifths principle, very well; extend the reflection period, very well; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this work, between us, is going to be very interesting but it would be a really big mistake not to do something else right away. so we are going to deal with the four fifths, the declaration 30 of an intergovernmental conference; maybe we'll change this or that in the draft constitution, otherwise, we'll never get through the two countries that said no. these are obviously necessary and are the first steps. but it would be a huge mistake not to open up a second way without amending the treaty. but all that i have said in my introduction, all the proposals i have made do not call for any amendment of the treaty. another great advantage is that france and the netherlands are already part of the eurozone. we don't have to start a whole debate about whether they want to participate or not. the second aspect i want to stress with regard to cooperation within the euro area is that it is an open cooperation, not a closed club, but a reality that exists and will be expanded with the entry of slovenia no later than 1 january 2007. i do not know whether the ecofin council has completed its examination of the other countries, on the basis of the commission and the european central bank's opinion, but these other countries will nevertheless join, perhaps not in 2007, but then, it will be on 1 january 2008. so we're sure that this group is growing. why not move forward with him in concrete ways? because if the citizens said no in the referendum in france, it is because there is no socio-economic convergence and we cannot meet their expectations at the social level. we must therefore go both ways and, while it is true that it would be a mistake to abandon ratification of the constitution, it would be a grave mistake to take the other way, that of the socioeconomic governance that everyone wants, without delay. this is perhaps the most view that the provisions of the international covenant on civil and political rights and the un convention against torture apply to guantánamo bay. in this connection, we welcome the united states’ intention to adopt a new army field manual for intelligence interrogation, which will hopefully ensure that interrogation techniques fully comply with the international prohibition on torture or cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment. moreover, in our view, every person who has been detained must enjoy a status under international law and is entitled not to be detained arbitrarily. a person must, in addition, receive due process and a fair trial. the commission would also stress that no one should be subject to incommunicado detention and that the international committee of the red cross must always be allowed access to detained persons wherever they may be. finally, we have repeatedly made clear to the united states our opposition to the use of the death penalty in all cases. the the rapporteur. - mr president, this house will vote tomorrow on the report on energy efficiency for which i have been responsible as rapporteur. this report comes at a very opportune time. following the energy crisis last january, the steady rise in the price of a barrel of crude oil, among other factors, has reopened a deep debate on the lack of a common energy policy within the union, the vulnerability of our supply system, the worrying increase in protectionist attitudes and the need to substantially improve our habits and the efficiency of our consumption. it has taken extreme situations for citizens and governments to become aware of the seriousness of the situation in which we find ourselves. and it is to be hoped that, once and for all, the necessary measures will be taken to solve these problems. in my view, which i believe is shared by the vast majority of members of this house, improving energy efficiency is the fastest, least expensive and most job-creating and economically growth-promoting way to reduce our external dependence and combat climate change. in addition, the promotion of energy efficiency is perfectly in line with the lisbon agenda, which is in dire need of a revitalizing boost. the report also aims to remind member states that, if the various directives in force were respected, the union could reach 50% of its energy saving targets and a large part of the commitments under the kyoto protocol without having to take any further action. i think it is important to stress this message because a large part of the agreements between member states at the last spring council correspond to the fulfilment of existing obligations. we are often accused of producing a lot of legislation which is difficult to implement, but this is often a poor excuse for national governments who are not diligent enough to comply with community legislation. the report we are going to adopt tomorrow also contains recommendations which are worth highlighting here: the need to invest massively in infrastructure improvements - taking into account that we suffer an average loss of 12% in transmission networks, with losses of up to 20% in some member states - the completion of the internal energy market; increased investment in research, development and innovation of more efficient technologies; the introduction of more stringent requirements for household appliances and stricter control of products offered on the european market which do not meet minimum standards; the inclusion of efficiency criteria in relations with developing countries; and a reinforced dialogue with the main energy producing countries. last but not least, several parts of the document highlight the importance of the public sector, including european institutions, playing an exemplary role in implementing energy efficiency measures, whether in the design of public buildings, the renewal of vehicle fleets or the inclusion of energy efficiency criteria in public tenders. i believe that the commission will find in this document many useful suggestions for the preparation of the action plan. we hope that commissioner piebalgs, who is always so attentive to the feelings of this parliament, will incorporate them into his final formulation. let me conclude, mr president, by thanking the shadow rapporteurs for their excellent cooperation in the preparation of this report, which i hope will receive the same broad majority support as the vote in committee tomorrow. it is the right time to take bold steps in the right direction, since we have on our side, simultaneously, the willingness of the member states and the will and interest of the citizens. we can't afford to miss this great opportunity.
mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to congratulate mr vidal-quadras on the broad consensus reached and the spirit he has shown in the process of drawing up this report. we all agree that europe is facing the effects of climate change, rising oil prices and tensions with russia over gas supplies. however, the european political response to our energy vulnerability may not yet be up to the challenges we face. in recent years, priority has been given to the completion of the european energy market. however, reality shows that progress towards a common energy policy is essential and that the commitment of the member states is necessary to move decisively towards this objective. on the other hand, greater financial commitment to research and development in the field of energy and, in particular, to increase efficiency, especially in buildings and transport, is also essential. in any case, one of the essential ways is to improve energy efficiency, which can save europe a huge amount of energy. the citizens can play an important role in this in their daily lives, but we will need a global approach, because this objective will affect all european policies as a whole.

and it calls for women victims of these practices to be able to appeal directly to international judicial bodies. however, it is also necessary to emphasize the fundamental role played by women in peacebuilding processes and, therefore, we call on the commission and the council, as well as on the member states involved in conflict management, to be more sensitive in ensuring the technical and financial assistance needed to promote programmes which enable women to be actors with their own voice in these processes, as, for example, has been requested by groups of kosovar women, who are calling for inclusion in the negotiating delegation, which, for the moment, has only men among its seven members. but we also ask that international missions, whether civilian or military, take a gender perspective into account in their practice on the ground and that those who abuse their status and impunity and commit - as we have unfortunately seen on several occasions - degrading acts and violations against women and girls are severely punished. member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank the european parliament, the committee on the environment and the rapporteur, mrs klaß, for the excellent work they have done on the second reading of this proposal. i totally agree that clean water is more important and more valuable than diamonds. there is no doubt that there is a need for an effective system to protect the quality of groundwater as a natural resource for drinking water, industry and agriculture. groundwater also has great environmental value. they are an essential component of the water cycle and therefore need to be protected for both the aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems to which they are linked. the proposed framework directive complements the water framework directive. first, it sets out clear criteria for assessing the good chemical status of groundwater and for identifying and reversing trends in the degradation of groundwater quality. secondly, it requires the application of measures to prevent or limit the direct inflow of dangerous substances into groundwater. at first reading the commission accepted many of the 89 amendments adopted by the european parliament, since they clarified and improved the text while remaining consistent with the structure of the original proposal and the commission's overall approach. the common position now incorporates 54 of parliament's amendments, either in substance or in spirit. before the common position was adopted, the scope and applicability of community standards for groundwater quality, and in particular the issue of nitrates in relation to the nitrate pollution directive, were discussed. in this respect, the commission considers that the nitrates directive, the water framework directive and this directive pursue the same objectives in terms of preventing and reducing nitrates pollution. the commission considers that the common position improves the provisions on the fixing of threshold values for groundwater and the corresponding compliance regime. the common position also simplifies the criteria for the detection and reversal of pollution trends and clarifies the measures to be taken to prevent and reduce pollutant inflows. i hope that we will be able to complete the legislative procedure as soon as possible, because we really need this new directive, which will allow the environmental objectives of the water framework directive to be assessed on the basis of clear quality criteria and groundwater protection measures.

number of proposals to the council, and i hope that the council will take them up. environmental policy at european union or national level depends heavily on spatial data, or in other words information that can be geographically placed on a map. all other sectors also depend on similar high-quality data. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment from the adverse effects of pollution of the atmosphere by nitrates and their salts is a very good one. our policy making is hampered by the fact that spatial data are often isolated in systems that are not easily accessible. in addition, in some cases, data are recorded in such a way that they cannot be combined with other sources, thus preventing the necessary policy-making assessments. the proposed inspire directive aims to address these problems by improving the accessibility and interoperability of spatial data systems held by public authorities in the member states. this is the best way of making the most of the possibilities offered by modern technology in terms of access to the information we need. the fact that the member states' experience is being brought together is a clear example of the added value of the proposed directive at european union level. the commission has accepted most of parliament's amendments at first reading. unfortunately, the mr president, the seventh framework programme is not only disappointing for the common fisheries policy, it should be openly described as hypocritical. it should not be forgotten that one of the union's major objectives is to lead a policy of competitiveness and economic efficiency in a framework of sustainable development. and when we talk about sustainable development, we immediately think of the marine environment and, in connection with it, the consequences of fishing activity. there is no fisheries management rule that does not end with the whiplash that decisions will be taken on the basis of the best available scientific advice. in presenting the green paper on the future maritime policy of the european union last week, commissioner borg reiterated the urgent need to know how the oceans work and that new fisheries management measures cannot be developed without knowing how ecosystems work and how economic activities affect them. and yet we have gone from having specific chapters for fisheries research, with 150 million euros in the fifth framework programme, to 60 million in the sixth programme, where, for the first time, the thematic approach to fisheries is no longer present. the fishing industry needs to know the size and evolution of species, to research new and more selective fishing gear, to develop the cultivation of new species to feed the exponential internal consumption of fish and to depend on imports. without this kind of specific research, any rules applied to fishermen will lack a sound scientific basis and will have no credibility. it is not by stepping back at this scale that we can lead sustainable development policies. i therefore ask everyone - and especially the rapporteur - to support the amendments tabled by various political groups and by various members which reflect this thematic approach to fisheries.
mr president, tunisia is indeed a key country in the euro-mediterranean process. so much so that it has had an association agreement since 1998, an action plan since 2005, and even its parliament has been chairing the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly for a couple of months now. that is precisely why the situation in that country is even more serious in terms of human rights violations. i would reply to mr busuttil when he says that we are too concerned about tunisia, that we cannot simply leave a friend behind and that we will therefore have to draw up as many resolutions as necessary. let the tunisian authorities not come to the conviction that, however much they insist on human rights violations, they will tire us out and we will be silenced. we would be unfair to the euro-mediterranean process, we would be unfair to the tunisian people and we would be unfair to ourselves if we did that. just because tunisia is doing it wrong, doesn't justify others doing it wrong too. and this is the political problem, mr president, that we have on the table. the euro-mediterranean process is a success, but there is at least one area where we have not yet achieved the objective, and that is that human rights should be a common currency in the political situation of all the countries in the process. what has happened in tunisia is the latest example, but it will not be the last of the last, unfortunately. that is why i would call on the tunisian authorities to think about being an example of a secular and democratic state, respectful of human rights, and to stop being an example of a secular state and not respectful of human rights, and they understand well what i am trying to tell them.

member of the commission. mr president, the sustainable development and lisbon strategies together address issues that really concern people. european value and quality of life surveys tell us that citizens want prosperity, but they also want a clean environment, good health, social protection and equality. the commission put forward its proposal for the review of the european union’s sustainable development strategy in december. this has been the subject of in-depth debate in the council, culminating in the adoption of a review of the strategy at the european council scheduled for tomorrow. i welcome parliament’s input from january on the stocktaking and orientations for the review, and i appreciate the involvement of many of you in the stakeholder debate on this subject. i look forward to working with you further on this, on the issues raised in the motion for a resolution amongst others. sustainable development is an over-arching objective of the union. the european union sustainable development strategy and the lisbon strategy work hand in hand towards this objective, although they should be kept separate. together the strategies are an agenda for change, for europe to adapt to a changing global context: new competitors, an aging population, and the impacts of demographic change, increased resource scarcities, climate change, biodiversity, and ecosystem loss, for example. they aim to stimulate innovation, including behavioural change, create level playing fields and engage all. the lisbon strategy and the sustainable development strategy are complementary. the much-needed economic growth must be decoupled from environmental degradation and must better safeguard social cohesion to ensure it can be sustained. at the same time, though, the worldwide drive towards more eco-efficient products and services creates opportunities for growth and jobs that we must seize. for both we need to act. by achieving results on sustainable development, we improve our chances of regaining citizens’ confidence in the european union. to achieve results, we need to focus and be clear about who does what. this implies a certain practical distribution of work between the two strategies. the lisbon strategy addresses concerns about medium-term economic performance, looking to stimulate growth and jobs and helping the european union to adapt to global competition and increased pressures on resources. to achieve this aim, the lisbon strategy comprises actions in a wide range of policy areas, many of which are central to sustainable development strategy, such as energy efficiency, environmental technologies resource use, and others. the sds addresses concerns about our prosperity, both in economic and quality of life terms, including issues that are more slow-burning, where time-lags mean that actions now have impacts into the long term. a good example is climate change, but also unsustainable modes of transport, social exclusion, health and how we use our natural resources. it also looks at broader global challenges and impacts beyond the european union’s borders. but let us be clear: lisbon and the sds are mutually reinforcing. the success of one depends on the success of the other. the priority now is to achieve results. there have been more than 20 years of debate on sustainable development, but progress in addressing unsustainable trends is too slow. we must move from words to action. some say that we are not ambitious enough. i disagree. the commission’s revised sds provides a new political drive for sustainable policies that apply to all policy areas. we also welcome the priority given by the austrian presidency to the revisions of sds and the draft conclusions that will be discussed at this week’s european council. we are talking about a new drive aimed at making the difficult changes across society that are necessary for sustainable development. the review of the european union’s sustainable development strategy is about how we can do things better to get results: first, about how we design policy, including policies within the lisbon agenda; second, about implementing what has been agreed; third, about making sure that we involve all those who need to act. the european union institutions cannot achieve sustainable development alone. the new strategy addresses some of the weaknesses of the previous strategy: unclear priorities, little ownership and absence of a clear monitoring mechanism. it confirms the main challenges, but clarifies the objectives and sets out a new and more rigorous monitoring mechanism. it includes regular reports from the commission, which are to be submitted every two years, drawing on the latest eurostat indicators. it includes national strategies, to be updated to bring them more into line with the european union strategy, and it includes peer review of national strategies to allow mutual learning. we need to learn from best practice and use every opportunity to multiply successful initiatives. by clarifying priorities, we will also facilitate the coordination of the lisbon and sustainable development strategies. the renewed sustainable development strategy re-emphasises the importance of an integrated approach. the problems are interlinked and so are the solutions. good use of impact assessments that address the economic, social and environmental impacts of proposals is key. horizontal measures, such as getting prices right, investment and research and innovation, education and skills are also important. the new strategy is about all of us assuming our responsibilities. involving stakeholders, businesses and citizens in delivering results is a priority. it is also about all european union institutions and member states working for the implementation of the strategy. we believe that the european parliament, the european economic and social committee and the committee of the regions should play a more active role in helping to implement and monitor the strategy.

member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by expressing my thanks and gratitude to the rapporteur, mr ó neachtain, who has presented an excellent report. i should also like to extend my thanks to the whole committee on fisheries for having taken up this important subject in the form of an own-initiative report. it is clear that small-scale coastal fisheries are in many ways different from fishing activities conducted by larger boats. many of these differences are highlighted in the report, and i should like to mention just a few. small vessels stay close to the coast and mostly conduct fishing trips of a single day. the businesses are small and mainly family-based, and in most cases only one person operates the vessel, with the maximum being not more than three. the catches are landed and also often marketed locally, thus making this segment more dependent on the local economy. this part of the fishing industry is fragmented and not equally represented in shipowners’ organisations. these vessels operate in coastal areas, which are often biologically fragile, and where there is a lot of competition with other users, such as other fishing vessels or recreational fisheries and tourists. however, i should like to stress that not all of these differences are disadvantages. in fact, some of them are distinct advantages, such as the freshness of the landed fish. however, it is also true that coastal fisheries have handicaps, and i agree with most of your conclusions in this respect. i absolutely agree that it is not an easy task to define coastal fisheries, but this is exactly why i would strongly recommend basing ourselves on the definition which is used in community legislation: vessels of up to 12 metres not using towed gear. this definition was agreed almost ten years ago and is a good basis for further action. however, it does not mean that at national or local level additional criteria could not be used when defining the role of the different players in coastal fishing areas. on the contrary, coastal management actions and plans should include further criteria depending on the specific settings of the area and the fleets involved. let me now turn to your specific suggestions. here, again, i agree with most of your proposals, and in particular the establishment by local fishermen of coastal management plans, the harmonisation of data on coastal fisheries, the improvement of training for men and women involved in this type of fishing, better coordination of all aspects affecting coastal areas and fishermen, the improvement of vessel safety and of the safety culture for those involved, the need to recognise the role of women and improve their legal work status and, last but not least, the better involvement of coastal fisheries in decision-making and representatives bodies, such as the racs. but this leads me to the question: who does what? i am deeply convinced that it is first and foremost the local fishing communities themselves who have to come together, get organised and propose actions and initiatives. secondly, many of the aspects that were mentioned are under the responsibility of the member states, for example education and vocational training, jurisdiction over coastal areas up to 12 nautical miles, and the control and enforcement of safety standards, etc. however, i also agree with you that we have a role to play at european union level. you, the european parliament, have started with a study, the hearing of last november and this own-initiative report we are discussing today. the commission has already started work too, and i have proposed specific treatment under the european fisheries fund, which will hopefully be adopted next week. among other possibilities of particular interest to coastal fishers: the proposed european fisheries fund reduces to 20% the private contribution for the modernisation of vessels for owners of smaller ships. it gives them more favourable treatment in the conditions for engine replacement and urges member states to give ‘safety tonnage’, preferably to smaller vessels. i think that this is a package of better treatment for this segment, which will contribute to bringing about some of the improvements mentioned in your report. in addition, there are several areas of the common fisheries policy where coastal fisheries are treated differently or exempted from obligations, such as the requirement to use a logbook, remote sensing and vms requirements. in relation to conservation, however, small-scale fisheries have to take full responsibility in the management of fish stocks, because coastal waters are often the place where fish spawn and grow in the early stages. before concluding, let me just mention that my services have recently commissioned an important study, which is under way at this very moment, and which will give us a new and up-to-date insight into several cases of small-scale fisheries located in different regions and seas of the community. the findings of this study are expected in the coming year and i am sure that they will help us to assess whether further action is needed and how to tailor it. i take up your suggestions and, building on your valuable work, will join forces with all the stakeholders, the member states and, last but not least, all those who make a living from coastal fisheries in order to engage in concrete action to improve the situation and the conditions for this segment of the fishing fleet. thank you for your attention.
opinion of the committee on women's rights and gender equality. mr president, i am speaking on behalf of the committee on women's rights and gender equality and i have to say that the work of women in the whole fisheries sector, and in particular in shallow-water fishing, should be given greater legal and social recognition. although only 3% of women are involved in extractive fishing, a high proportion of women are active in other fisheries-related activities. in an economic structure built mainly on small family businesses, most women work hard but without economic or social rights, as they do not have a sufficiently clear employment status and, moreover, in working conditions that are, in many cases, highly detrimental to their health. it is therefore urgent - and we say this in the report - that both the commission and the member states take the necessary measures to guarantee the rights of all these women. women working in this sector should also have access to finance, credit and vocational training on equal terms with men. it is also necessary to ensure the participation of women in the decision-making, representation and consultation bodies of the communities involved in shallow-water fishing. at a time of transformation in the sector, important changes are taking place that directly or indirectly affect women and therefore both men and women must be involved in finding solutions. we therefore ask the commission to recommend to the relevant bodies that appropriate measures be taken to ensure a balanced presence of men and women. the lack of gender-disaggregated data makes it very difficult to find solutions to the problems of women working in the sector. we therefore call on the commission, through the european institute for gender equality, to provide a rapid solution to this issue. making these women more visible also means using the right language to reflect that in the fishing sector there are women and men and not just men. i therefore think it is very appropriate, and we support, the proposal, which the rapporteur has just also defended, to change the word 'fishermen' in the title of this report to 'fisheries communities'. ladies and gentlemen, we cannot allow groups such as the women who work in shallow-water fishing to be left unprotected. the committee on women's rights and gender equality calls for greater recognition of the work of these women and for solutions to the specific problems arising from it.
i would like to thank the rapporteur, whom i congratulate on behalf of my group, for his excellent report, which would not have been able to be adopted if he had not had the generosity to accept many amendments and suggestions from other members representing different fishing areas with very different concepts of small-scale fishing. it should be borne in mind that these vessels represent about 80% of all community vessels and that this type of fishing is practised in all coastal member states, although each has its own particular characteristics. it is precisely the treatment of this aspect which seems to me to be one of the best achievements of the report, since it has specified a number of criteria which may be common to most of the small-scale fleet, which in some member states is defined by length, in others by the type of treatment of fishery products, or by distances to the coast, or by the duration of the tides, or by a combination of several criteria. the definition of small-scale fishing, which, as community legislation does, is limited to 12 metres, is therefore a fiction that is not in keeping with reality and which we hope will be amended in the near future in community legislation. it is also important to stress the responsibilities and obligations of this fleet in the conservation of resources, since, although they are small or medium-sized vessels, it must not be forgotten that they are very numerous and operate in waters that are very sensitive to overexploitation, being areas characterized by a high concentration of juveniles. finally, i would like to record an unfinished business that has a large part of the fleet with security. i would like to stress once again that the future european fisheries fund must take account of the need for modernisation and renewal for reasons of safety and also for reasons of energy saving, in order to alleviate the crisis in the fisheries sector caused by the increase in diesel prices. and i do not think that the agreement reached in coreper and which is going to the council of ministers offers all the measures that this parliament called for in the house report on the european fisheries fund (eff), where there were many more measures that would certainly make the situation of renewal and modernisation of small-scale fishing much more flexible.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, in this report the european parliament explicitly recognises the fundamental contribution of shallow-water fishing not only to local economies but also to the maintenance of the social fabric of coastal communities, which is in dire need of cohesive elements. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, our colleague mr ó neachtain, on the happy thought of proposing this own-initiative report at a particularly sensitive time for small communities, which are faced with problems that are urgent and need to be addressed. the first is the ageing of its vessels, whose modernisation needs to be supported further, in particular to improve living and working conditions on board and to establish a safety culture, starting with safer and more modern vessels. the second, the absence of young people. i agree with the rapporteur that a commission initiative on training is needed to encourage young professionals to enter the sector. but the training has to go further. it must include safety at work on board, protection of resources and protection of the sea and coastal areas. low-water fishing, when well regulated, is an essential element of ecosystem conservation. and training must also include improving the quality of catches, marketing and management of small businesses, because these are the issues that can enable small fishermen to consolidate their business results and improve their living standards. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate in particular the rapporteur for the committee on women's rights and gender equality, mrs riera, who has made very valuable contributions which have enriched the report. indeed, women play a key role in the sector and, if well organised, can make an important contribution to the socioeconomic development of fishing-dependent communities.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i join in the general appreciation of the work of my colleague herbert bösch for his tenacity in protecting the community's financial interests and his follow-up of olaf's activities. this year we are therefore pleased - i am particularly pleased with references to aspects of agriculture which affect my country - with the marked improvement in quality and the reduction of fraud in the member states and, in particular, with the success achieved in the smuggling of cigarettes, which shows that the union can impose itself on those multinationals which sometimes seem impossible to control. but this year we also have a new development which is very worrying and which confronts us all - but especially the commission - with a greater responsibility: is the respect for the fundamental rights of the persons under investigation guaranteed? author. - mr president, north korea is sadly still one of the most frequent offenders against human rights. and far from helping to improve its image, certain attitudes of the north korean government only make it worse. an example of this is the repeated decision of the government of the democratic republic of the congo to deny access to the un special rapporteur on the situation of human rights and the un special rapporteur on the right to food, as well as to various humanitarian and human rights ngos. numerous reports warn of the increasing departure of people from the country as refugees, as well as the existence of practices such as torture, summary executions, arbitrary arrests and imprisonment in inhumane conditions and without procedural guarantees of defence. any opposition to the regime is forbidden and any expression of criticism of government policy is harshly prosecuted. the case of sonj nam, who was tortured and sentenced to death, despite repeated calls for the case to be reviewed with greater guarantees, is just one example of this, as has already been mentioned by other speakers. in view of all this, we must once again take this opportunity to call on the north korean government: first, to assume the human rights commitments and principles laid down in international law and to incorporate them into its own legal framework; the president of the council. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i would like to answer the questions briefly. first, the subject of the us summit. i shall start with this subject immediately, since it has been raised by several speakers. you are quite right that we must pay great attention to the transatlantic dialogue and its results. if america and europe work hand in hand and not head to head, then something can really be done. everybody needs to know that. and with all the legitimate, critical aspects of american behavior that you can't just blink an eye and ignore: the american-european friendship and partnership is an important cornerstone for the future. that is my deep conviction. and i want to say that here, even if it's not popular everywhere. (applause from the centre) we are therefore going to make some very important milestones at this summit, for example. firstly, an agreement whereby america and europe will defend themselves against product piracy with very precise concrete actions. we want to cooperate on energy, where the americans are ahead of us. the americans are far ahead of us in research into renewable energy sources, and we will make a joint effort to achieve the kyoto targets, to protect the climate and much more. foreign policy is also important, of course. the middle east, iran, iraq, afghanistan - these are all very important issues, and it is self-evident that we should not lose sight of the long-term goal, such as a transatlantic free trade area and a comprehensive agreement. you can be sure that the subject of human rights, guantanamo and cia overflows will come up naturally. i did that myself when i auditioned in washington in december. i say this also because during the austrian presidency - it is perhaps not so well known that hans winkler was also one of the pioneers and i agreed this with bush in december - we started a dialogue at the level of legal experts - john bellinger from the state department and now the international law office in austria - and we started to work out what to do. because it is clear that there are gaps in international law. and these gaps are going to be debated very intensely in america, right up to the decisions of the highest courts. yesterday an interview with john bellinger was published in the austrian standard, which i find very interesting. we have also been able to eliminate certain elements - and i hope that this will continue to be the case tomorrow - which are very important to me: there must be no legal space! there must be no torture under any circumstances. there must be no kidnapping of people and no detention in secret prisons or detention centres or whatever those fine new-spoken terms are called. this must be said in the knowledge that we can and must do a great deal at the same time - and this is also thanks to the americans - to export democracy, to strengthen ngos and to strengthen civil society. these issues are being addressed. secondly, on transparency: i really don't want to make an austrian campaign because that is not my intention at all, but it is interesting that the austrian greens have all left the hall. i think it is a little unfair to accuse me of not seeking dialogue with the citizens. because the café d'europe was really an attempt to go into everyday life. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. from coudenhove-kalergi to many writers, thinkers and journalists, europe is still made in coffeehouses. to dismiss this as an elite project, if i may say so, is just not right. we also used the new media. i was surprised to see that our own website, future europe, europe hears, had 8 million hits. think about how many politicians have the opportunity to speak directly to 8 million people! we've had 32 million hits on the presidential website. i think we can do more and we should be more confident. this is not about self-praise, it's about professional work with new media. on enlargement: this question is very important to me because i was austrian foreign minister and president of the council in 1998 when we started enlargement. sometimes it was an uphill struggle, an uphill battle. i have sometimes had the majority opinion against us and against my strategy in austria. but we have stood firm and today we have, for example, on the czech republic, which was a very sensitive issue, a majority in favour of the czech republic joining. i'm very pleased. that means it's okay. it is only necessary to advocate for it, and olli rehn, in particular, who has invested a great deal of time and energy, can confirm this. ten years ago, the wage/income gap with the new member states was 10:1. today it's half. this is a win-win situation. we can export, we have hong kong on our doorstep and we can benefit from these growth impulses. we just have to have the courage to stand up and tell people what's going to make a difference, and not just spread bad breath all the time. (applause from the centre) the question of turkey is also part of this. you have to tell the truth. i have fought hard to open negotiations with turkey and to close a chapter. but one thing must be clear: the commitments must be respected. the commitments contained in the ankara protocol must be respected absolutely, and it was not a particularly good sign of european timing to make these declarations last week, which are very disappointing for all those who have been very committed to this european path, to turkey's integration into europe. the second and last point is the constitutional treaty. let me be very frank here. we need some new elements. this is clear to anyone who is fond of this child of european unity born in pain. everybody knows that. i'm not a fan of the term "constitutional treaty". it was a very strange compromise anyway. it is not a constitution, it is not a treaty, it is a constitutional treaty! let's call it something else because it resonates with other things. you should know that. and we're going to need interpretations, of course. that is why this explanation of the messina type is very important. why was the opposition to this constitutional treaty mobilized in part? because there was concern that more liberal or other tendencies were being overemphasized. i disagree. i believe that it contains massive individual social rights. it contains 12 specific fundamental rights which can be challenged before the european court of justice. no one knows. i believe that we must try to put this element of european life and the social model more at the centre. and if we do that, then we're better positioned and we don't have to worry about the critical section. because in the eurobarometer survey, at least - if i read the figures correctly - 63% of european citizens were in favour of such a constitution or treaty. it is not possible for a minority to leave its mark on the whole of europe. it must be possible to reach a common consensus solution, which some of us, of course, object to. of course, that's part of democracy. but it must be possible for the majority to fight for a majority view, and i do. (applause from the centre) this is the real success of the european model, that we become voluntarily curious about our languages. i'm very pleased about the praise that we brought a bit of realism into it. i don't care about the sounding phrases, they're exposed as hot air the day after tomorrow. you have to prepare very professionally for what you have to do, and the finns will do that good luck! exactly like that. matti vanhanen and his team, erkki tuomioja and all the others will do it just like we do and later the germans. but we can still learn a little, not only culturally, but also sportingly from what is happening now. i have just calculated that so far we have played 32 games in the world cup, 20 of them against europe and the rest of the world, that is, against other continents. our record is 12 wins, 4 draws, 4 losses. that's not bad for a global player, and if we replicate that now politically on other levels, then nothing can go wrong.
