vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs sornosa martínez, for her work on this proposal. it is a very important directive. it is part of the community's actions on mercury, the community strategy on mercury was recently debated here in parliament. it's about working together to prevent more mercury from being released into the environment. just so we're clear, we're not talking about any poison here, we're talking about a particularly dangerous one. mercury and its compounds are highly toxic to human health and the environment. the directive we are debating today is aimed at preventing new measuring instruments containing mercury from being placed on the market. we would be able to achieve that 30 tonnes of mercury per year would no longer be able to enter the environment. and 30 tons of mercury is a lot of health hazard! the proposed directive will ban the placing on the market of mercury-containing thermometers altogether, because there are already equally good alternatives. it will also prevent the sale to the general public of all other measuring instruments containing mercury. the proposals were based on a risk assessment and a detailed impact assessment developed for the mercury strategy, followed by consultation with industry and other stakeholders. the directive not only protects human health and the environment but will also serve to preserve and strengthen the internal market, since harmonised rules on the placing on the market of measuring instruments containing mercury apply throughout the community. there are now a number of amendments from your group aimed at derogations. i agree with you that it should indeed be allowed that antique measuring instruments may continue to be marketed. antique measuring instruments are those which are at least 50 years old. antique instruments are largely collector's items, they are handled very carefully because of their value, they are traded in very limited quantities, and the risk of such pieces ending up in the garbage is low. i can also support a temporary derogation for new mercury barometers manufactured by a few small specialist companies. a transitional period of two years will allow these companies to adapt their production to the new regime without creating a disproportionate risk to the environment and health. two years is more than enough. i must make it clear that there is no reason to use mercury in these devices produced by these manufacturers. you can get the same result without mercury, and maybe even better. there is no argument that newly manufactured devices must contain this type of mercury. it is not that a new technology has yet to be developed; the alternatives are already there. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. i am very strict on this point, two years of adjustment period should really be sufficient. the situation is somewhat different with regard to health measurement instruments. it has been proposed here in parliament that blood pressure monitors should be exempted from the restrictions, subject to further review. i think that's the way it should be. blood pressure monitors are still needed in certain medical applications. they are indispensable in certain medical cases where the utmost accuracy of measurement is required. we have been working very hard on this question. medical professionals consider blood pressure monitors of this type to be indispensable, especially in certain life-threatening situations. this means that we should consider extending the rules to the health sector when safe alternatives have been developed for these devices with the same reliability. so we are not at the end of this process, but there is still work to be done here. finally, i would like to note that the negotiating process was characterised by very close cooperation between parliament, the council and the commission. the commission can therefore also agree to all the compromise amendments - that is, paragraphs 12 to 18 - proposed by your rapporteur. i very much hope that we can get this directive adopted at first reading.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we all share the view in this house that the demand for mercury in the manufacture of products must be reduced and its replacement accelerated. it is appropriate to introduce restrictions on the marketing of measuring and monitoring equipment intended for use by private individuals containing mercury at community level, with some exceptions in the health sector. we must prevent considerable amounts of mercury from entering the waste stream. in this way we will contribute to ensuring a higher level of protection of the environment and human health and to the preservation of the internal market, in accordance with article 95 of the treaty. mercury and its compounds are extremely toxic to humans, ecosystems and nature. mercury pollution, which began as a diffuse local problem, is now recognized as a serious, chronic, global problem. as regards the possibility of a total ban on the use of mercury in all measuring devices, which is the subject of this proposal, it should be noted that the experts consulted by the commission came to the conclusion that hospitals need very precise devices to treat potentially life-threatening conditions such as hypertension, arrhythmia and preeclampsia. mercury sphygmomanometers ensure the precision and reliability necessary to preserve patient safety, and so, for the time being, in this proposal, we advocate exempting these instruments from the ban until there are full guarantees in the operation of possible alternative instruments. i would also like to stress to the commission the need to take short-term measures to ensure that all mercury-containing products currently in circulation are separately collected and safely treated, otherwise this directive would lose its practical effect. dumping or improper disposal causes mercury residues to seep into wastewater and disperse into the environment. the presence of mercury in food products is thus observed, with particular risk to the aquatic food chain, making fish and shellfish consumers particularly vulnerable. you have said it, commissioner: 30 tonnes can be treated inadequately in landfills. i also ask the commission to take measures to raise public awareness by organising information campaigns on the health risks of exposure to mercury and the environmental problems that this substance can cause, as i fear that citizens are still not sufficiently informed about its toxicity. as regards the amendments tabled, i was hoping, as were most of the political groups, that there would be agreement, as there has been with the council and the commission, on the barometers. the agreement we have reached concerns the exemption from the obligations of this directive for scientific instruments containing mercury, such as barometers which are more than 50 years old and are intended for sale or trade on the international antiquities market. as regards the production of mercury from new conventional barometers, we proposed an agreement: that there should be a transitional period for manufacturers to adapt to the new standards. unfortunately, not all the political groups have signed it, although i believe that we will have a sufficient majority in this house to approve it. finally, i hope that parliament will endorse the agreement with the council at first reading, so that it can be implemented as soon as possible and thus reduce industrial demand for mercury and speed up its replacement by other materials which are not harmful to human health and the environment. in short, commissioner, i agree with what you have said. i thank the commission for its work and for the possibility of reaching agreement at first reading. i also thank the council and the political groups who support this proposal.
member of the commission. mr president, honourable members, the white paper on financial services policy 2005-2010 sets out a roadmap for opening up europe’s fragmented retail financial services markets. one of the core elements of this strategy is our ongoing initiative on mortgage credit. the challenges of integrating european mortgage markets should not be underestimated. differences in product characteristics, distribution systems, consumer behaviour and many other economic, structural and indeed social factors all have a significant impact on the sector. we should not forget that for most european consumers, taking out a mortgage is perhaps the most significant financial decision in their lives. given the economic and social significance of mortgage lending, the commission has adopted an open and consultative approach. deliberations began in 2003 with the establishment of a forum group on mortgage credit, and a green paper was published in july 2005. a cost-benefit study was published in august 2005 to provide insight into the potential benefits of initiatives in the field of mortgage credit. the public consultation that followed the publication of the green paper confirmed that the commission was on the right track. at the same time, however, it identified areas where further analysis was required, for example on mortgage funding, before the commission could decide on the appropriate policy responses. your report comes at an important moment in our deliberations. the consultation phase is drawing to a close and we are fast approaching a time when the commission must decide how to proceed. i wish to thank the rapporteurs for their hard work in preparing what i believe is a carefully thought-through and pragmatic report. i would like to focus on commission to ensure that actions do not hamper innovation and competition. a wide range of products is currently available to borrowers in the european union. however, in no single country can with parliament on how best to address the policy challenges emerging from this in the interests of assisting the development of a genuine single market for mortgage credit that creates new opportunities for lenders and borrowers alike, and that ensures appropriate protection for what remains for the vast majority of europeans the most important financial decision the make in their lives.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the consumer in respect of the placing on the market of consumer goods. mr president, i think the commission has taken the right approach to mortgage credit because, as the commissioner has said, it is probably the most important commitment that european citizens make in their lifetime: credit to buy their own home. it is therefore necessary to remember that we are moving towards a single market and that in that single market it does not make much sense to have 27 different national laws or 27 different mortgage systems. it is also a matter of the most essential elements of the legal system of each state. therefore, achieving results will not be immediate or easy; it will take some time. in any event, the committee on the internal market and consumer protection would like to stress the importance of making progress in the legislative area. it is not possible, of course, to adopt a complete european union regulation on mortgages, but some progress can be made, for example, in the field of information, maximum authorized rates, repayment of mortgages at a given time, so that when a citizen moves from one country of the european union to another, he does not find himself in a completely different legal environment from the one in which he is accustomed to living.

but nothing would be more dangerous to a fledgling democracy than to artificially manufacture an opposition. it is bad for an aspiring government not to have a strong opposition which will be more responsible and more competent and which will test the government. i'm sure that this kind of opposition will be created as society develops. perhaps one day but i hope not that soon it will prevail in open and fair elections. we have certainly established a political and legal environment in which that can happen. now it is up to opposition groups to take the next step. our path of transformation began with a very simple idea: that every citizen must feel secure. to achieve that, corruption had to be stamped out and that was our major goal. in order to provide a social safety net, we have been aggressive and imaginative in our economic reforms. georgia today is an attractive target for investment. for a country with relatively few natural resources, we are left to work with our own ingenuity and discipline. that's why we have established the lowest tax rates in europe, some of the most flexible labour laws and some of the simplest trade, customs and regulatory procedures. liberal reforms have proven to be the best tool to fight corruption, while guaranteeing the freedom of business and protection of property rights. it has also proven the best way to generate revenue, so that we can build more roads, schools and hospitals. today, i am proud of the fact that two years ago not a single school in georgia had access to the internet, but now 80% of our schools have computers and internet access, and next year the process will be finished. we are building new schools comparable to the best schools in the netherlands, germany or the czech republic. this year we built 340. that's a lot for a small country. more roads have been built this year alone than since independence in 1991. at its annual meeting in singapore this year, the world bank ranked georgia the most successful reformed country in the world and one of the best places in the world to do business. in two years we have switched from being one of the worst to one of the best places in the world to do business. georgian economic growth this year will be strong, since, according to the world bank, we are also the top-performing country among transitional economies in eurasia in fighting corruption. in fact, the ebrd ranks us among the three most non-corrupt nations in europe. maybe other figures will say more about our achievements. the year 2004, the first year after our rose revolution, was the first time since 1991 that we had a positive immigration and birth rate. last year, in a country of just under five million people, almost 100 000 more georgian citizens came back to georgia than left. they were in fact voting with their feet. it is an amazing story. so i don't think europe should be afraid to open up to these areas, because georgians are not going to flee to europe overnight they are coming back. (applause) i would like to thank you. an amazing symbol of this is the main central hospital in tbilisi. it stopped being a hospital and was occupied by internally displaced persons from the war in abkhazia. last year a large team of georgian high-level professionals came from the united states, spain, germany and russia. they re-established the hospital. we helped them and carried out repairs. we provided the idps with assistance to leave and now it is one of the best hospitals in the world. some europeans said that there is only one other hospital of its kind in europe. this is the symbol: georgians like nina gedevanovna ananiashvili, who was a top ballet dancer at the bolshoi, are coming back and trying to recreate our country. she left a very lucrative career with the bolshoi to come back and recreate our ballet group from scratch. it is now a very powerful group, perhaps one of the best in our part of the world, and it will soon be touring worldwide. our goal now is to focus on steady job creation. with my economic advisor mr marklar, former prime minister of estonia, who was one of the architects of the estonian economic miracle, we have established very successful on-the-job training programmes. our reforms in that sector will only be complete when every georgian feels that he or she has a real opportunity for employment. georgia is a country of tremendous warmth, hospitality and beauty. in fact i was just showing president borrell an album of georgian sites. it is a country that european travellers have enjoyed in the past and are now rediscovering. we are, in fact, europe's best kept secret from that point of view. i would like to share with you a brief quote from the writings of sir oliver wardrop, who in 1888 wrote a book entitled the kingdom of georgia. he wrote: there is no reason why georgia should not become a popular resort. it is not so far away as people think. it has the great advantage of being almost unknown to tourists, there is none of the impudent extortion which ruffles our tempers nearer home and it is, after all, cheaper than scotland. please, those of you from scotland, do not be angry with me. i am only quoting. but in fact it is true! (laughter) reviewing the combined effect of our reforms, i believe it is fair to state that these steps have allowed us to move closer to europe institutionally and culturally. you have provided the framework for further growth through the neighbourhood policy. today we will be signing the action plan that translates many of our mutual priorities into detailed results. but in the spirit and the substance of that effort we must continue to build, for i want my country to work with europe so that europe knows it has an utterly reliable partner and friend in georgia. for some, however, our strategy has proven an irritant, and it seems georgia's reform path means we are departing from former and, in their eyes, still applicable spheres of influence. i believe, as you rightly said in your landmark declarations two weeks ago on georgia, that the time of "spheres of influence" is over. (applause) i would like to thank you for that declaration and for the very appropriate and specific language it contained. each nation must have the chance to freely decide how and with whom it wants to build their future. we base our strategy on being a secure and reliable partner, not a tame and weak satellite. we are a nation with a long history of independence. that independence was interrupted 200 years ago with the violent expansion of the russian empire. for three brief years between 1918 and 1921 we enjoyed another moment of independence. that again was taken away from us. what were the circumstances? in 1921 the bolshevik army, claiming to protect a minority population in one of our regions, entered georgia and reconquered it. during that period, more than 500,000 georgians perished in the gulags, including several members of my own family. it was too expensive a price to pay and we are not willing to pay it again. we will not allow that history to be repeated, whatever it takes. after all, we are living in 2006, not 1938 or 1939, 1956 or 1968. at what point are small countries asked to sacrifice their aspirations for liberty? how often can we ask the smaller party to tone down its voice and resist reacting to provocation? let us hope that we will never be asked to succumb and say that justice lies with size, numbers and power in this age, that might makes right and not vice versa. let us hope that never again, when our or any other european nation is threatened, will the spectre of that famous reference by one statesman in the 1930s to "quarrels in a far-away country between people of whom we know nothing" be seen as an adequate response. thankfully, i hope that policy has been left permanently in the past. i hope one day that georgians, as well as proud representatives of that then far-away country the czech republic, will be equals in the european family. (applause) i would like to thank you. today, because we have chosen to move as close as possible to europe and to align ourselves with euro-atlantic institutions, georgia is punished. because we are a democracy, the pressures we are under have only resulted in further consolidation of our society. people who exercise pressure do not understand: you do not pressure democracies, because you get exactly the opposite result from that you want to achieve. that has become increasingly challenging because, as you know, russia has closed its market to georgian goods. our prized georgian wines and mineral water major sources of revenue are now banned from the russian market. the situation has worsened in the last few months as russia unilaterally introduced a complete ban on transport and postal links with georgia. just a few days ago gazprom announced a non-commercial more than doubling of the price georgia must pay for gas. altogether, in plain language, the sum of those measures can be called an economic blockade. i do not wish to use this opportunity to further elevate tensions between georgia and russia, or to see this afternoon as a chance to create anti-russian feeling in the heart of europe. we have enough tensions and enough mudslinging. such rhetoric would serve no constructive purpose. rather, it is now time for diplomacy, discussion, the constructive identification of areas of mutual interest and mutual responsibility. (applause) on behalf of my government and my people, i stand ready to pursue that approach, for it is the only path. let these words once again stand as an open invitation to our colleagues and all interlocutors to return to the path of normality and harmony through dialogue. i believe that the leaders of both countries share the responsibility for making sure that, under our leadership, relations between the two countries do not deteriorate beyond repair. let us move forward with haste and good intentions. like all of you, the people of georgia are not and never will be anti-russian. please allow me to make reference to another great european statesman, konrad adenuaer, who, in his memoirs had this to say about his situation then: we were a small and very exposed country. by our different today, but i could apply some of those words to my country as well. chancellor adenuaer's words still resonate today. our european aspiration is simply to be allowed to develop according to look upon the caucasus. it is generally believed, even by some of those who have been in the country, that transcaucasia is inhabited by a vast number of tribes, more or less wild, having nothing in svan, the pshav, the osset (and the abkhaz), it is sufficient for us to know that all these people are, politically at least, georgians, and have fought under the kartvelian kings since the days of william the conqueror. georgia is a multi-ethnic state and i believe that diversity, that tapestry, is one of our greatest strengths. not a weakness, but a strength. i was proud that just a few days ago i opened a new ossetian language school outside south ossetia, the territory we control, because right now we have twice as many ethnic ossetian language schools outside south ossetia as there are inside. we are still a unitary state, but we are certainly open to all kinds of arrangements under which all minorities are accommodated and there is considerable wide autonomy for all of them, such as the ones in south tyrol and in many other places in europe. for these reasons, our task is to extend our hand in peace, justice and reconciliation, to try and solve our problems through negotiation and compromise so that these areas and all the peoples who call them home can share and be blessed by the same prosperity and guarantees of security enjoyed by the rest of georgia today. some suggest that our separatist problems are simply an internal georgian affair. unfortunately this is not so. our disputes have continued because they are based on recidivist territorial claims remnants from the soviet period when an empire collapsed and elites sought to retain their privilege and fiefdoms. generals fought wars for dachas in abkhazia because that was the main private property in soviet times, and they are still clinging to those dachas. in this scenario, the tactic so visible today is to provide support to local proxies and create institutional blockages to bilateral discussions and negotiation. in this scenario it is the people and future generations born into a climate of fear and hate that lose. my message this afternoon is one of reconciliation, of openness and of recognition and protection of minority rights. we cannot have 19th or 20th century solutions. we appeal to your objectivity, interests, and above all sense of fair play when evaluating these challenges. ladies and to take advantage of our successes and progress to send a positive signal. in the 1990s, russia used the economic blockade to prevent the integration of the baltic states into the european union, member of the commission. to be successful, any action on migration and development must be comprehensive and integrated, and we must use our short and medium-term financial instruments and engage in pillars. first of all, it is a question of responding to the urgency of the situation by mobilising the instruments available: i am thinking of the b package and the rapid reaction mechanism. for reception to facilitate the reintegration of irregular migrants returning to their country of origin. financial support for national and regional programmes for the reintegration of migrants. promote information and awareness campaigns for potential migrants on the risks of illegal immigration. i would like to add, however, at the risk of sounding a little out of date, that it is obviously necessary to ensure that any accompanying and reintegration measures do not manifestly favour migrants who return to their country over those who do not leave. otherwise, you will obviously have a knock-on effect and i think it is extremely important to ensure that. finally, in the long term, and we know this, the real answer is a policy of training and employment for young people which the european community supports, inter alia, through its support for economic integration policies, through the negotiation of economic partnership agreements designed to attract investment and increase economic growth, which are the necessary conditions for the creation of attractive jobs. these policies are at the heart of the development priorities and strategy for africa. i must tell you that from this point of view, i am one of those who think that if growth does not necessarily lead to poverty reduction, it is certain that there is no poverty reduction without growth: we must remember this. so i am convinced that the long-term answer is to promote economic partnership agreements, to support the emergence of integrated regional markets which, moreover, can go hand in hand with etc. in conclusion, madam president, i would like to make a rather personal digression which is worth reflecting on. there are immediate measures which must be taken and which, unfortunately, are policies, which are development policies. in addition to these immediate measures and policies, i wonder whether it would not be useful to start thinking about what i shall call accompanied migration. it's not about quotas, an old idea, which i'm not very keen on at the moment. i imagine, for example, that we could fund migration agencies in the countries of origin of the flows, agencies which could inform applicants for migration, which could also work with the western european countries where there are job opportunities, without encouraging the brain drain which is another of my concerns. phenomenon. there's always been migration. it is as if europe were suddenly discovering a phenomenon which had not existed before. ever since the world was created, there have been migrations. i'm rapporteur. – mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the colleagues who helped me draw up this report, and especially the members of the committee on culture and education. i also wish to thank commissioner figeľ, who has kept in contact with us, for his positions on plurality and on the issues related to minority languages, etc. thanks are also due to all the other colleagues, from several groups, and other people involved in the report, especially the members of the various ngos for the normalisation of languages who were in contact with us during the preparation of the report. i would like to mention in particular vicent santaló, a member of the legal staff at the catalan parliament, who worked with us until his death last summer. the main aim of this report is to move forward the concept of plurality in languages. plurality and diversity are common values of the european union. there should be unity among all europeans in this area, which should have plurality as one of its main aims, because a non-plural europe is a false and devalued europe. this is reflected in a certain manner in languages. as you know, in sociolinguistic terms there are ‘normalised’ languages, which are the fully official languages used in all walks of our lives. there are also ‘minorised’ languages, which are not fully official and cannot be used for every purpose, despite the fact they are the main languages in specific language communities. there is also a third group, which is that of minority languages. all these groups must be respected and preserved, and the preservation of language diversity is one of the aims of the european institutions. europeans are not as multilingual as we think. unfortunately, many european citizens have only one language – usually their mother tongue – and one of the main goals of the european union is to have a citizenship able to speak several languages. in order to achieve that, it is very important for there to be a change in mentality. our society was formed under the influence of jacobinist states. most european states are unilingual officially, and this is a remnant of jacobinism. however, this is not a true reflection of the facts. the aim of the european union is not to maintain this point of view, but to preserve genuine plurality and work towards citizens being able to speak several languages. we need a european language policy. that policy should promote multilingualism, improve the language skills of european citizens across the european union and preserve all languages, whether or not they are official eu languages. to this end, the budget and european programmes must support not just the main languages, but all languages, in order to improve diversity. in this way we must make a special effort to support endangered languages. every language is good for mankind, and if a language is lost we have all lost something because each language has its own unique expressions. it is for this reason that we must preserve genuine plurality and true diversity. in this sense, it is necessary to draw up a full report on the actions still to be developed.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to see that a framework strategy for multilingualism in the european union has been launched. our motto 'united in diversity' is a testament to the importance of the diversity of cultures, customs, beliefs and also languages in the construction of the union. the charter of fundamental rights has made respect for linguistic diversity one of our basic values. this principle applies not only to the official languages but also to the many regional and minority languages spoken in the union, including those of immigrant communities. this rich coexistence of different linguistic communities in europe sometimes results in extraordinary difficulties in the practice of daily work in the community institutions. regardless of the fact that all languages are equally important from a cultural point of view, i think it would be wrong to think that the institutions of the european union can function by using all of them at the same level. in my view, progress in promoting, defending and making known this linguistic diversity must be supported by the member states' pursuit of active policies to promote and defend their languages at educational level and in the more social sphere, including the media, and by promoting the learning of at least two foreign languages, with the aim of facilitating the knowledge of other cultures, encouraging mobility and contributing to awareness of european citizenship. finally, in the community institutions, it is a question of making it possible for citizens to communicate with the union in their mother tongue. and to make the use of mother tongues compatible with the day-to-day work of the institutions, it is necessary to establish different uses of the different languages and this is where we must work to agree on the basic criteria we use to agree on these working languages, without leaving out any element, either cultural or in relation to the number of speakers or the status of the languages in their respective states. i hope that the new commissioner for multilingualism, mr leonard orban, will share this idea and work in this direction.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, in the minute i have to speak, i want to support in a clear and explicit way the report presented by my colleague, mr joan i marí. if the european union is to live up to its slogan 'united in diversity', it must take multilingualism beyond the official languages as a flagship. just as the protection of biodiversity is and should be a core value in today's societies, so too the protection of linguistic diversity must be understood as a core element of progress, the promotion of peace and development. given that the violation of cultural, linguistic and identity rights is at the root of many of today's armed conflicts, it is urgent to see the promotion of multilingualism as a tool for promoting dialogue, encounter and peace. and if this is important in the world in general, it is especially so in a european union which, being already a union of values, aspires to be, one day, a political union. promoting multilingualism in europe therefore means wealth and progress. tending towards monolingualism, on the other hand, will make us poorer.
mr president, in its first communication on multilingualism, the european commission set three absolutely reasonable objectives a year ago: to promote language learning and linguistic diversity, to promote a multilingual economy, thereby improving labour mobility and the competitiveness of the european economy, and to provide all citizens with access to information about the union in their own language. the close link between this communication and the overall european objective, which we set at the barcelona council in 2002, of ensuring that children learn at least two foreign languages in addition to their mother tongue, will be obvious to everyone. that is precisely what the report which this parliament will vote on tomorrow should be about, offering the 450 million european citizens a wide range of tools to enable them to learn languages and thereby benefit from the enormous social, economic and cultural advantages of participating in our great project of integration, a project rich in national histories, languages and cultures, which today represents a dream of unity in diversity, for the benefit of all citizens. the rapporteur's opportunistic attempt to use this report to promote nationalistic and particularist approaches is highly inappropriate and completely distorts the meaning of the communication. in this respect, the work of the committee on culture and education is to be commended, which has responsibly and sensibly revised the original text and its ideologically biased approach with its amendments. it is enough to say that the rapporteur's intention was radical, since he ended up opposing his own report in the committee vote. respect for diversity is a principle of the union, but the use of languages to disintegrate member states on ethnic or linguistic grounds is nonsense and the people's group will always oppose it with all our strength.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i fully share the statement by commissioner mandelson and, as rapporteur for the report on the generalized system of preferences, i also stress the importance of the gsp plus as an incentive to engage the most vulnerable developing countries in sustainable development and good governance. i welcome the commission's decision of 21 december to grant its benefits to 15 countries which requested them and the steps taken subsequently by countries such as colombia, venezuela and el salvador in ratifying important ilo conventions. i would like to draw attention to three fundamental points concerning the way the system works. first, the purpose of the gsp plus is to promote, inter alia, human and labour rights through trade. this partnership is essential and must not be lost. trade must be an incentive for human and labour rights; protectionist deviations from this objective must be avoided. secondly, the success of the system requires an increase in the number of beneficiary countries. one of the commission's priorities must be to increase this significantly, since these countries now represent only 3% of the world's population. thirdly, the effectiveness of the system must be ensured by intelligent implementation, involving the european parliament. it is important that the commission cooperates with the beneficiary countries in fulfilling their commitments, through various initiatives and in particular by strengthening the monitoring and evaluation of their implementation, in a rigorous and regular manner, with transparency and involvement of the main social actors and the beneficiary countries, as stated in the parliament's report. the penalties provided for should also be applied where there are serious and systematic breaches of the principles, thus punishing the offenders but not the operators who comply adequately with their commitments. finally, as the motion for a resolution reiterates, the commission must prepare a study before the next revision of the regulation to assess the impact of the system, analyse its operation and assess the reforms that are being carried out.

mr president, the basic motto of the european union is 'united in diversity'. and it is that from its origins we are trying to build a common space, not only economic, but, above all, a space of opportunity for life and freedom. and we are doing it between people and nations who have a lot in common; i do not mean only the strategic, political and social interests we share, but also values, behaviours and ways of understanding life itself. we have a common cultural background, coined in greek thought, roman law, christianity, the reformation, the enlightenment, the renaissance and even globalism. but at the same time it is indisputable that we still maintain particular cultural and identity differences, and especially languages and dialects. this diversity, which might be seen only as an obstacle, turns out to be a great wealth and a source of vitality. that is why, although it has not been adopted, i have voted in favour of the proposal to amend the treaty on european union so that there can be community legislation on the respect and protection of languages, particularly minority languages, and the creation of a european agency for linguistic diversity and multilingualism. i also voted in favour of encouraging all european citizens to learn at least two other languages in addition to their own, as a better way of promoting mutual understanding, coexistence and unity.

mr president, the development of the european security strategy was influenced by three major debates on an international scale: the new threats it had to face and how to deal with them, especially after 9/11, the difficulties of the united nations as a multilateral and universal forum for preventing and managing disputes, and the commitments the european union must make in order to become a or, if you like, a complement to the 25 existing armies, and not as a replacement, as i think it should be. although we seem to agree that large numbers of national armies are no longer necessary to meet the challenges of today, we still have 25 national armies in the european union, totalling some two million personnel, whose first and foremost mission is to defend the borders and interests of the states and which together cost more than eur 160 million a year. on the other hand, we would like to see figures that are equally dedicated to conflict prevention and management. in short, the facts and the decisions of governments do not seem to be keeping pace with the paradigm shift in security that we are experiencing in recent times, especially at european level.
vice-president of the commission. madam president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate mr gargani and the committee he chairs on having put forward a proposal which, if approved by this house - as i hope - will not be translated into a legislative proposal. i too would like to start with a statement. we have worked for a long time to understand the thinking of legal practitioners, experts in the field, but above all the citizens of the european union, as regards the possibility of having an instrument which clearly identifies the applicable law and thus makes it possible to facilitate the creation of a genuine european area in the field of successions and wills. a eurobarometer survey carried out in july 2006 on the various aspects of family law in europe showed that an average of 80% of european citizens believe that the recognition of last wills is necessary throughout europe. there are of course countries where the consensus is even stronger: for example, in germany, a large founding country, and in latvia, a smaller country, there was a 92 per cent consensus in favour of such legislation. in my country, italy, 88 percent, as well as in hungary. there was therefore a broad response, with an average of four fifths of european citizens in favour of facilitating the european regulation of wills. in march 2005, the commission published a green paper on the subject, which enabled us to collect hundreds of responses of great interest from academic circles, the judiciary and the relevant actors. we also got a lot of good ideas from the hearing on transnational successions, which parliament had the good idea of organising. i should also like to inform you that the commission has itself organised a public hearing on the same subject, to be held on 30 november, which will enable us to gather further ideas which, together with the report by mr gargani, will, in my view, enable us to submit a legislative proposal soon. the last point i want to make is the one which president gargani has already mentioned, namely the european certificate of succession. i also believe, as does the rapporteur, that if we want a european instrument to be truly effective, it must have binding effect within the european territory. in this connection, many of you will recall other instruments of private international law on which we have reached agreement. if a given instrument, once adopted in one member state, could be called into question each time in the other member states where it is to be applied, since it does not have binding effect, one of the cornerstones of the area of free movement of decisions would be undermined. it could of course be objected that a certificate of succession, as such, always has a binding value, because otherwise it could not certify situations. i think it is appropriate to stress the binding nature of this directive in this case, because we are creating, perhaps for the first time, a useful instrument for solving the problem of circulation between european citizens, which is also expressed through the recognition of last wills, that is, successions and wills. i therefore take the liberty of expressing in advance an opinion which is in full agreement with that of mr gargani.
on behalf of the pse group. madam president, mr gargani has presented us with a report which expresses the desire of the committee on legal affairs to see the european institutions intervene in the field of succession law. commissioner frattini pointed out that 80% of european citizens believe that the law of succession should be regulated and recognised in a uniform manner throughout the european union. we are not talking about theories, but about the realities of people living in different countries, who have families in different countries and who, when the succession event occurs, find themselves in an absolutely desperate situation. unfortunately, the treaties of the european union do not provide for the possibility of harmonising substantive law in matters of succession. it is something that will probably have to be rectified in the future, because it is difficult to understand that the consequences, the legal system, the rights of heirs, change completely because of the fact of crossing a few kilometres, depending on whether a person settles in one country or another. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. commissioner frattini has expressed the commission's willingness to do so. we probably can't get much further at this point. in the committee on legal affairs we have discussed the merits and content of the proposals which mr frattini includes in the annex; there are some amendments tabled by my socialist colleague, mrs maria berger, which are aimed at correcting some of the shortcomings which are found in that annex, but the most important thing is that the commission, as mr frattini has said here, is prepared to make concrete proposals. it is a subject on which improvisation is not possible, since we must rely on our experience. anyone who has ever had to deal with the problem of international succession within the european union will have encountered tremendous difficulties, especially of a judicial nature. it is probably necessary to start addressing the issue from the point of view of jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of courts, the recognition and effectiveness of decisions, by eliminating, as mr gargani recommends, the 'exequatur' procedure, which has no meaning in the european union. i hope, therefore, that the efforts of mr gargani and the contribution of mr frattini will enable us to have concrete proposals on the table soon for the development of community law in this area.

the rapporteur. - mr president, when mrs wallström gave the european parliament the white paper on a european communication policy and i was informed that she had the honour of being the rapporteur for the report on that book, a journalist friend of mine who works here in the european parliament told me that the best thing i could do was to make a very short report, with only one point to say: 'mrs wallström, the only purpose of this book is to use it as gift paper, because it is an exercise of goodwill, but useless'. and i said to my friend, "i think you're unfair. i think mrs wallström is trying to make a good information and communication policy and, moreover, call me naive, i have seen with her on several occasions that this is her purpose. the circumstances in which an information and communication strategy in the european union needs to be articulated do not exist today. so why don't you give? because there is no legal basis to enable us to articulate this information and communication strategy and, therefore, to enable us to set out actions and monitor them properly. so let us go one step further - as i said when i was making this report - and try to make things different from what they have been until now, because every time we meet to discuss information and communication strategy, we make a kind of general set of recommendations which are always toasted to the sun. let's try to get what we don't have yet. let us have that legal basis which will enable us to act much more effectively in the future. i have done some research and found that there is only one way to achieve this legal basis: the application of article 308 of the treaty. when i was told the circumstances in which this article could be applied, i was tempted to say 'it's impossible, we're not going to get it'. because three very difficult conditions must be met: first, the commission must ask for it; secondly, parliament must agree; and thirdly, and this is the most difficult, the council must approve it unanimously. i spoke to mrs wallström and she said that the commission was in agreement. i spoke to all the alternative rapporteurs and they said that parliament could agree. and we had the opportunity to hear the view of the minister in the interinstitutional group, who was at that time acting as the council's representative, and who told us that she was in a position, not to guarantee that, because she cannot do that, but to believe that unanimity could be achieved in the council. we are therefore faced with a circumstance in which an astral conjunction occurs which is very difficult to re-occur again. and in politics the most important thing is to take advantage of the circumstances that the moment presents. we have an opportunity now that we will probably not have again in the future. a very good opportunity to improve, to have a legal basis. it does not mean that it is the panacea or the cure for all our ills, but it is clearly going to be progress. and we have only two choices: either we accept it or we reject it. my proposal is that we accept it. mrs prets, christa, i ask you, please, to help me, because i know that your party, because of mr corbett's intervention, is going to vote against the application of article 308. mr corbett believes there is another formula for obtaining a legal basis. there isn't one. and if there is, tell me which one. let's negotiate it. let's talk about it. no amendment from the committee on constitutional affairs has given us an alternative. gérard onesta, the rapporteur for this report, to mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in the debate on this report we are again looking at the distance between the community institutions and the citizens and how to reduce it. i believe that, while acknowledging the great effort made by the commission and parliament to deal with this distance, it is absolutely essential to have the complicity of the media and the national parliaments. there is a widespread feeling that the media in the member states consider what is happening here to be neither news nor of interest to the general public. the first thing we should do is to involve the media more directly, so that they can help us to translate and bring the community dimension closer to the citizens without technical problems. with this complicity, we would probably also be able to broadcast the news of the european union at prime time in the media programme. we must make it easier for these professionals to do their job, and we must simplify and make procedures more transparent: we must be complicit and work together with the national parliaments so that they can convey the issues of concern at national, regional and local level and thus generate feedback which normally incorporates questions of european policy. on the other hand, i think it is right to continue to rely on the internet as one of the main providers of community information. however, the internet only reaches a part of the public, which is already interested. we have another audience, which only accesses the traditional media - television and radio - through their respective national, regional or local channels or stations. in this field, new technologies can open up a new horizon, integrating different services and products that can facilitate the transmission of information in a multimodal way, thus broadening the target audience.
mr president, on 1 february 2006 the commission presented the white paper on a european communication policy, and mr herrero's report, which was approved by a large majority in the committee on culture and education, takes up the main guidelines suggested by the commission, but introduces a major innovation, which has given rise to a serious and thorough debate, both in this parliament and at interinstitutional level. the report by mr herrero, in paragraph 10, calls on the commission to explore the possibility of launching a european information and communication programme, in accordance with article 308 of the treaty. as vice-president responsible for information and communication in this parliament, i have followed this debate very closely and i must point out that the interinstitutional group has given a positive assessment to the creation of a legal basis and that all the institutions, as mr herrero reminded us, have also shown their support. my conclusion is that it's worth a try. i am aware of the reservations raised by this proposal, all based on the loss of control by parliament, which is curious, ladies and gentlemen, because it is difficult to lose what you do not have. however, three things must be kept in mind. firstly, the report makes it clear that if the commission submits a proposal, parliament must be fully involved in the elaboration of its content; secondly, parliament has the powerful tool of budgetary control; and thirdly, there is the interinstitutional group on communication, whose mandate is to set the basic guidelines of communication policy. we must shed our complexes and create a communication strategy that is able to present, explain and defend europe through reason, but also with enthusiasm, passion and emotion. i therefore wholeheartedly support mr herrero's report and his proposal to create a programme on the basis of article 308 of the treaty.

institutions. the treaty of nice was a marathon, and it resulted in a treaty which was considered unsatisfactory from an institutional point of view. that treaty, the treaty of nice, was rejected by the irish people in a referendum in 2001. but the irish prime minister took up the challenge of an intensive public information campaign and got ireland to approve the treaty of nice in a second referendum 18 months later in 2002. the european parliament welcomed this and congratulated him warmly. he then presided over the european council during the intergovernmental conference on the constitutional treaty in june 2004. those of us who were at the convention remember his pilgrimage through various european capitals in search of a delicate compromise which he finally succeeded in prime minister of ireland. president borrell, it is a great honour to be here again. i am very grateful for the invitation to exchange views on the future of europe with all the members of the european parliament today. as someone who has spent more than half of my lifetime as a member of parliament, i cherish this renewed opportunity to address the only directly elected, multinational legislative body in the world. since i last addressed you in 2004, the constructive influence of the european parliament in advancing the concerns of europe’s citizens has continued to grow. your vision is needed as we face the difficult challenges ahead. i wish you every success, mr president, for the remainder of your term of office. i also wish your successor well. i wish you continued success and congratulate you on all that you have achieved. we look forward in particular to your visit to dublin in the days ahead as part of the forum for europe, into which we have put an enormous amount of effort. i thank you for your kind remarks about the forum for europe. it is not a government body: it represents all the organisations in the country and it is hugely successful. you do us an enormous honour by coming to address it. explaining europe to the public remains probably our greatest challenge, at both european and national level. therefore, mr president, i particularly welcome and look forward to this discussion and to discussions with you in the days ahead. you will be visiting a country that has benefited enormously from its membership of the european union. some key facts stand out. since we joined europe in 1973, our national wealth stood at just 60 per cent of the european average at that stage. even after accession, we were plagued by emigration, unemployment, high inflation and spiralling debt. these dismal conditions have been completely reversed in recent years. the role of the european union was vital to all of that. europe provided invaluable assistance to us at a critical period in our national development. the phrase ‘the future of europe’, like so many phrases, has become part of our jargon. but let us recall for a moment the significance of what those words ‘the future of europe’ really mean, for ourselves and for the wider world. for our own people in europe, as we approach the 50th anniversary of the treaty of rome, it means consolidating and developing our extraordinary union – a union which has been so successful that many now take its success for granted. in a world which knows so much uncertainty, oppression, deprivation and violence, the union is a bedrock of prosperity, stability and deep-rooted democracy. the very essence of the european union – this powerful blend of pragmatism, of patience and vision – was captured by robert schuman when he observed that: ‘europe will not be made all at once, or according to one single plan: rather it will be formed by taking concrete measures which bring about real solidarity.’ our union is not, and must never become, an inward looking one. from 1 january we will be a union of 27 with the very welcome accession of bulgaria and romania. we will remain open to further enlargement in line with our commitments, our responsibilities and our principles. we also have growing responsibilities in relation to the wider international community. it is indeed a paradox that, at a time when we appear to be unsure internally of the precise direction which the future development of our union should take, our role externally has never been more important or more clear. the wider world increasingly looks to europe for leadership, for support and for the promotion of our values. the founding fathers of europe would be proud to see the europe of today – what we are and what we bring to our world. however, they would insist that our benchmark must be set not against where we have come from, but rather against what we must still achieve. today europe faces as great an array of challenges as ever, including globalisation, technological change, migration, energy security and terrorism. these challenges have not been dreamed up in brussels or strasbourg: they have risen up the union’s agenda because they are very real and directly relevant to all our citizens. the challenge must not only be met but also addressed in a way which reassures our citizens and responds to their anxieties and aspirations. the union, in approaching these issues, is rightly pursuing two broad parallel tracks. in respect of both tracks, the role of the european parliament will be crucial. on the one hand, we are continuing to reflect on the question of the constitutional treaty and we will return to it next june on the basis of a report by chancellor merkel. on the other hand, we are seeking to address the concerns of our citizens in practical ways under the existing treaties. both of these tracks are essential. we cannot put practical progress on hold; neither can we wish away the need to provide the union with a coherent, streamlined basis for addressing the challenges of a new century. the constitutional treaty is designed to provide a much-needed basis for practical progress; and the practical progress we strive for will continue and contribute to a positive context for reaching agreement on the urgent institutional questions. i would like to address these two twin issues in turn. nobody can predict with any certainty what the future holds for the constitutional treaty. there is, of course, no easy answer. i would, however, like to share with you briefly my own reflections and i look forward greatly to hearing your own perceptions in this afternoon’s debate. a good starting point for trying to evaluate what lies ahead is often to reflect briefly on why and how we got to be where we are today. history is important because it can help us to make wise choices about the future. since the irish presidency had the privilege of bringing the intergovernmental conference negotiations to a conclusion, i have a particular awareness of the processes which made that agreement possible. so let me start by recalling what seem to be three fundamental realities about the situation we have reached. first, it is important to remember that the constitutional treaty was agreed because it was necessary. the need for the substantive provisions has grown rather than diminished. we need its more coherent external policy to meet our growing international responsibilities. we need its subtle, balanced and effective provisions in the area of justice and home affairs to strengthen our fight against crime. we need its more open, comprehensible, democratic and effective procedures, including its significantly enhanced role for the european parliament. we need its principles and its values. moreover, apart from the constitutional treaty’s specific elements, we need it because the long term stability, prosperity and coherence of europe are of fundamental importance for our people as well as for people beyond our borders. second, the process which led to the agreement of the constitutional treaty was long, complex and difficult. the convention was unprecedented in its openness and achievement. the european parliament was highly influential at the convention, which also benefited greatly from the direct involvement of national parliaments. the subsequent igc involved intensive bilateral and collective negotiations in which the views of each member state, as well as of the commission and parliament, were taken very carefully into account. the process leading to agreement was a comprehensive and inclusive one. i visited every capital, as the president kindly recalled, and everyone was listened to and helped to shape the outcome. third, participants were in the end able to accept the outcome of the negotiations because they saw it as a balanced overall package. the institutional provisions in particular were closely interrelated and formed a single whole. the difficulties of moving forward with the constitutional treaty are significant, but any analysis of what europe needs, of how we got to where we are today and of the alternatives convince me that the right and realistic option is to return at the appropriate time to the substance and balance of the constitutional treaty. i understand that this is also broadly the view of this parliament. in moving forward, we must ensure that the basis for progress must be an inclusive one in which the concerns and views of all are taken into account, including the legitimate concerns expressed by the citizens in many member states. chancellor merkel will be consulting closely with each member state and with the institutions. i have no doubt that her report to the june european council will be soundly based and well judged. however, let me at this stage offer four reflections. first, we must continue to work to change the context in which we will return to consider the constitutional treaty. this means continuing to address, as effectively as we can, the concerns of our citizens on issues from employment to mobile phone charges, from enlargement to the fight against crime. that is what you, the directly elected representatives of the people of europe, do so effectively week-in, week-out. second, the 50th anniversary of the treaty of rome next march offers an important opportunity to highlight for our citizens the achievements and potential of the union. a succinct, consensual and eloquent declaration on that occasion, in the name of the council, the commission and the european parliament, could represent a very positive element in creating a new context for our wider institutional debate and perhaps also in addressing some of the specific concerns which have arisen in the national debates on the constitutional treaty. third, as was the case on previous occasions when european treaties ran into difficulties at national level, additional elements could be introduced to address concerns that have arisen. such additions could enrich rather than undermine the substance and balance of the treaty. fourth, the presentation, the length and, in some respects, the nature of the constitutional treaty could also be amended significantly without affecting its basic substance and balance. to give some examples, it could be brought out more clearly that what is involved is a treaty and that, in many respects, it essentially amends rather than replaces the existing treaties. for the irish government’s part, we remain resolutely and enthusiastically committed, as soon as the situation has been fully clarified, to holding a referendum on the substance of the constitutional treaty. the treaty remains important for europe, for our people and for those who look to our values. as i said at the outset, it is essential that europe also pursue the second track which we have set for ourselves, namely addressing, as best we can under the existing treaties, the priorities of our citizens. i believe it is important to maintain broadly the distinctiveness of the two tracks. we should be wary of the selective advance application of elements which form part of the balance in the constitutional treaty. let us not be unduly pessimistic about what we have achieved so far in terms of practical progress. the european economy is gaining in strength. more people are in work. an enlargement of historic proportions, which not long ago seemed unimaginable, has taken root and has greatly enriched our union. but we are not here, at either european or national level, to congratulate ourselves. the successful football club is not the one that focuses on the trophy room: it is the one that focuses on the matches ahead. one only has to look at the agenda of any of your parliamentary sessions to appreciate the range and depth of the challenges we face. time requires me to address what seem to be the strategic underlying challenges. allow me to address briefly five of those challenges. first, there is the competitiveness challenge. this has many important european dimensions: better regulation, a strong and appropriate competition policy, research and development, the removal of barriers in the internal market, and perhaps above all innovation, in relation to which the proposed european institute for technology can make an important contribution. our objective should be to make europe attractive for investment. i have repeatedly stressed to my colleagues in the european council and to the commission that europe is increasingly in competition not within itself but with other parts of the world, notably asia. the reality of this competition must give urgency as well as direction to the development and implementation of policies at european level. our second strategic objective should be to ensure that achieving competitiveness does not threaten the european social model, and that competitiveness and social inclusion are partners, not rivals. this is the key principle underpinning our own national system of social partnership. our experience of extensive and intensive social dialogue has delivered 18 consecutive years of economic growth, improved living standards and greater social inclusion. in our approach at european level, including where appropriate through legislation, we should reflect the principle that economic and social policies can and should be mutually reinforcing. we must, above all, ensure that solidarity and opportunity are at the heart of the union and must drive europe’s future. the test of europe’s credibility today is whether it can deliver policies which build up solidarity within the european union and secure opportunities for all our people. i also strongly believe that we need to give greater substance to the social dialogue at european level. at both european and national level, we must engage the social partners, in particular the trade unions, in a real debate on the reform of the european social model and on the modernisation of labour markets. our third strategic challenge is to confront the downsides of globalisation, including cross-border crime, human trafficking, illegal migration, and the scourge of illicit drugs that ruin so many lives. we know about the potential for pollution to trigger calamitous climate change. of course, the responsibility in many of these areas falls significantly on the member states. but as long as our climate and our criminals do not stop at the borders between our countries, we must work together to ensure all appropriate action at european level. fourth, europe must play its full role across the range of its external competences. i shall not dwell on this further because i have already highlighted in my introduction the increasingly important role which the union plays and is expected to play in the international arena. it is, of course, essential that europe is adequately funded, including in the cfsp area, for addressing its growing responsibilities in the western balkans, in our wider neighbourhood and further afield, especially towards the poorest who need our support and to whom europe should continue to strive to be a special friend. the fifth, and perhaps greatest strategic challenge is – i am sure you would agree – to connect europe better with its citizens. of course, this challenge is not unrelated to the other challenges. we can only communicate a positive message if we have a positive message to communicate. but we have to demonstrate clearly that europe is part of the solution to globalisation, not part of the problem. we have to show that the european social model remains at the heart of increased competitiveness. our people must not only be secure but also feel secure. we need to act, but we also need to explain what europe is doing and can do to provide security for our citizens. we have to bring home much more effectively to the public that, through our external policies, we are increasingly and effectively promoting their interests, their priorities and their values. i fully accept that a large part of the responsibility of explaining europe accurately and fairly falls at national level. it is certainly a priority for my government. respect for diversity can play a particularly important part in connecting the union with its citizens. i thank you, mr president, for announcing that today is the first day that irish will be used and that from 1 january 2007 it will become the 21st language of the european union. ní fhéadfadh aon rud meas na heorpa ar charachtar indibhidiúil a cuid ballstát a léiriú níos fearr ná an stádas feabhsaithe a bheas ag an ngaeilge ó 1 eanáir. tá europe, when it was founded half a century ago, was the determination to bring permanent peace ‘among peoples long divided by bloody conflicts’, as the first treaty put it. the union has been resoundingly successful in that aim within our borders. the union is also an increasingly important factor for stability beyond our borders. i would like to pay particular tribute to the fact that the articulation of mechanisms to ensure the participation of smes in all the actions of the programme. a minimum target of 15% of the total budget has been set for their participation and the maximum contribution of all community institutions, including the european investment bank, has been sought in the financing of projects involving their participation. our proposal enshrines the principle of scientific and technological cohesion as one of the objectives of the programme and points out the need to seek maximum complementarity and synergy with other national and regional european funds. mechanisms are required to establish joint approaches to scientific and technological issues of interest to more than one theme and also mechanisms to address complex issues of thematic priorities specific programme 'cooperation' by this parliament. these new instruments for technical and financial management and participation in the specific programme 'cooperation' required mechanisms to the rapporteur. - thank you, mr president. i thank mr potočnik for his open and cooperative attitude; i thank mr buzek and all the other alternate rapporteurs. we are all part of the family of the seventh framework programme, and in this family there has been a long, hard birth, with few sanitary facilities, but the baby has been born healthy, although a little underweight. because when will we realise that european research is even more important than agricultural subsidies and the building of motorways? it is not a rhetorical question; we must ask ourselves coldly what the priority is for the future of europe, this europe which wants but cannot. we have set out some challenges with this framework programme and we have largely covered them. we have made some progress in opening up science, in achieving the maximum transfer of scientific knowledge and technical information and in supporting all incentives that encourage the transfer of technology, so that companies, civil society and universities can develop bridges between research and the necessary economic and technological renewal in today's european societies, thanks to this communication and thanks to the rules on the mandatory publication of results, the promotion of free software or the obligation, for example, to promote interoperability; we have made some progress, but we must continue to make progress. we also have to ask ourselves whether we are going to do science for and for people, because the opinions of researchers have to be in line with those of those who are not necessarily experts. in this connection, we should express our satisfaction at the support and important work of the science and society section of this programme, the financial reinforcement of this area and the opening up of the programme to civil society organisations. i also wonder whether small is beautiful in european science, because we all talk about smes, but is that empty rhetoric or a firm commitment? mr president, in the fight against hiv/aids we are indeed still far from victory; however, victory is possible simply with political will. the numbers are clear: the vast majority of new infections occur in developing countries, making hiv one of the main factors currently holding back progress in thousands of towns and communities. this is a global emergency, both from the health, social and economic point of view. today we know what the problem is and we know how to prevent it and how to treat it. but this requires resources, political responsibility, responsibility of the economic sectors and social and cultural responsibility. among other measures, for example, it is necessary to ensure universal access to essential medicines, something which is not yet possible today because of the greed of certain economic sectors, especially the pharmaceutical industry, which has no scruples in this matter, thus becoming clear co-responsible for a mass murder on a global scale. in addition, certain discourses by ultraconservative sectors against sexual and reproductive health are also responsible for this situation. to oppose today, for example, with the information we have, that everyone, and especially younger people, have proper sex education is, no matter how you look at it, an attack on life and dignity and, of course, immorality. and so, one more year, it is time to demand action, commitment and, above all, that promises be kept.
