the next item is the report by elizabeth lynne, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the situation of people with disabilities in the enlarged european union: european action plan 2006-2007 (2006/2105 (ini)).
madam president, commissioner špidla, ladies and gentlemen, today is an important day for this house, and that is why i want to congratulate mrs lynne on her report, because we are taking another step in building the europe of opportunities for which we are working. today we will adopt with broad agreement new measures to advance equal opportunities for people suffering from some form of disability. i believe that this new european action plan 2006-2007 is a great challenge to eliminate all forms of discrimination and also addresses the needs of people with disabilities throughout europe. i will highlight a number of points. firstly, it seeks to establish a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation, not only in education and access, but also in promotion and continuing training. secondly, it certainly improves the conditions and rights of disabled passengers in the use of air, sea and land transport. but i must warn - and i did so in the report - against creating a new and hitherto non-existent barrier: the economic barrier. the compulsory accompaniment of disabled people is a positive factor in improving the quality of their travel, but it is not the case that the disabled person has to pay for the ticket of the person accompanying him, because in that case these people would have to pay for two tickets, while the rest of us would only pay for one. thirdly, improving access to new technologies. new technologies could, without a doubt, break down many barriers for people with disabilities, provided we achieve universal access to them and provided that technological advances take these people into account from the outset in their designs. fourthly, we need to have integrated and coordinated responses to the disability of children and of people already discriminated against, such as women and the elderly. and finally, the prevention of occupational hazards. we have made a great deal of effort to reach an agreement on occupational hazards, which has already been tabled in this house, but which has not yet been accepted by the commission - and i remind you, mr špidla - and in which special attention will have to be paid to the risks that people may suffer in the workplace. i would also like to point out the important role played by disabled people's associations. i certainly think that this is a great challenge and a new step forward in achieving the europe of opportunity that we are all committed to.
the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are now discussing a report which will be voted on this morning and which in turn summarises a set of reports presented by the commission with a fundamental and very well defined objective, which is none other than to establish a set of measures which will make it possible to develop a society, an economy, based on knowledge in europe, which, in the end, is the fundamental instrument for creating jobs and for generating growth and therefore for generating prosperity for all europeans. in this report, as in other expert reports, such as the aho report, which is an extraordinarily complete and precise report on the same subjects, or other previous reports by the commission, we find ourselves in a situation where we have a fairly good diagnosis - i would say - of where we are, why we are in this situation and what we need. there is probably no area in which we have such precise knowledge as this to be able to drive europe's growth. the diagnosis is there, the diagnosis is there and the remedies are there. we all know that to drive forward a knowledgebased society, we need to drive forward innovation. we all know that we must promote training which enables people to adapt to all these changing times in employment and thus to be able to retrain and find a new form of work. we all know that innovation is necessary if the social welfare system is to continue to respond to citizens in health, education and so on. we all know that companies also need a friendly framework, a framework that helps them, that encourages them to develop innovation and that prevents them from encountering bureaucratic problems, difficulties in a whole series of areas of action. it is not a question of going into detail about each and every aspect of the report, because they are there and you all know them; i would like to take this opportunity to stress as much as i can the need to stop, for once, talking, talking and talking and to give very attractive titles to reports and analyses, while there is still a certain paralysis in action in the national states. the step taken with the 25 national reform programmes is important, but i think that a very strong assessment of the progress made in these national programmes should be particularly emphasized. as time goes on, we're missing more of the train. when the lisbon agenda was defined, there was an expectation of development. when we are halfway through the development of the lisbon agenda, the european average - naturally some countries are in one situation and others in another - was further behind than it was when the lisbon agenda was defined. and we may find that in 2010 we have indeed continued to be behind and have therefore been accumulating backwardness. i really believe that if we were to hire an external auditor, he would be impressed by how good the diagnosis is, how good the remedies and the solutions are, and that, despite this, the paralysis in the application of those remedies is so complete. societies, like life itself, are made of collaboration between different generations. you're carrying a witness; it's like a relay race, but relayed in the background. many europeans are growing up and being born today. others, like those here, will be, in the not too distant future, retired. and we all need a society in which europe can continue to have the competitive capacity, the leadership and the future it has had in previous periods, because there were europeans who decided, with their heart and soul, to leave the best legacy for the future of their country and for the future, in this case, of all the countries that make up european society. so that is our responsibility and we have to put our heart and soul into it.
i would like to refer to the directive on the marketing of pyrotechnic articles. i should like to begin by saying that i voted in favour of this because we have really improved the overall safety aspects, the environmental aspects, the aspects relating to the health of people and also the interests of european companies. but i think we have missed a good opportunity to make a clear distinction between pyrotechnic devices, used in public celebrations or shows, in theatres, cinemas and so on, and percussion pistons, which are used in toys, in car airbags or even in seat belts. i think we have drafted a text which creates a little confusion in this respect. i hope that this can be improved in the future; for the moment i have voted in favour, although i do not consider the text to be fully satisfactory.

member of the commission. mr president, first of all i should like to thank members for their efforts to speed up the discussion on this banana proposal, and express special thanks to mr fruteau, who delivered an excellent report within a very tight time frame. i am convinced that we all have an interest in approving the banana proposal before the end of the year, to give the producers a clear framework within which to operate in the future and also, of course, to achieve budget stability; but also to reassure the banana producing regions that they can count on the tangible solidarity of the european union. bananas are very important for the social and economic viability of our outermost regions. they provide revenue to more than 15 000 holdings and jobs to some 24 000 farmers. those regions face very specific handicaps and the treaty itself grants them a specific status, in article 299. they are, in all respects, part of the european union and have every right to enjoy the benefits of european union policy. the banana reform is the practical expression of our commitment to confirm solidarity within the union. i am very happy that the european parliament agrees with the commission on the need to reform the current banana aid scheme and to try to bring it into line with our common agricultural policy. a crucial consideration is the budgetary unpredictability of the current expenditures within the banana sector. i am delighted that the european parliament agrees on the very substance of the proposal, namely, the choice of the posei solution, which represents quite a number of different advantages. first of all, it is consistent with the cap reform; it is a very flexible tool for member states and for the regions in question; it permits member states to give additional financing; and, last but not least, it gives predictability from a financial point of view. another important point on which you agree with the commission’s proposal regards the budget, which is based on the average support granted over the period 2000-2002, and a marginal assurance has been added to take into account the variability of the banana market. the recent change in the import arrangements and a possible agreement with banana-producing third countries have also been taken into account. you have requested that the commission should submit a specific report on posei in 2009, if the livelihoods of banana producers, in particular, were to deteriorate following a change in the external regime. as a matter of fact, our proposal already focuses on, or foresees, the submission of a report on the whole posei regime in 2009, and that will include the banana sector. let us not forget that the banana sector represents more than 50% of the agricultural revenue in some producing regions. it goes without saying that this report will be submitted sooner in the event of a deterioration of livelihood in the outermost regions. as concerns crete, cyprus and the algarve, we should keep in mind that banana production involves less than 400 hectares and some 300 holdings overall. that hardly justifies a derogation from the general principle that allows farmers the freedom to choose their crops according to the market and the best advantage they can derive from their production. i am looking forward to the discussion with you tonight. again, thank you for being so quick in your action on this issue.

understanding of the council in the conciliation committee. groundwater supplies around 65% of all drinking water in europe. the fact that we have achieved the definition of deterioration and that precaution and prevention are now considered as a principle is really a very positive thing. in order to protect the environment as a whole and human health in particular, it is necessary to prevent and reduce the harmful concentration of harmful pollutants in groundwater, and i think we are on the right track with the drafting of this directive. the quality of water and, consequently, the health of humans are threatened by the presence of high concentrations of nitrates, pesticides, heavy metals, hydrocarbons and a long list of pollutants. i am therefore particularly pleased with the agreement we have reached with the council, which will make it possible to implement a whole series of rules to prevent pollution and protect groundwater. these rules will oblige the member states to prevent or limit the entry of dangerous substances into groundwater, and in this area i also think it is very important to take account of the different hydrogeological conditions in the different regions of europe, because soil that is continually inundated is not the same as dry soil, which suffers from other problems. i would also like to stress the possibility for member states to establish protection perimeters of the size that the general basin management body, or another competent national body, deems necessary to protect the drinking water supply. i think this is one of the most important elements that has been introduced. finally, i would ask my colleagues to vote in favour of this report and i hope that the member states will implement these measures as soon as possible, in order to preserve the environment and protect human health, and to move towards that sustainable europe which we all want.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we all know that democracy is a system of public opinion, and the freer the media, the better the quality of that democracy. this directive regulates the media in the audiovisual sector and the question i think we have to ask is: does it make them freer or less free than before? the equation we have to consider in answering this question is: the more interventionism of the public authorities, the less freedom of the media and vice versa, the less interventionism of the public authorities, the more freedom of the media. in my view, ladies and gentlemen, this directive is unfortunately too interventionist: it is so in the field of advertising, it is so in the field of quotas for audiovisual productions, it is so because it unnecessarily extends the scope of coverage unduly to non-linear services, but above all it is so because it gives the national regulatory authorities the capacity to protect the fundamental right of freedom of expression. any democrat knows that the protection of fundamental rights is the exclusive responsibility of the courts of justice. but this directive, and not because of the rapporteur, who has been very brave about it - and thank you for that, ruth hieronymi - gives the national regulatory authorities the ability to decide what is true and what is not true, what emissions can be given or what emissions cannot be given or, as has happened in catalonia, which is one of the european regions with the lowest democratic quality in the whole of the european union, which operators can issue or which cannot issue. in this way we are opening the door to prior censorship. and i ask you, please, mrs reding, to take this seriously, to see if we can avoid it, among other things because we will have to listen carefully to what organizations like reporters without borders, the world association of newspapers or the world committee for press freedom have to say on this point. they're going to color us. i hope that at least this suffocation will help us to correct our mistake in time.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to present to you today the european union's annual human rights report. the first human rights report was published in 1999, when finland, as in this case, was involved in the preparation of the report in its role as the presidency of the european union. the purpose of the report has not changed since then. it continues to deal in a unique way with the european union's human rights policy and the issues raised within it. the report now presented examines the eu's actions and policies aimed at promoting universal respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms during the period 1 july 2005-30 june 2006. the report follows seven previous annual reports published between 1999 and 2005 in accordance with the declaration adopted by the european council in 1998. in that declaration, issued on the 50th anniversary of the universal declaration of human rights, the european union was called upon to step up its human rights work. the same declaration also called on the eu to draw up an annual human rights report. the human rights report provides an overview of the work done to promote human rights and democracy in the european union institutions. the eu's external policies and internal aspects are examined. this year, the european parliament's activities in promoting human rights and democracy will again be examined in its own section. the european parliament is grateful to raise human rights issues and to ensure that these issues receive the attention they deserve in the other institutions of the union. the report highlights specific priorities of eu human rights policy, such as mainstreaming human rights.in practice, mainstreaming has meant increasing interaction between human rights experts and country working groups and raising human rights concerns in different areas of eu activity, such as crisis management and arms exports. the european union has developed ways of addressing specific issues such as women and security and children in the context of armed conflict. the personal representative of the secretary-general, acting as high representative, has been active in mainstreaming human rights in the common foreign and security policy and in raising awareness of the eu guidelines on human rights. the european union has adopted specific guidelines on certain issues and thus defined the priorities of its human rights policy. the union opposes the death penalty in all circumstances and has identified individual cases in which the minimum standards of international law have not been met. in the reporting period, the union has paid particular attention to countries whose approach to the death penalty has been changing. the european union has encouraged various countries to accede to the international convention for the elimination of torture and thus contribute to strengthening efforts to eliminate torture. the union has also identified a number of priority areas in which it intends to improve the human rights situation by alleviating the suffering of children in armed conflicts in various ways. it has been important to raise this issue in multilateral international fora and to enhance the eu's own capacity to address this issue in the context of european security and defence policy operations. as regards the eu guidelines on human rights defenders, the union has undertaken global campaigns on freedom of expression and women's human rights. as human rights defenders are themselves quite often the target of attacks, their rights remain a priority for eu action. the council appreciates the central role of the european parliament in our common mission to defend and promote the realisation of human rights. the annual sakharov prize for freedom of expression is central to this task. in previous years, parliament has paid tribute to notable figures such as nelson mandela and kofi annan. it is positive that this year's sakharov prize has been awarded to the belarusian opposition leader, aleksandr milinkevich. it is to be hoped that the international honour awarded will encourage milinkevich and others to continue their important work in strengthening democratic forces in belarus. during the period covered by the report, i.e. between the summer of 2005 and the summer of 2006, the un structure underwent a significant change. the negotiations for the establishment of the un human rights council and subsequently the first session of the new council provided the key framework for eu action in the field of multilateral human rights policy. the eu has always aimed to create a council which would give human rights the status guaranteed by the un charter. although we did not get all the things we were working on into the final text adopted in march 2006, the union nevertheless considers that the establishment of the un human rights council is an essential part of strengthening the un human rights system. it is also a significant step forward in the whole process of reforming the un. the promotion of human rights and the development of democracy and the rule of law is of the utmost importance in the fight against terrorism and various extremist movements. the eu has reiterated in several statements at the un and other forums its view that ensuring respect for human rights is also essential in its counter-terrorism work. the presidency has emphasized on several occasions that effective counter-terrorism and the protection of human rights are complementary and mutually reinforcing. political dialogue is undoubtedly one of the key instruments for the promotion of human rights. the mainstreaming of human rights has sought to ensure a consistent approach to human rights issues in eu-third country contacts at different levels. this also applies to countries with which the eu has a special human rights dialogue, such as china and russia. this year's human rights report highlights for the first time the eu's commitment to promoting intercultural dialogue both within the union and with third countries. victims of human rights violations and human rights defenders around the world have high expectations of the european union, and rightly so. as a community of values, the european union can be expected to be very ambitious in its efforts to promote human rights and democracy. this report will help us to assess how well the union has been able to meet this challenge.
member of the commission. mr president, i very much welcome the publication of the 2006 annual report on human rights. this is the first time that this report has really been a combined effort. we have battled for that. last year we had the debate here in plenary and i said that i would be very happy if we could prepare the report together. i would have liked to have one of the prefaces. unfortunately it seems it was too late, but i think the commission should have been visible. it now seems to be an established practice always to have a special session on human rights and democracy before christmas. it is a good tradition; it is a noble tradition, to see what has been implemented and what the new developments are. the annual report this year is again a valuable record of the combined efforts of us all in promoting and protecting human rights around the world, and a reflection of the positive way in which the european union has come together to produce it. this debate gives me the opportunity to quickly highlight some activities in 2006. first, mainstreaming human rights into external policies ranked high on our eu priority list in 2006, thanks to the austrian and finnish presidencies. it is indeed a source of satisfaction to note that all actors within the eu are more and more committed to this very important aspect of our policies. however, let us not forget that mainstreaming or, as i also like to call it, ‘integrating’ human rights into all policies, is not an end in itself, but an approach to achieving overarching goals. for the european union, these goals have a clear basis in our treaty, which calls on us to develop and consolidate democracy, the rule of law, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms through our various external policies. in this context, we are particularly pleased that human rights and democracy issues have been integrated into the legal texts of all the new financing instruments under the 2007-2013 financial perspective. secondly, mainstreaming is a never-ending process; we need to constantly maintain our efforts and introduce new tools. i am happy to inform you in this context that last june the commission revised the mandates of its heads of delegation, following up on the report by mr agnoletto. these mandates now specifically mention human rights and democracy issues, and therefore place greater priority on reporting and acting in this regard. similarly, in the context of the ‘human rights clauses’ of our agreements, we have seen the creation of the new forums for dialogue or exchanges of views with third countries. the number of occasions to discuss the promotion of and respect for human rights has been growing, from argentina and bangladesh to india, jordan, morocco, turkmenistan and vietnam. that is in addition to the institutionalised human rights dialogues and consultations and the various political dialogues where human rights issues are regularly raised. last but not least, the commission continues to include the human rights and democracy ‘essential elements’ clause in the negotiation of the new bilateral partnership and cooperation agreements. this is, for instance, the case for the agreement with six asean countries. likewise, preparations are being made for negotiating an agreement with china, and the commission remains fully committed to the inclusion of this clause in conformity with our standard practice. thirdly, while mainstreaming or integrating human rights issues in all our policies, we also need to focus on some specific aspects of the human rights policy. these have been exemplified by two communications from the commission: one called ‘roadmap on equality between women and men’ and the other ‘towards an eu strategy on the rights of the child’. the year 2006 has also been characterised by the pivotal changes seen within the united nations human rights machinery, with the new human rights council that has already been mentioned. whilst there was initially great cause for optimism, for example the active participation of ngos in debates or the desire to move away from the failure of its predecessor the commission for human rights, the overall picture at the end of the year is a cause for concern, not least because of the discouraging signs of politicisation of this new forum. we, the european union, have to renew our efforts and engage more with a number of actors in geneva in order to convince them that the international community needs an effective human rights council. we still have the possibility to make this new body work and deliver. indeed, we have to remain hopeful that today’s special session on darfur will yield some positive results. i cannot conclude without indicating once again my personal satisfaction, as well as the commission’s satisfaction, with the vote that took place earlier today on the proposal for a regulation establishing the new european instrument for democracy and human rights. this instrument will make it easier for the commission to establish priorities when implementing the objectives contained in the regulation and in keeping with its scope. however, we know too well that measures to promote human rights and democracy deserve to be as worldwide, numerous, multisectoral and cross-cutting as possible. the fact that the number of beneficiaries has expanded will also have to be taken into account. but the enhanced complementarity with the various tools, which range from political dialogue and diplomatic demarches to various instruments of financial and technical cooperation, including both geographic and thematic programmes, is warmly welcomed. finally, we are looking forward to developing more integrated approaches to human rights and democracy under the new instrument. there continues to be some debate about human rights and democracy as if they were two different issues. however, we think that human rights are the foundation for democracy and democracy is necessary to develop and protect human rights. therefore, let us not create artificial demarcations. in any case, we think this is a good basis for continuing our work in the year to come.

member of the commission. i should like to thank the honourable member for her question concerning the commission’s follow-up to the recommendation set out in the report on women’s networks, fishing, farming and diversification adopted by parliament on 15 december 2005. the commission considers the situation of women working in the fisheries sector, and in particular their legal and social recognition, to be a very important issue. it is using all the instruments at its disposal to promote equal treatment and opportunities for women and men in the sector concerned. as regards the four specific questions raised by the honourable member, the commission would like to point out the following. firstly, the european fisheries fund, which is the new structural instrument for fisheries for 2007-2013, explicitly states, in article 4(g), that one of its objectives is to promote equality between men and women in the development of the fisheries sector and fisheries areas. the eff is based on the principle of partnership with all stakeholders in the fisheries sector, and this explicitly covers partnership with bodies responsible for the promotion of equality between men and women. the eff contains specific provisions promoting gender equality, both through better women’s representation in decision-making processes and in the programmes to be implemented by member states. in particular, the commission is encouraging participation by women in the various stages of implementation of the european fisheries fund, including the design, monitoring and evaluation of the member states’ operational programmes for the next programming period. the fund can also support measures aimed at promoting equal opportunities between men and women through networking and the exchange of best practices among relevant organisations. the commission will strive to ensure that member states reflect these provisions and priorities in their operational programmes. secondly, the commission recognises the importance of training in the fisheries sector, and education and professional training are eligible for support under the european fisheries fund. training measures are also expected to promote access to employment for women. moreover, under the fund’s new priority axis 4 on the sustainable development of fisheries areas, support can be granted for the diversification of activities and the promotion of alternative employment for fishermen through a large variety of measures. under this axis, special measures for the improvement of professional skills, work adaptability and access to employment for women can also be supported. it should be stressed that the commission is promoting the involvement of women in the local bodies, managing the measures supported under axis 4. thirdly, as mentioned above, the eff requires member states to ensure broad and effective involvement of all relevant partners in the different stages of programming, and this includes bodies responsible for the promotion of equality between men and women. the fund also requires the operational programmes to contain information on how the partnership principle has been implemented, the list of the parties that have been consulted, the results of those consultations and how they have been taken into account. the new priority axis 4 on sustainable development of fisheries areas, supported under the fund, will be implemented through a bottom-up approach. it will be the local players, including women’s associations, that will serve as the engine for designing and implementing local development strategies. this allows women’s organisations to get involved in decision-making at the local level and ensure that their specific concerns and suggestions are taken into account in local development strategies. women and their representatives are also encouraged to participate in the regional advisory councils, which were set up to improve the governance of the reformed common fisheries policy. for instance, women’s associations already have a seat in the north sea rac, which was the first rac to be formed. women are also represented in the north western waters rac. finally, in the present programming period, under the financial instrument for fisheries guidance, member states can co-finance studies and innovative projects covering the specific situation of women shellfish gatherers. this possibility is also offered under the european fisheries fund, under priority axis 3 on collective actions. the commission has since 2003 been launching a series of calls for proposals for innovative actions in the fisheries sector. these actions are now almost completed. in 2005 the commission conducted an ex-post evaluation of these actions in order to assess their impact and added value. the results of this evaluation showed clearly that such actions do not have an added value, whereas innovative actions included in, and financed through, the operational programmes of the member states, were more successful and better monitored. taking into account these conclusions, the commission decided to integrate the implementation of those actions into the european fisheries fund regulation and to support their implementation through the operational programmes of the member states.

president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the june european council decided that the debate on enlargement and the future enlargement strategy of the union would be continued and improving the quality of the enlargement process on the basis of the experience gained so far. the european council will conduct its general debate on enlargement on the basis of the enlargement strategy announced by the commission on 8 november. the strategy also includes a special report on the union's capacity to integrate new members. the presidency aims to ensure that the european council's discussions will consolidate a common vision for the future of the enlargement process. the european council's conclusions on enlargement were discussed by the general affairs and external relations council on monday. the council held a constructive and thorough discussion on the matter. enlargement is part of the process of european integration. when the finnish presidency presented its work programme to the committee on foreign affairs last july, we stressed that enlargement has undoubtedly contributed to growth and prosperity in europe. enlargement has benefited the union and its member states as well as europe as a whole. the prospect of membership has encouraged the candidate countries to undertake the necessary reforms. the enlargement has made the union a more powerful actor in international politics. the enlargement of the internal market has enabled the eu economy to better respond to the challenges of global competition. the historic fifth enlargement will be completed when bulgaria and romania, whose future commissioners were approved here yesterday, join the european union on 1 january. this round of enlargement has already proved a success. the enlargement process has already extended the area of peace, stability, democracy, the rule of law and prosperity to almost all of europe. we must now ensure that this success continues. the union must pursue enlargement as an open and objective process, without imposing any new restrictions or conditions. to ensure this, more attention needs to be paid to the practical promotion of enlargement. it is natural to seek to improve the quality of the enlargement process and to develop the union's preparation for enlargement. as we know, and as the speakers have also shown, the capacity for integration or the capacity of the union to welcome new members is not a criterion for membership. nor should the capacity for integration be such. however, the ability to integrate is an important consideration to ensure successful enlargement. maintaining the capacity for integration is in the interest of both the union and the candidate countries. however, if we were to impose conditions on enlargement within the union which the candidate country itself could not influence, we would risk undermining the willingness of those countries to reform. in order to maintain the union's integration capacity, it is necessary that the acceding countries are prepared to accept and implement the obligations of membership of the european union. it is also essential that the union is able to function effectively and develop. it is important that the union can welcome new members when they are ready, on the basis of the progress made in the negotiations. both of these aspects are also important for securing public support for the enlargement process. the union's capacity for integration must be examined in the enlargement process. it is necessary to ensure that the union is able to function politically, economically and institutionally as it enlarges. the impact of future enlargements on the union's institutions, policies and budget must be carefully assessed. it is important that the union sticks to the commitments we have given to croatia and turkey in the accession negotiations and to the countries of the western balkans. as regards turkey, i would like to say that the presidency has done everything possible to enable the negotiating process to continue. we are pleased with the decision taken by the council on monday. it provides us with a basis for moving forward. the candidate and potential candidate countries have the responsibility to implement the necessary reforms in these countries. progress in the accession process depends on the progress thus made. the only way to advance in the process is to meet the conditions. mr president, there has been a strong feeling of expansionary fatigue in the air recently. providing timely and factual information can also help to dispel existing suspicions. the truth is that the union benefits from and needs the new member states. finally, mr president, on behalf of the presidency, i would like to thank the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank you for this opportunity to discuss the european council on 14 and 15 december in advance in this house. the main topics of tomorrow's summit will be enlargement, improving decision-making in the fields of justice and home affairs and immigration policy. the european council is the meeting of heads of state or government to discuss in depth how the enlargement of the union should be pursued. the june european council gave the president a clear mandate to organise this debate. the european council's discussions will be based on the commission's enlargement strategy, which was published on 8 november, and on the in-depth discussion which took place on monday in the foreign affairs council. as i said this morning, the enlargement debate is intended to confirm the commitments we have made to croatia and turkey, which are now negotiating accession, and to the countries of the western balkans. the european council's enlargement debate is intended to confirm the renewed consensus of the member states on the continuation of the enlargement process. it is based on the principles of the commission's enlargement strategy commitment, conditionality and enhanced communication. at the same time, the union's capacity to welcome new members must also be taken into account. enlargement is not the only issue which will have a significant impact on the future of the union at the summit starting tomorrow. the european council is expected to hold a dinner in which prime minister vanhassen will present to his colleagues his assessment and the main general conclusions of the confidential consultations held during our presidency on the future of the constitutional treaty. the aim of our presidency was to bring the debate on the constitutional treaty into a more active phase after a year of silence. consultations have now taken place with all the member states and with romania and bulgaria, which joined the union at the beginning of the year. it has been positive to note that internal reflection is under way in the member states and has been activated. it is still too early to look for ready-made solutions, but there are certain priorities in the member states' views. we will pass on our detailed analysis to the next german presidency as a basis for further work. one conclusion, which is very important for the future, is that all the member states see the need for treaty reform in order to ensure the union's ability to act. the way forward should now be sought together and the solution should be acceptable to all. the finnish parliament approved the constitutional treaty earlier this month and the president of the republic decided to ratify it last week. finland thus became the 16th member state to ratify the treaty. we wanted to send a signal that we believe the constitutional treaty is a balanced whole. it is a good basis for finding a solution acceptable to all the member states. mr president, citizens expect the european union to take effective action in the fight against international crime, trafficking in human beings and terrorism. however, it has become clear from many experiences that the union is currently unable to respond to this wish of the citizens in the best possible way. we repeatedly find that a small minority of member states veto the adoption of decisions. it is unfortunately easy to give examples: the negotiations on the european arrest warrant took over three years; we have not made any progress in the last two years on the anti-racism framework decision; the negotiations also failed to develop cross-border police investigations. unfortunately, last week the framework decision on the transfer of prisoners also fell to the opposition of one member state. these examples illustrate why finland's eu presidency has made it a priority to develop decision-making, especially in matters related to improving the safety of citizens. we also received a clear mandate from the european council in june. police and criminal justice cooperation is a difficult area. the willingness of the member states to compromise on many important issues is unfortunately very low, since they are able to veto a decision at the very last moment. the results of the negotiations are meagre and progress is slow. some member states have stated that the union should focus on enhancing practical cooperation rather than on improving decision-making. it is by acting that we can best advance our common cause. however, practical cooperation must be based on mutually agreed rules, and we have had great difficulty in agreeing on these rules. this is a problem that cannot be ignored. it is clear that not only citizens but also the member states have been frustrated by the union's actions. this has led to an increasing number of member states considering the possibility of moving to an enhanced cooperation model. some member states have decided to promote their cooperation outside the union's structures, as exemplified by the prüm agreement. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european police college, which would be a new instrument for the protection of the rights of the defence. however, it has become clear during the finnish presidency that the member states are not willing to accept this solution. however, we still believe that we need a more efficient, transparent and responsible decision-making model for police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters. we therefore want to make full use of the mandate given to us last june to improve the efficiency of decision-making. the european council is to discuss the question of improving the efficiency of decision-making in the field of justice and home affairs. we hope that the principals will commit themselves to finding a solution to this problem, which has already been solved in the negotiations for a constitutional treaty. the european parliament has made its position on this very clear. the presidency greatly appreciates the speech made by president borrell at the informal meeting of heads of state in lahti, in which you, mr president, clearly expressed the view of the european parliament that the decision-making process in the field of justice and home affairs should be strengthened. ladies and gentlemen, during the finnish presidency a great deal of work has been done on various immigration issues. good progress has been made in implementing the comprehensive approach. it has also proved to be the right approach to this subject. immigration is currently one of the union's greatest challenges, but also an opportunity. the finnish part of the programme has focused particularly on cooperation with african countries. we have organized two successful ministerial conferences focusing on immigration and development. in addition, the european border and coast guard agency (frontex) has coordinated successful operations at the southern borders of the union. the next important step is to extend the principles of the comprehensive approach to other geographical areas and to extend its scope to other policy sectors. we have consistently stressed that the union must be able to create a comprehensive immigration management policy that addresses both illegal and legal immigration issues, including integration. the priorities for next year are to be agreed at the european council tomorrow. the measures to be agreed are based on two communications issued by the commissions last week. it is important that we are able to agree not only on long-term measures but also on those which the union can use to respond to sudden and unexpected flows of migrants. mr president, since finland will only be holding one official european council meeting during its presidency, there are high hopes and expectations for the conclusions to be drawn from the meeting. however, we have long held the view that the conclusions of the european council must be regarded by the capitalists as the true outcome of the discussions. conclusions should not be a mere list of all pending cases and all cases dealt with. this is why we have taken the view in the preparations for the european council that the conclusions should only cover matters which are discussed by the heads of state or government or which require political guidance for the future work of the union. in addition to the topics of discussion i have president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the hague programme on strengthening freedom, security and justice in the european union, adopted in november 2004, and the related 2005 council and commission action plan, establish the framework for developing an eu policy on legal immigration. the hague programme already recognises the important role of legal immigration in promoting, among other things, the economic development of the union. the same programme states that it is the responsibility of the member states to decide on the number of legal immigrants. on this basis, the commission is to submit for adoption a number of legislative proposals set out in the action plan on legal immigration adopted in january 2006. the first of these is the proposal for a general framework directive, the main purpose of which is to guarantee common rights for all third-country nationals who are already legally working in a member state but who are not yet entitled to long-term resident status in the eu. in addition, the commission will submit four separate proposals for directives based on the categories of workers that member states generally require. these proposals concern the conditions of entry and residence of highly qualified workers, the conditions of entry and residence of seasonal workers, the conditions of entry and residence of trainees on a paid basis and the procedures governing the entry and residence of persons temporarily posted by their companies to another country. improving the availability of information on the different aspects of migration, the exchange of information on them and the dissemination of information more effectively are also key. to this end, a number of instruments are to be developed in the coming years. there are five in all, the first being the european year of labour mobility this year and the second the european year of equal opportunities next year. the second instrument is the eu immigration portal, which is due to be set up by the end of next year. the third instrument is the system for mutual information on member states' measures in the field of asylum and immigration. the fourth instrument is the european migration network and the fifth instrument is the further development of the european professional mobility portal and the eures network, which are considered to be able to contribute to the management of economic migration. as regards the integration of third-country nationals into the society of the host country, which was already discussed in the previous question, the union supports the integration policies of the member states through various financial instruments, including preparatory measures for the integration of third-country nationals. in the context of the financial perspective 2007-13, the new dedicated solidarity instrument, the european fund for the integration of third-country nationals, will give new impetus to integration policy in the member states. the objectives of the fund are linked to the challenges of integration and thus complement the activities of the european social fund. these objectives are based on the general principles on integration adopted by the council in november 2004.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the hague conference has been working since 1893 to bring about a progressive unification of the rules of private international law worldwide by means of conventions. on 5 october the european council, after consulting parliament, adopted a decision on the accession of the european community to the conference. the current initiative arises in connection with the convention on the law applicable to certain rights in securities deposited with an intermediary, which was negotiated at three sessions of the diplomatic conference in december 2002. the convention is open to all parties and, although the european community was not a member of the conference which drew up the convention, the commission submitted a proposal for a decision on 15 december 2003 for its signature. the first objective of this initiative is to demonstrate the need to respect the european parliament's powers in this area and to ensure more democratic control of the work of the conference. the scope of the convention directly affects the competences of the european union on judicial cooperation in civil matters with cross-border implications to the extent necessary for the proper functioning of the internal market, in which the european parliament has the status of co-legislator. in addition, in the view of the european central bank, it may have implications for the definition and implementation of monetary policy, the operation of clearing and payment systems and the effectiveness of the provisions forming part of the community acquis. the proposed signing of the convention raises important concerns and serious concerns at the level of the european union, affecting both form and substance. the heart of the convention, contained in article 4, which states that the law applicable in this matter is that of the state expressly agreed by the contracting parties, raises enormous risks and questions which have not yet been resolved. the magnitude of the legislative impact it can have requires the application of community standards to better legislate, hence a process of consultation and public debate, as was done in the united states when legislative changes were made that were inferior to those proposed in the convention. the convention introduces further complexity and uncertainty by opening up the possibility for numerous legal systems to apply to a single system of registration, clearing and settlement. this, in the absence of harmonisation on substantive issues, can lead to adverse effects and systemic risk. the solution he proposes, far from contributing to the unifying purpose of the conference, increases its incoherence and is incompatible with community legislation which establishes the criterion of the location of the portfolio of securities. this criterion had helped to increase certainty and efficiency at community level. under the convention, the bargaining power will determine the applicable law. this opens the door to legislative delocalisation, to the detriment of investors and financial institutions. its entry into force may encourage an uncontrolled process of global and regional consolidation of clearing and settlement activities, increasing the risk of concentration outside the european union and with perverse effects on prudential supervision, the prevention of terrorist financing and the fight against money laundering. the formula chosen may have an impact on investors' political rights, transparency and good corporate governance. it raises a number of doubts, and therefore, commissioner, either a more thorough impact study is carried out or the proposal is abandoned and withdrawn.

justice and home affairs is one prime example. the citizens expect concrete action to improve security and justice. there is a serious problem with the justice and home affairs. the requirement of security and combating crime. today, however, decisions on cooperation are either watered down or unable to be taken, as we have seen recently with the transfer of prisoners. the unanimity requirement is a legal and internal affairs bullet that prevents genuine progress. we would have a method for improving the efficiency of decision-making in the field of justice and home affairs, article 42 of the treaty, the so-called passerelle, which would allow us to decide unanimously to move to qualified majority voting. finland, as the presidency, went out in earnest to explore this possibility, but already in september, at the meeting of the ministers of justice and the ministers of the interior in tampere, it became clear that many member states were opposed to this. this avenue is closed to us. i am therefore pleased that, despite all this, the european council has now sent a clear message that it is important to improve the efficiency of decision-making in the field of justice and home affairs by adopting the principle enshrined in the treaty, namely the qualified majority. this is a major attitude breakthrough, and we can be pleased about it. this decision must be respected by future presidents. i would like to say in this context that if i could change one thing in the union at all, with the experience of the presidency here and now, i would significantly increase the qualified majority decisionmaking. it is by far the most efficient, fairest and best way to reach good decisions. the unanimity requirement is unreasonable in the interests of the european union as a whole in all matters other than those which are absolutely necessary. the european council discussed in depth the union's immigration policy. we all remember in a spirit of solidarity the problems meeting in lahti we had a good discussion with russian president putin and the eu was able to present a unified message to russia. it is clear that russia is an important partner for the eu. a glance at the map will suffice to illustrate this fact. russia is important to the eu, we are bound to each other by many ties, but at the same time we must be honest and say that we are concerned about many aspects of russia's development. i'm not convinced that russia is going in the right direction. we need a more determined commitment to democracy, the rule of law and the market economy. we don't want russia to go in an authoritarian direction. we have every right to be concerned about russia's development. russia is the touchstone of european unity. finland would have liked to reach an agreement on the opening of negotiations for a new and comprehensive agreement with russia. this is the understanding which we have not yet reached, for reasons which are well known. i think the new agreement clearly shows what the problem is that we have on our hands. we need a common and strong agreement that contains the most important foundation of our cooperation, the values, and provides a sustainable basis for trade and energy cooperation. if a single agreement is not reached, the unfortunate and short-sighted development is the network of bilateral agreements in which russia can treat eu member states differently. some get good deals, some get bad deals, some may not get any. at the same time, it is self-evident that the eu as a whole is such an important partner for russia that it is able to negotiate a proper agreement as a whole. what kind of united europe is it if we compete with each other to see who gets the best terms? this is not european solidarity. ladies and gentlemen, the presidency is beginning with the greatest ambition, but a lively life will bring us all back to the country. we have achieved a great deal, but we have missed many essential things. finland is seriously seeking a solution to the reform of the working time directive and i believe we are getting quite close. but it wasn't enough. the problem is not gone, however, and i wish the future presidents the best of luck in solving this european question. i am sorry to say that this is the last time i will be speaking in this house as the representative of the finnish presidency. i have excellent memories now of good cooperation with parliament and i would like to thank all of you for the support you have given to finland's efforts. i believe that the future of europe is shared. a more united europe, where borders disappear. i am particularly pleased that we have achieved a result in the enlargement of the schengen area. this is the practical progress that the citizens expect from us as decision-makers. once again, i would like to express my warm thanks to the european parliament for its excellent cooperation. president of the council. mr president, thank you for giving me the freedom to comment on any and all opinions, especially those which were agreed with me. but i want to highlight one where the speaker clearly disagreed: nigel farage, who said we want more power for the union. that is not the point, but the union has been given very broad powers. it is a question of the union also having the means and instruments to exercise its powers. in politics, in all the exercises of power, the most important thing is that when you give someone a task and power, you must also have the means to use it. in particular, the council does not currently have this means of action because of the decision-making and voting systems and the unanimity requirements. the work of parliament shows that despite ideological differences it is able to take decisions almost always by voting, but votes are usually preceded by very long negotiations in which compromises are sought and from which results are also obtained. i would like to confirm what françoise grossetête said about 2006 being a year of parliament in particular. this year has seen the passing of perhaps some of the biggest legislative projects of the decade. the debate raised a number of issues and themes which are european in nature and in which the union has competence as such, but also the capacity to make decisions. one of the challenges for the future will be to decide next year on the european institute of technology, for which the european council has declared 2007 the year of decision. this is where the commission and the council will have a lot, a lot of work to do next year. in the enlargement process, i believe that the western balkans should be given special attention. enlargement is the way to link the peoples of the western balkans in a healthy way to stability and democracy, and we have time in the union both to make our own changes to the treaties and to continue the enlargement negotiations. we have only to assume our responsibility within the union and the member states to ensure that the negotiations on the treaty on a constitution are concluded in such a way that the target timetable for the european parliamentary elections in 2009 is achieved. if we succeed in this, i'm sure expansion will be no problem. i am grateful, mr president, for the privilege of being here at the last sitting of parliament this year and witnessing a lively political dialogue where cooperation is possible across ideological boundaries. the evidence of this was particularly evident in the opening part of this discussion. we in finland have also learned to cooperate across ideological boundaries, including at government level, and it has been a great pleasure to be involved in this same cooperation here at eu level. with these words i express my heartfelt thanks. a few specific questions were asked: one concerned agricultural trade in russia. i believe that the president of the commission will answer that. (applause) i would like to thank the
president of the commission. mr president, we in the commission are used to having the more difficult questions to solve! this was indeed a successful presidency and, as someone said, it was the last presidency of a european union of 25 members. on 1 january 2007 we are going to welcome romania and bulgaria. one of the achievements of these last six months was the finalisation of all these processes – the ratification in the member states. the good work that has been done was important, as was the election, with a great deal of support, of the two new commissioners from romania and bulgaria. once again, i would like to thank parliament for its support. it was a very clear signal of this parliament’s support for the enlarged european union. regarding russia, i think the debates we have had over the past six months have been helpful in establishing the basis for our relationship with russia. russia is a very important partner, a close neighbour and a partner with whom we want to have a strategic long-term relationship. we should avoid two risks. one is the ‘business as usual’ approach, pretending that everything is going in the right direction. it is not. there are some concerns. another risk is a kind of confrontational position with russia. i do not think this is in our interests, nor is it in the interests of all those who want a democratic, progressive russia. we should have a constructive, positive engagement with russia, trying to make it a win-win situation, namely on the energy issue. i have said before that we were divided from russia and the soviet union for so long because of our ideologies. let us not now be divided from russia because of energy. let us make it a positive factor. they need a stable market as much as we need a stable supplier, but at the same time, while we are engaged with this constructive position, we should also be very firm on matters of principle, namely on human rights. on this matter we have to tell our russian partners that this is non-negotiable. that is the position we have been taking publicly and privately in the talks with our russian partners. when it comes to russia, we will be able to control some events but not others. the future of russia will depend mainly on the dynamics of russia. it is a huge country. it would be a mistake to think that we can control its future. we do not and should not control that. however, there is something we can control, which is solidarity among our member states. we have to ask all the member states to keep a united and coherent approach to russia and not give in to any pressure to divide us, for instance on the issues that are now on the table. that depends on us. we can have a common approach to russia if we really want to. there have been some attempts to divide us but at the lahti summit we were able to speak with one voice on energy. now, in the face of an embargo on one of our member states, we can also express a common position. we hope that common position is maintained when it comes to the mandate for the future framework agreement with russia. i hope that matter can be solved. i hope the member states will be unanimous in supporting a mandate so we can continue with the strategy i have just outlined as a good position for europe and a position that is also useful for the future of our relations with russia. this principle of solidarity has to be a cornerstone in our external relations and also in how we build the european union. finally, since we now know that mr poettering has addressed us for the last time as the chairman of the ppe-de group, let me also express my gratitude and recognition for everything he has done as leader of such an important group in the european parliament and say how much i appreciate his sincere commitment to our european values. i hope that the commitment he has shown in leading such an important political group will be maintained in future for the service of europe, so we shall not say goodbye or adieu but just auf wiedersehen. i wish you all a merry christmas and a very good 2007.
